Chapter Two, The Arising of the Sublime Body.

Commentary on the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra, Fascicle Two,
Composed by the Śramaṇa Fazang:
Explanation of the Chapter on the Manifestation of the Sublime Body.

Why does this chapter follow? It is because the preceding chapter extensively explained that only those great bodhisattvas who have fully cultivated pure karma within the Pure Land of the Buddha’s Secret Adornment (Guhyavimala) are able to be born there;
therefore, it is called the "Chapter on the Birth of the Sublime Body" (Miaosheng pin). Regarding the "birth of the sublime body," there are generally three meanings:
first, the transformation-body (*pariṇāmiki-deha*) experienced within the ten stages (*bhūmi*), which abandons the coarse death of the fragmented aggregates (*bhedaka-maraṇa*).
Because it is a body of weightiness, it is called the "Wondrous Body" (*miao-shen*). Thus, the Sūtra says it is the "body born of the *dharmatā*.

Second, as for the body received within the *Ghanavyūha*, because it is preeminent and subtle, it is called "Wondrous Birth" (*miaosheng*). Third, the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) manifested by the Tathāgata is called the "Wondrous Body.
This chapter extensively clarifies the meaning of the birth of the Wondrous Body; since the chapter title is derived from the subject matter elucidated therein, it is titled "The Wondrous Body."
This is the Chapter on Birth (*Janma-parivarta*).
Regarding the explanation of this chapter, it is divided into four major sections: first, the inquiry and response between [Vajragarbha] and [the Buddha] regarding seeing things as they truly are;
second, the inquiry and response between Vajragarbha and bodhisattvas such as Samantabhadra and Viśvarūpa, which elucidates the matter; third, the various [bodhisattvas] of the Śuddhāvāsa...
The various great bodhisattvas of the heavens questioned Vajragarbha, who then explained [the matter] through their dialogue.
The great assembly in the four assemblies heard the Dharma taught and, having paid homage, practiced it. Within the initial section, there are two question-and-answer exchanges:
the first explains the virtues accomplished by cultivating the causes; the second clarifies the basis for that cultivation. The first of these further has two parts, the first being as follows:
The Realization (Saddharmadarśana) asks the question, and Vajragarbha answers it. Within the text of the inquiry, there are three sections: first, praising the virtues of the questioner;
second, the desire to inquire while performing the rules of ritual propriety; and third, from the phrase "thereupon he spoke these words" onwards, the actual formulation of the questions.

Within the section on praising the virtues of others, "one who sees according to reality" refers to praising those who possess internal virtue; this is called "seeing according to reality" because they are without error regarding the ultimate and conventional truths.
This marks the stage of a Bodhisattva. Furthermore, these Bodhisattvas—whether lay Bodhisattvas or otherwise—cause all the common people to submit and be subdued.
For this reason, it is said that they possess great majestic power and are able to act as lords among the common people.
Therefore, he is sovereign in the world. His inner body is upright and handsome; thus his name signifies that his physical form is exquisite.

The King’s body is adorned with ornaments made of the seven treasures; for this reason, it is called "adornment with superior garments. Having finished praising and questioning the person, the following explains the practice of ritual salutation.
Because he wishes to make a request to the Buddha, it says, "standing before the Buddha" and so forth, up to "with single-minded reverence"; this is evident from the text.
Following this, he speaks to Vajragarbha to formally present his request. Within this, he first praises the virtues of the person to whom he makes the request;

subsequently, with the words "Therefore, I now," he requests a resolution of his doubts. Regarding the initial praise of virtues, the phrase "well able to penetrate the realm of one's own wisdom" [is explained as follows].

This praises his wisdom and virtue. That which is not shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) is termed "one's own wisdom. Next, it praises the virtue of realizing the principle and being free from confusion;

this refers to the passage concerning "dwelling in happiness in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). Next, it praises the virtue of transforming others; this means that his mind does not conflict with the three vehicles or the world.
Regarding the phrase "a master of great concentration who possesses mastery over meditative absorption," this praises his mastery over what he performs.
This is the meaning. "One who can explain the characteristics of the various stages in accordance with them" praises the virtue of skillful teaching.

"Always present in all Buddha-lands" praises the virtue of accomplishing pure karma. "Acting as the foremost among all to expound the profound and wondrous Dharma" praises the virtue of upholding the profound Dharma.
Below this, the requested methods of practice are presented: first, the request for the methods to be practiced; subsequently, the section on "peaceful and happy cultivation."

"I request the benefit obtained. Therefore, "I now [request]" and so forth concludes the preceding and introduces what follows. Next, from "Furthermore, I request the various sages" onwards, it clarifies the Dharma requested.
Finally, from "May I and others" onwards, it concludes the request for the teaching. The first passage is easy to understand. Regarding the second, the Dharma requested is of two kinds:
first, the practice of the path of instruction (*śikṣāmārga*); second, the practice of the path of realization (*adhigamamārga*). "The various sages" refers to the former...
From the first bhūmi upward, the various sages are not one; therefore, they are called "all sages" (*sarvārya*).

"Not following the practice of others" means that he has emerged from the essence of the path of teaching (*śāsana-mārga*) and does not follow the narrow and inferior self-benefit of the Hīnayāna, but constantly practices impartial, objectless great compassion (*anālambana-mahākaruṇā*);

for this reason, it is said he "does not follow the practice of others. As for "the path of realization" (*adhigama-mārga*), it is non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*); because its manifest realization is not distant, it is described as "manifest" (*pratyakṣa*).

The Dharma is called "abiding in bliss" because it is free from distraction and agitation; this refers to the state of abiding. The realm of internal realization is the principle that is the object of abiding.
Now, as requested, one sees this reality exactly as it is. The concluding text of the request below may be understood by reference to the preceding.
Regarding the methods of requesting from here on, there are briefly four kinds of benefits sought: first, freedom from enmity, which means proceeding toward the practice of peace and happiness.

This refers to the passage concerning the stage of Buddhahood (*buddhabhūmi*). Second, the attainment of the supporting body (*āśraya-kāya*), which refers to the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) and the body of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-kāya*).
As for the mind-made body, it is the fruit of realized practice; because it arises solely from the mind and is free from verbal expression, it is the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*).

As for the body of verbal expression, it is the fruit of the practice of teaching; it is the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*). Third, the manifestation of distinct qualities, namely the powers (*bala*).

This refers to the mastery of the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). "Powers" (*bala*) refers to the ten powers; "supernormal powers" (*abhijñā*) refers to the six supernormal powers; and "mastery" (*vaśitā*) has eight types. It is thus beyond verbal expression.
Because one intends to seek and aspire to the one hundred and forty unique qualities of a Buddha (*āveṇika-buddhadharma*), it is concluded by saying that all are fully attained.

Regarding the four non-abiding paths (*apratisthita-mārga*) that transform the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): "not abiding in saṃsāra" and "not abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*)" means not [abiding in either].

Abiding in nirvāṇa. The following provides an analogy: just as a mani jewel of many colors manifests various forms and images, because he does not abide in [a static] nirvāṇa, he is ever present within all buddha-fields, teaching the practices of the *Ghanavyūha* to the bodhisattvas.
The questions have concluded above.
From here below, the questions and answers are provided. This section consists of two parts: first, a brief response to the preceding questions in prose;

second, a detailed response to the questions in verse. Within the prose section, there are two sub-divisions: first, praising the questioner; second, from "One should first awaken to... onwards, demonstrating the underlying principle through a formal answer.
Regarding the praise of the questioner, the phrase "Excellent, O Lord of Beings" praises his excellence in being able to request that I speak, and so forth.

This is an exclamation praising the excellence of the request. The people of Ghanavyūha have thoroughly realized the principle of the two-fold selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-nairātmya*).

Since this Benevolent King is now precisely inquiring about this matter, he is praised accordingly. Below follows the answer to the preceding question: first, the response is presented by awakening the understanding and indicating the core tenet;
next, "All the worlds" explains the reason for the answer; finally, "I shall now... grants permission to speak and commands the audience to listen. This is the first section.

This can be seen. Next, regarding the second passage which states that "the objects of various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) are the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the mind," this cites the Mahāyāna principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) and the doctrine of the non-self of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).
As for "the objects of various conceptualizations," because the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are not singular, they are referred to as "various."
The distinct demarcations of each are called "discrimination" (vikalpa), pronounced with a high tone. Regarding these "characteristics of the mind," there are three kinds of mind:
First, the true mind of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara-citta*). Such are the six sense objects; they are the phenomenal arising of the true mind, appearing as if manifest.

Upon thorough investigation, one finds that it is only mind; outside of mind, there are no phenomena. Second, the deluded consciousness-mind. This refers to the division [of consciousness] from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to the manifesting consciousness within the mind.

Because it manifests the two parts—the grasped (nimitta-bhāga) and the grasper (darśana-bhāga)—it is called "consciousness-only" (*vijñapti-mātra*). Third, regarding the mind of the *vikalpa-vastu-vijñāna* (discriminative consciousness of objects):

this refers to the mind of manifesting consciousness which falsely clings to the manifested *nimitta-bhāga* as being real. Since that which is grasped as real does not exist, it is called "consciousness-only.

This is the answer to the previous question concerning "not following others," and so forth. If one can thoroughly penetrate the principle of consciousness-only and the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), [one will attain liberation].
This is because one abandons the deluded mind of grasping and discrimination. For this reason, it is said that within the objective realm, one relinquishes all discrimination.
The preceding section concludes the response by stating the fundamental tenet. Next, the reason for the response is explained:
"All worlds are views of discrimination" means that the essence of the world is indeed suchness (*tathatā*); however, due to the deluded grasping of ignorance, one perceives differences.
It is distinct. Thus, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky.

To see the essence of the world is called "seeing" because the seer is clear, pure, and thoroughly penetrating. This may be described as realizing that the essence of the world is merely suchness (*tathatā*).

A person such as this attains the samādhi of suchness (*tathatā-samādhi*) amidst the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) which serve as the focal points. The explanation of the reason has concluded; below, [the text] grants permission.
I shall now explain it for you and reveal its meaning. Because the preceding section expounded the principles of the Mahāyāna, it refers to "those dharmas.
The following section is an injunction to listen, which can be understood from the text itself. Thus, the prose section above has completed the response that sets forth the central thesis.

The following verses provide the answer. This consists of three sections. The first four lines extensively explain that the various conceptualized objects mentioned in the prose are the manifestations of the mind.
The subsequent seven lines explain the passage from the prose concerning "conceptualizations within objects."
Thereafter follow seven lines, which explain the passage from the prose section beginning with “all worlds are conceptualized views,” and so forth.
The first part of this further consists of two sections. The first is one line, which explains the various objects of conceptualization mentioned in the prose. The latter consists of three lines.
In the prose commentary (*śloka-bhāṣya*), this explains the characteristics of this mind. In the first verse, the upper two lines present the objects of discrimination:
that which is the objective referent (*ālambana*) of the distracted consciousnesses of all ordinary beings is called "all worlds.
Such worlds appear as if they exist though they do not, like a mirage in the heat. The lower two lines explain the reason for this: how can such unreal characteristics [appear]?

It can be so. Therefore, the present commentary explains this by stating that although [the object] does not exist, it arises through false discrimination. This concludes the explanation of the initial passage. Below, the long prose (gadya) is explained as "the characteristic of this mind.
Within this, the first one and a half lines clarify that the object and the mind are established in mutual dependence.
The subsequent one and a half lines explain the reason for this mutual dependence. The initial term "awakening" (*jue*) refers to the cognizing mind; that which is "awakened to" is...
Regarding the object of perception (*ālambana*): when the body arises, it arises in dependence upon an object; therefore, it is said that the cause of cognition arises from the cognized.
The objective sphere cannot manifest by itself; it manifests in dependence upon the mind; therefore, it is said that the cognized depends on the cognizer. These are the two phrases.
The preceding explains establishment through mutual dependence; the following explains non-separation.

"If one is absent, then the other two are not" means that if the self-aspect (*svabhāga*) of consciousness is absent, then the seeing-aspect (*darśanabhāga*) and the image-aspect (*nimittabhāga*) do not exist. There is another explanation: if the seeing-aspect is absent, then the image-aspect is absent;

therefore it is said that if one is absent, then the other two are not. Next, this is illustrated by a metaphor, hence the statement: "like light together with its shadow," which clarifies consciousness.

It is like light; the appearance of the object is like a shadow. The following clarifies the explanation in terms of phenomena (*dharma*): if there is no perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) of the mind, then there is no perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Therefore, it is said that without mind, there is also no object. As for "the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the object of cognition (*prameya*)," this explains their distinct characteristics.

That is to say, within the perceiving aspect, there are various modes of mental engagement (*vikalpa*), such as wholesome, unwholesome, or indeterminate; with outflows (*sāsrava*) or without outflows (*anāsrava*), and so forth. The objects of cognition are likewise the same.
This is so. The cases of contrariety, conformity, and equanimity can be understood by analogy. From the next line and a half onwards, the reason for the general conclusion is established.
The preceding two lines establish the reason for the characteristics of conformity; that is to say, the two aspects—the perceived and the perceiving—rely solely upon the single mind.

Such provisional conceptualization lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Next, there are two lines that establish the reason for the refutation of faults; that is to say, the phenomena of the subject and object [are each...]

Regarding "individually": this refers solely to the false conceptualization and attachment within a single mind. There follow two subsequent phrases which conclude by explaining the reason for the comprehensive understanding;
this can be seen according to the text. The initial passage has been explained.
From here below are seven lines. This explains the passage in the prose [sūtra] concerning "within the object" and "among various conceptualizations. Within this, there are two sections.

The first consists of four lines, which provide an explanation through the teaching of the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*). The latter consists of three lines, which employ analogies for illustration. The initial text, in turn, has three parts.

The first two lines concern how the mind arises from conditions, taking the formation of phenomena as its basis. The next one and a half lines describe the reversal of the flow to return to the source.
The final two lines clarify the fruit that is attained. Regarding "the mind is the self-nature of dharmas": the "mind" here is the true mind;
it arises from conditions to produce all phenomena. Nevertheless, all produced phenomena do not depart from the true mind, for they take the mind as their substance.
Therefore, it is said that the mind is the self-nature of dharmas, and that which is turbid for persons. From the true mind arise dharmas such as ignorance;
one becomes deluded in reverse regarding the mind and clings to it as being various dharmas. Thus it is said, "and that which is turbid for persons. The explanation of the first passage is complete.
Below, the return to the source—the true mind—is explained. Within this, one line clarifies the stage of returning the flow, followed by...
These two lines clarify the return to the source. Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage attain the contemplation of dual illumination;
only then are they able to forever relinquish all conceptualizing minds. For this reason, it is said that upon entering the eighth stage, they attain purity.
"That" refers to the conceptualizations that were relinquished, which are designated as "that. Bodhisattvas of the ninth stage rely on the dual practice attained in the preceding eighth stage.

Because they practice meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), they do not give rise to conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Although they are without discrimination, because their causal practice has not yet reached fulfillment, they occupy a middle position.
When the cultivation of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) bodhisattvas reaches its ultimate completion, they awaken to all phenomena as a Buddha;

therefore, it is called "Great Awakening" (*mahābodhi*). The following clarifies the return to the source: within the adamantine mind (*vajracitta*), subtle transgressions are forever exhausted without remainder. This is the virtue of cultivation.

Perfectly [awakened], he receives the rank of Dharma King; his basis is transformed and he returns to the source. Therefore, it is said that the water of the Dharma is poured upon his crown, and he becomes one honored by the world.
The preceding section has completed the analysis and explanation of abandoning all conceptual constructions within the objective sphere.
Below, two lines explain the fruit attained. There are two kinds of fruit: first, the fruit of initial existence; second, the fruit of fundamental existence. The first three phrases explain this.

There is first the fruit; there is first the reward body (saṃbhogakāya), which is named the Dharma-body (dharmakāya). Because it is non-dual and indistinguishable from the principle realized, it is inexhaustible.
The following two lines may be understood by analogy. The subsequent section explains the originally existing fruit, which consists of two lines.
This explains that the originally existing fruit is inexhaustible and indestructible. Below are three phrases concerning its being the locus of virtues.
"The mind-consciousness is precisely the originally existing Dharmakāya, the Tathāgatagarbha-mind; it is also thus" is explained according to the preceding analogy.

Since the initially existing Sambhogakāya is of one flavor with realization (*sākṣātkāra*), it can still be eternally abiding; how much more so the originally existing Tathāgatagarbha-mind—could it not be so?
It is eternal. Therefore, the illustrative statement is also like this. "Inexhaustible" means there is no cessation. "Indestructible" means there is no change.
Furthermore, the first two phrases clarify the empty *tathāgatagarbha*, while the latter three phrases explain the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*.

The remaining text is easy to understand and need not be explained at length; I shall now explain it point by point in response to the difficulties. Regarding the phrase "the pure lands of the *Ghanavyūha* Buddhas," it says:
The Ghanavyūha is a land of pure purity. As for the lands of all Buddhas, these refer to lands that are a mixture of the pure and the defiled, which are termed the "pure lands of all Buddhas.
This is because the true mind pervades all places; there is nowhere it is not present, yet its characteristics of existence or non-existence cannot be known.

Therefore, it is said that one "dwells in the inconceivable. The explanation of the Dharma through its textual exposition is now complete. Below follows the citation of analogies, which consist of two sections:
first, the analogy of the broken jar, which illustrates that which is to be remedied (*pratipakṣya*); second, the analogy of the fire, which illustrates the remedy (*pratipakṣa*).

Within the analogy for that which is to be remedied, the first line presents the analogy and the latter half of the verse provides the application (*yoga*). Regarding the phrase "the jar is broken," this is an analogy for the *vijñapti-mātra-vikalpa-vijñāna* (the discriminating consciousness of phenomena).

Cessation: This refers to the practitioner who first relinquishes the consciousness of objects, just as when a jar is broken. Although the jar is completely destroyed, the shards still remain present.
Similarly, although the coarse, manifest mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) has perished, the four afflictions, the *manas*, and their continuity remain undestroyed.

It is like the manifestation of shards. Furthermore, as the practitioner proceeds to sever the continuity [of the afflictions], the non-interruption and so forth still remain manifest within consciousness, up to and including ignorance.
This is like the destruction of a jar where the dust particles have not yet vanished. Furthermore, as he proceeds to exhaustively sever ignorance, the karmic consciousness, and so forth.

There is only the true mind, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Just as when dust is pulverized, there remains only the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*), the following two lines join this with the cited metaphor;

such is the synthesis. Regarding "because of the out-flowing" (*sāsrava*): by cutting and destroying the out-flowing until reaching the ultimate state, only the *tathatā* (suchness), the non-out-flowing dharma, remains.
There is no further birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) to be severed or eliminated. As for the out-flowing...

The suchness contained therein is untainted (*anāsrava*); thus, through this analogy, it is shown that while the phenomena have ceased, the principle remains. The subsequent analogy illustrates the capacity for remediation.
The first two lines introduce the analogy by way of illustration; the following passage concludes the analogy by applying the dharma.
Regarding the initial section, the phrase "like fire burning wood" means that within the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*), non-conceptual [wisdom] removes conceptualization.
Because it takes the object-consciousness as its mind, it is like fire burning wood until it is exhausted.
Furthermore, as the practitioner proceeds to sever the increasingly subtle remaining obstacles, it is therefore metaphorically said that "it burns again in another place.

In the subsequent application of the analogy, there may be doubt as to whether this antidote should function by taking meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) as its object or by employing true cultivation (*bhūtā-bhāvanā*). Therefore, it is generally stated that it functions solely through meditative cultivation, and not otherwise.
True cultivation. By this, one speaks of the immovable wisdom regarding flavors. "Flavors" refers to attachment; that is, the wisdom of dependent cultivation, which takes ignorance as its essence.
One looks up toward and seeks the true immovability that is free from such attachment.

Now, wishing to exclude the true immovable wisdom and take only the wisdom of dependent cultivation—though if discussed generally, both wisdoms are attained—the limits of non-extinction are transformed, and by departing from discrimination, one undergoes the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
This refers to cessation. Because the very substance of ignorance, which is the basis of transformation, is extinguished, the cultivation based upon it can no longer be established;

hence, it is called "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). That which is free from conceptual discrimination is true cultivated wisdom. If cultivation based on conditions were still present, it would occupy the same locus as the wisdom of conditioned cultivation, and one could not say it is "free.
Now that cultivation based on conditions has been exhausted, true wisdom alone remains; thus it is said to be "free from conceptual discrimination."
Below are two lines that conclude by indicating the location; this may be understood according to the text. The explanation of the metaphorical passage is finished.
From here on is the third section, consisting of seven lines of verse, which explains the prose statement that "all worlds are conceptualized views" and so forth.
This section has three parts. The first part consists of three lines, explaining the prose statement that "all worlds are conceptualized."
[The term] "seeing" (*darśana*) appears. Next, there are two lines that explain the "seeing of the world's essence" (*loka-svabhāva-darśana*) within the prose section.

Following this, there are two lines that explain "attaining samādhi upon the very object of focus" (*ālambane samādhi-lābha*) within the prose section. Within the first three lines, there are also three sections.

The first line clarifies "discriminative seeing" (*vikalpa-darśana*) by way of discriminating the world. The next line [clarifies it] by way of the afflictions and karma of transformation (*pariṇāma-kleśa-karma*).
This explains the cause by clarifying the view of discrimination. Following this, there is one line that addresses the fruit of transformation to explain the view of discrimination.

It demonstrates the correct principle that various categories of phenomena do not arise: namely, that worldly dharmas are false discriminations falsely reckoned as existing when they fundamentally do not exist;
just as dream-objects and the dreaming mind falsely appear yet are originally unarisen, so too is the discrimination of the world. Thus it is likewise.

This is so because it exists due to the false conceptualization of the *vikaṭpavijñāna* (discriminating consciousness of objects). Therefore, it is said that "it does not give rise to various categories.

Regarding the two phrases, "Do not dwell in the world," etc., they are an exhortation to ordinary people not to be attached to the world and an encouragement to abandon all views of false discrimination.
"Dwelling" means attachment. The subsequent phrase indicates the ultimate source (*pratiśaraṇa*): "non-self" refers to the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
There is no abiding and no attainment; it pervades the entire dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) without a single characteristic. Therefore, it is said to be "selfless" (anātman).
Those who wish to abandon all views must take refuge in the doctrine of selflessness. Thus, the True Suchness (tathatā) realized at the first stage (bhūmi) constitutes this selflessness.

Below, [the text] explains that the world is established through the discrimination of the causes of afflictions and karma within the transformational existence (pariṇāmika-saṃsāra); if one cuts off ignorance up to the [notion of] characteristics...

When various conceptualizations such as the continuity of consciousness are not perceived because the world is no longer seen, it is said that all continuities are severed, and there is neither arising nor destruction.
As for "continuity": from the initial ignorance up to the sixth consciousness of the continuity, it is called "continuity" because it flows in succession without interruption. [The following two...]

The phrase indicates the correct principle: that is to say, if one exhausts the causes of death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*), all those who hold views take refuge in the doctrine of non-self (*anātman*).
"Taking refuge" means realization. This is precisely the *tathatā* (suchness) realized through the effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*) of the eighth stage, which is termed "non-self.
Following this is one line that explains the result of transformation; it says: "All those who suffer" refers to the retribution of transformation, which is called...
Regarding "afflictions": at the very last moment within the *vajra-mind*, when the retribution of transformation is exhausted, it is said that "all afflictions have already ceased.
In the second moment, within the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*), one realizes the fulfillment of original suchness; therefore, it is said that "one dwells in quiescence, inconceivable.
Since time immemorial, when all phenomena are seen as perfect suchness, there is only pure suchness itself; there is nothing whatsoever to be severed.
Because it is excluded. It is purified among all views; the subsequent phrase follows the same principle as the preceding one.

This refers to the *tathatā* (suchness) realized by the Vajra [stage] up to the fruit of Buddhahood, which is named "non-self. The explanation of the first passage is complete. Below this is the second section, explaining the essence of the world (*loka*) within the prose commentary.
This consists of two parts: the first line clarifies the essence of the world, and the following two lines [clarify its characteristics].
Next, I shall explain the character *jiàn* (see/manifest). Within the first section on practice, the first half explains the essence (*tǐ*), and the second half explains the reason (*suǒyǐ*).

"The various phenomena of the world" refers to the characteristics of the world. Since such characteristics are nothing other than Suchness (*tathatā*) without any distinct dharma, the statement regarding the essence says:
"originally, they have no nature of self. "No-self" (*anātman*) is Suchness. The following explains the reason. Someone may raise a doubt, saying: "We currently perceive..."
Although there are various distinctions among all phenomena in the world, the present explanation states that they are "only like non-self.

This implies that all phenomena must first cease and perish before they become non-existent, and that verbal expressions can reveal *tathatā* (suchness). Therefore, it is now stated generally that [suchness] is not revealed by striking or destroying [phenomena], nor by means of metaphors;
for "metaphor" (*dṛṣṭānta*) is another name for verbal expression. This concludes the section on the supramundane essence. Hereafter follows the second...

2. Next, I shall explain the character "view" (dṛṣṭi). To investigate and seek [the truth] is called "view. Because one employs the wisdom cultivated through practice to investigate that the essence of the world is suchness (tathatā), it is termed "view.
Within this, first there is a simile, followed by its application to the Dharma. Fire has no separate essence; it takes wood as its essence.
Once the fuel is completely consumed, its own essence perishes along with it; therefore, it is said that "it is extinguished therein. The following two [verses]...
The phrasing is consistent; it may be understood by comparison. The explanation of the second passage is concluded. From here on, the two lines explain the prose section:
"one attains samādhi within the very object of focus. This contains three sections: the first two lines present the essence of samādhi;

the next three lines concern the progressive cultivation based upon that concentration; and the final three lines clarify the benefits obtained. This is called "bliss in the present life" (*dṛṣṭadharmasukha*).
Regarding "the essence of emerging from samādhi" and "the realm of the sages' own wisdom":

this praises the profundity of samādhi, stating that the meditative concentration associated with the *tathāgatagarbha* is not something entered by ordinary beings or those of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). Therefore, it is praised as "the realm of the sages' own wisdom.
Next, there are three phrases clarifying the advancement of practice: based on the samādhi of the first stage (*bhūmi*), one enters the subsequent stages; thus it says, "relying on this, one enters."

Regarding the various stages (*bhūmi*): the latter two lines clarify the faults to be abandoned. There are two kinds of faults: first, faults of the cause, which refers to the purification of beginningless evil;
second, faults of the result, which refers to the relinquishing of worldly dependence. The following three lines concern the benefits obtained.

Regarding "transcending the world and abiding therein," there are three aspects to transcending the world: first, transcending the world of segmented existence (*paricchinna-loka*), which refers to the initial [stage]...

In the stage of the ground (*bhūmi*). Second, the world of manifesting function, which refers to the eight stages (*aṣṭabhūmi*). Third, the world of transformation (*nirmāṇa*), which refers to the stage of Buddhahood.
In these three locations, one attains the benefit of stable abiding;

that which is called "the mind" here is the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), meaning that throughout the aforementioned three stages, as obstacles are gradually eliminated, it gradually manifests purity. Once the mind has attained purity, it remains constant...
"Abiding in the Buddha-field" is what is called the benefit obtained. The preceding section of one round of question and answer is concluded.
Below this follows another round of question and answer, which clarifies the place of refuge. Within this, there is first the question and then the answer.

Regarding the interrogative text, the term "Vajra-Svāmin" (Vajra Sovereign) is an exclamation addressed to the person asking the question; the meaning of the remaining text is evident and can be understood by inference. Thus:
The following provides an answer to the preceding question. It consists of two sections: first, a brief response expressed through verses that state the central thesis;

second, an extensive explanation of the reasons for this, beginning from the prose section below. Within the initial statement of the thesis, there are four lines of verse, which are divided into four sections.
The first two lines explain the Buddha as the object of refuge. The next single line identifies the Dharma as the object of refuge. The subsequent three lines...
The Sangha is the place of refuge. Following this, there is one line concerning the country as the place of refuge.

Within the Jewel of the Buddha, the first line of verse clarifies that the Buddha transcends the hundred negations; the subsequent line clarifies that because the Buddha is preeminent, he is worthy of taking refuge in.
The initial passage consists of two parts. The first two lines clarify that the Buddha’s essence is subtle, transcending the characteristics of existence and non-existence;

the latter two lines clarify the faults from which it is free. Regarding "the Buddha’s essence," this refers to the *dharmakāya* of true suchness (*tathatā*). Transcending the characteristics of existence and non-existence, it is subtly beyond the hundred negations and accords with the Middle Way;
therefore, it is called "Buddha. The following section explains the freedom from faults. "The tree of the aggregates has already been incinerated" means that [it is free] from the internal...

"Transcending the body" means that the demonic armies have all been repelled and destroyed; this refers to being free from external enemies. The former refers to the *skandha-māra* (the demon of the aggregates), and the latter refers to the *deva-māra* (the celestial demon).
The following line explains that the Tathāgata is supreme and thus worthy of reliance. The first two lines explain that because the destination reached is supreme, he is worthy of taking refuge in.

The next single line explains that what is realized is pure and stainless, and because it is suchness (*tathatā*), he is worthy of reliance. The final line concludes that he is worthy of taking refuge in.
This is understood. The explanation of the Jewel of the Buddha is concluded. "Far removed from all conceptual discrimination" clarifies that the Jewel of the Dharma is the locus of reliance.
"Removed" means "non-existent"; because it is called the Dharma as the sphere where conceptualized delusions do not reach, it is devoid of all conceptual discrimination.

Below, the Sangha is explained: "Realizing the state of no location" refers to those from the first bhūmi upward, who have realized the principle of True Suchness (tathatā) which is without center or periphery.
They are called the noble Saṃgha. Within such a Saṃgha, one selects the superior ones and does not include those of the lower stages;

thus, the latter phrase mentions "those in the Guhyavati samādhis," referring to those from the eighth stage upward as the superior ones. The concluding phrase is clear. There are two kinds of taking refuge:
first, the objects of refuge at the time of practice, namely the Three Jewels, as described above; second, [the state of] abiding...
The body, time, objects, and locus are as described below: the sublime realm of Ghanavyūha.

Because Ghanavyūha is the place where Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and above are born, it is called "supremely pure. The meaning of the remaining passages is evident and can be understood by inference.
The brief response expressing the fundamental tenet is hereby concluded.
From here below is the second section, which extensively explains the reasons [for the preceding]. This consists of three parts: first, an explanation in prose;
second, an explanation in verse; and third, a further explanation in prose. Within the first part, because it sets forth five chapters, there are five sections.

First, from "Having already attained the stage of the ground" onwards, it explains that all worlds are illusory and lack reality. Second, from "The multitudes of the world" down to "constantly non-existent."
1. "Severing" explains that worldly phenomena are created solely by the mind. 2. "The three [aspects] are among the eight kinds of mind...
up to "...there may be those who grasp them all at once" explains the meaning of the mind arising instantaneously. 3.

"The nature of the mind is fundamentally pure" down to "yet there are distinctions" explains the meaning that the mind is eternally pure and unchanging. 4. "Although the ālayavijñāna... [is as follows].

Regarding the phrase "with the perfuming agents... down to... it becomes clearly manifest," this explains that although the ālayavijñāna coexists in the same location as all phenomena, it is neither identical to them nor different from them.
In the first section of the text, there are three parts. First, "Having spoken these words" serves to conclude the preceding and introduce what follows.

Second, from "Having attained the various stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth" downward, the Dharma is explained to provide a direct demonstration. Third, as in the passage on the painted image, extensive analogies are cited for explanation. The first part is easily understood.

Regarding "having already attained the stages," this refers to the Bodhisattva who perceives reality as it is attaining the first stage. As for the various contemplative practices (*vipaśyanā-caryā*)...

"Those things"—the ten stages (*bhūmi*) are not one; they are not called "various contemplative practices" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). The rest of the text is clear. Below, the meaning is explained through metaphors.

There are ten metaphors, with the first great metaphor divided into four. The first metaphor illustrates the aforementioned falsely conceptualized characteristics of the differentiation among all phenomena.

The second consists of two metaphors, illustrating how various non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) falsely conceptualize a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to the self (*ātmīya*) within the body. There are four [remaining metaphors].
Metaphor. This metaphor illustrates that phenomena born of causes and conditions are established merely as empty appearances and possess no real nature.
The phrase "all four are false and deceptive" below concludes what was previously stated and resolves potential doubts and difficulties; this constitutes the first metaphor.

"As there may be high and low within a painted image" refers to a painting on a wall which, in reality, has no height or depth. Yet, ordinary children, seeing the large and small [forms] on the wall, perceive them as high...

This explains the characteristics of the lower distinctions. However, when one rubs [the surface] with the hand, it is level without any elevations or depressions; True Suchness (tathatā) is like a wall, and all phenomena (dharmas) are like images reflected therein.

As for the two similes of what is seen in a dream—the beautiful woman seen in a dream and the barren woman who, having dreamed, becomes pregnant with a child—these ultimately have no reality. These two similes below serve as metaphors for the "self" (ātman) as conceived by non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Just as the beautiful woman seen in a dream and the child borne by a barren woman in a dream are ultimately non-existent, so too is the self.
It is merely a confused calculation of a dream; the calculations of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) are also like this.

Next, there are four similes illustrating that all phenomena are empty and appear to exist only in semblance, yet lack any real nature. Not only do they lack reality, but even when seeking their characteristics closely, they cannot be found.

The text is clear enough to understand. Next, there are two similes illustrating that all phenomena are impermanent and perish rapidly, not lasting beyond a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). As [the text says]:
"Like the shadow of floating clouds, like a flash of rushing lightning; they perish swiftly and do not abide. This concludes what was previously stated.
"They are all false and deceptive, not truly existent"—this is the summary of what was previously stated.

"That which is accomplished through discrimination is like a craftsman fashioning a vessel"—this is the passage that resolves doubts and difficulties. There may be an external doubt: "If the characteristics of all phenomena are not truly existent..."
"Why is it that what is presently perceived each possesses its own intrinsic nature (svabhāva)? The Sarvāstivādins maintain such a position. To this, we now respond:
What you perceive is produced by conceptual construction (vikalpa); it does not exist inherently. Therefore, the subsequent analogy states: 'It is like a craftsman fashioning a vessel.'"

A skilled artisan, relying upon a single lump of clay, fashions various vessels whose appearances differ from one another. Yet, when one examines these distinct characteristics, there is only the clay;
no separate phenomena exist. Thus, it has been concluded that all aforementioned phenomena are empty and unreal.
From here below is the second section, which investigates how illusory phenomena are produced solely by the mind. This section contains two parts: first, an explanation according to the Dharma;
second, the citation of analogies. Within the explanation, there are further four sub-sections: (1) explaining that the eight consciousnesses arise in mutual dependence;

(2) explaining the five dharmas; (3) explaining the three natures; and (4) the absence of self. However, in the scriptural text, these are condensed into two segments; the first explains the eight [consciousnesses].
Regarding the meaning of the arising of the characteristics of consciousness: there are two explanations for how the five dharmas and so forth are established as being inseparable.
In the first passage, the phrase "worldly sentient beings... continuing in succession" means that the eight consciousnesses arise in mutual dependence.

"Worldly sentient beings" excludes external objects and refers only to the realm of sentient experience; this is the general statement. "Habitual tendencies (vāsanā) shroud the mind" is the explanation.
Therefore, as for the mind, it is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*). Although it is said that all phenomena are produced by the mind, the mind does not act of its own accord;

it must depend upon causes and conditions, namely the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time. These delude and obscure the true mind. Because the mind follows these conditions, it gives rise to all phenomena.

Once the mind-consciousness has arisen, one becomes attached to various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and fixations; because of this, the various phenomena evolve with their distinctions. From this point on—

Below, it is explained how the seven consciousnesses arise based on the mind. First, regarding "mind" (*manas*): from the consciousness of ignorance (*avidyā-vijñāna*) up to the consciousness of continuity (*prabandha-vijñāna*), these are collectively termed "mind," because they are capable of generating the discriminating six consciousnesses.
Regarding "consciousness" (*vijñāna*): this refers to the discriminating mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*).

As for "the other various consciousnesses," these refer to the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*). Regarding "evolving in succession": "evolving" (*pariṇāma*) means "arising. Thus, from the subtle aspect...
It continues to establish the end; in the interim, there is no interruption. Therefore, it is said that they "proceed in succession. This concludes the explanation of the first passage.
From here on is the second section, explaining that "dharmas are mutually inseparable" and that they are explained in a single location. Why does this passage appear?
It is because the True Mind cannot transform itself into the dharmas of birth and death; it must first acquire the habit-energies of ignorance and deluded thought before such a transformation occurs.

Regarding all phenomena (*dharmas*): all phenomena are likewise; they must rely upon the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) in order to establish their own essence. Because it is intended to reveal this, this passage follows.
As for the "five factors" (*pañca-dharmāḥ*): first, name (*nāman*); second, appearance (*nimitta*); third, discrimination (*vikalpa*), also called false conceptualization (*parikalpita*);
fourth, correct gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*); and fifth, suchness (*tathatā*). Regarding the way these five factors are subsumed within the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), the various teachings differ.

According to the *Madhyāntavibhāga* and other treatises, the two factors of name (*nāman*) and sign (*nimitta*) are subsumed under the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) are subsumed [under the same];

and correct cognition (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) are subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). As for the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, it states that the first, the imagined nature, is not included among the five dharmas because it is ultimately non-existent.
Those who speak thus have merely heard the names of the three natures from others; they do not recognize their actual substance.

Regarding the nature [of these categories] and the reason they receive their names: if the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) were not an object of the noble ones (*ārya*), the noble ones would certainly not have spoken of it.

If the noble ones did not speak of the principle of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), who else would speak of it such that the principle of the three natures exists? Furthermore, as for the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature):

depending on what and depending on what "other" is it called "dependent"? If its nature were to depend [on itself], one could say it depends on itself; why then discuss "depending on another"? Yet you say...
The term "imagined nature" (parikalpita-svabhāva) refers to that which is non-existent; thus, it is not included among the five dharmas.

As for the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), since there is nothing else upon which it depends, by depending on what "other" could it be called "dependent"? From this, it is clear that [the opponent] does not understand the explanation of the names.
According to the *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra*, there are two successive expositions of the meaning of the three natures. The first exposition states: "By means of the imagined nature..."
He first exists. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "The eye's cataract and dizziness are like the nature of parikalpita (imagined); the perceived hair-tufts are like the nature of paratantra (dependent).
By this one may infer that the *paratantra* is established only by depending upon the *parikalpita*.
Later, it further states: "By means of the *paratantra*, the *parikalpita* comes to exist. Therefore, the Sūtra says: "A crystal bead appears blue due to its proximity to a blue color."

A color appears; ordinary, ignorant people do not recognize it for what it is, but grasp at it as being truly blue. That which appears blue upon the jewel is a metaphor for the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature).
That which is grasped as being real is a metaphor for the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature).

According to the first sequence, the *parikalpita-svabhāva* is subsumed by "discrimination," while the *paratantra-svabhāva* is subsumed by "name and appearance. According to the subsequent sequence, the reverse of the former may be understood. This is also like [the explanation] in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

Thus it is said. Therefore, that sutra states: "The two dharmas of name and appearance are subsumed under dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is subsumed under false discrimination.

Regarding the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), there is a twofold analysis: first, the explanation of their names; second, the determination of their essential natures (*tattva*). As for the explanation of the names:
the first is the nature of discrimination, also called the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Regarding the term "nature of discrimination," it means:
The deluded mind constructs and conceptualizes; because it does not correspond to the actual object, it is called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*). This is a designation based on its functional capacity.
Furthermore, because this deluded mind universally conceives of and clings to the objects it grasps, it is termed "the nature of being thoroughly imagined and grasped" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

It is not that the object existing as it is grasped by the imagining mind is called the "imagined nature"; rather, this is a designation formed by combining the subjective and objective aspects. Some teachers have declared that the object...
The object of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) is called "pervasively conceptualized. One does not take the grasping subject itself to be the nature of pervasive conceptualization;

if one were to do so, it would contradict reason. This is because the three natures are the domain of the noble ones (*ārya*). The nature of pervasive conceptualization is ultimately non-existent, and the noble ones do not perceive it.
Since they do not perceive it, the principle of the three natures cannot be explained [in terms of that perception]. The principle of the three natures is the domain of the Buddhas.
The realm (dhātu) is not the domain of ordinary beings. How, then, can it be said that an ultimately non-existent thing constitutes the object of the noble ones?

This is the error of the proponents of the Buddha-nature treatise (*Buddhadhātu-śāstra*). As for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), it is also called the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda-svabhāva*) and the nature of arising in dependence on others (*paratantra-utpatti-svabhāva*).
All are obtained without injury. Because it exists only by depending on the differentiation of others, it is called the "dependent nature" (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
This is truly because, in the Mahāyāna, all phenomena are produced by the mind; these produced phenomena do not depart from the mind and take the mind as their essence.
If there were no deluded mind, the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) within the cycle of birth and death could not arise of itself;

therefore, the various sūtras explain the twelve links of dependent origination as being the dependent nature. Since ignorance is the first of the twelve causal links, we know that the dependent nature depends upon the *parikalpita* (imagined nature).
Furthermore, the sūtras speak of eight similes, such as dreams, to illustrate the dependent nature. If there were no dreaming mind, [the dream would not exist].

The dream-object does not appear; yet, based on the dream, there is an object. Thus, it is clearly known that the dependent nature exists through conceptualization. Furthermore, some say: "There is a pure dependent nature.

Is this pure dependent nature identical to or different from correct cognition (*samyagjñāna*)? If one says they are identical, then it is subsumed under the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) and is not the dependent nature.
If one says they are different, then it would follow that the remainder [of phenomena] exists only by virtue of ignorance (*avidyā*). This is a contradiction.

This is not understood as pure. If one were to claim it is pure because it does not arise from ignorance, then what scripture states that the twelve links of dependent origination have "ignorance" (*avidyā*) as a condition for "existence" (*bhava*)?
Therefore, it is known that to say the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is pure is a baseless and frivolous statement. To reveal its essential nature:
As for the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), its essence consists solely in the mental constructions, deliberations, practices, and understandings of the deluded mind.
Furthermore, as for those who claim that its essence is the deluded objects grasped by the deluded mind, this statement is profoundly erroneous; the faults are as previously described.

Regarding the essence of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there are two layers of meaning. The first is the establishment of all phenomena from their origin, which refers to [the process] from ignorance (*avidyā*) up to manifestation.
Regarding consciousness: within the mind of manifesting consciousness, the two parts—the perceived aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśana-bhāga*)—emerge simultaneously.

Because the perceived aspect arises based on ignorance and so forth through the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), it is termed the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*). Within this context, both the perceived and perceiving aspects are entirely of the dependent nature.

Second, through contemplative practice that eliminates obstacles and enters into principle, one establishes the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Within this context, only the *nimittabhāga* (the objective aspect) is established as the essence [of the dependent nature].
This is because the mind, as the *darśanabhāga* (the subjective aspect), does not know its own or the common objective aspects (*nimittabhāga*).

They grasp at [phenomena] as being truly existent dharmas external to the mind. However, that which is the objective essence (*ālambana-svabhāva*) grasped by the mental consciousness and its mental factors is a manifestation produced by consciousness;

it is not produced by the mind itself. When the practitioner of contemplation realizes their lack of true existence, although the semblance of the objective part (*nimitta-bhāga*) appears, it still exists and is not non-existent.

Based on this principle of practice, worldly deluded followers say that the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) is existent and not non-existent, while the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)...

The essence is, as usual, to be understood accordingly. Regarding the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*): the absence of a sovereign master within the aggregates (*skandha*) is called the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).
The absence of any real intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) among all phenomena (*dharma*) is called the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

As explained above, the eight consciousnesses, the five dharmas, the three natures, and the two selflessnesses—each and every one of these factors cannot exist independently, just like waves upon water; if there were no water, [the waves could not exist].
Where there are waves, they do not arise without a source; wherever there are waves, there must be water. All phenomena (*dharmas*) are likewise:

wherever there is a phenomenon, there must be *tathatā* (suchness). There is not a single phenomenon that is merely false and devoid of suchness. Therefore, it is said that [all phenomena] are eternally associated with it.

The explanation by Śākyamuni has been concluded. From this point downward, analogies are cited. Within this section, there is first the analogy, and subsequently, from "the ālayavijñāna" onwards, the application of the cited analogy.
Thus, the correspondence between these two passages can be understood.

The third section from here on explains whether the arising of the eight consciousnesses is simultaneous or gradual. This consists of two parts: first, explaining the distinction between the simultaneous and gradual arising of the consciousnesses;
second, from the passage "If, regarding houses and dwellings... onwards, explaining simultaneity and graduality.

Although there are no such various differences in substance, this clarifies that the eight consciousnesses share a single substance (*ekakāya*). There are two aspects to this single substance: first, the *tathāgatagarbha* as the dependent origination of phenomena.

Gate. [The mind] transforms into all phenomena (*dharmas*). Although phenomena differ in myriads of ways, their essence is solely the true mind; therefore, they are said to be "of the same substance" (*tongti*).

Second, prior to the manifestation of consciousness within the deluded mind, there is no mark of differentiation. Flowing until the manifestation of consciousness, it suddenly appears as the perceived object (*xiang*) and the perceiving subject (*jian*).
Thereafter, various phenomena gradually appear. Since these phenomena take the manifesting consciousness as their essence, they are said to be "of the same substance. And...
"Following conditions" (隨緣) below explains that when consciousness arises, there is the sense of being sudden or gradual. "Arising gradually following conditions" explains gradual arising.
"Or arising all at once" refers to the meaning of sudden arising. Thus, the substance of consciousness arises either suddenly or gradually.

Regarding "at the time the mind arises" below, it explains that within the grasped object (*grāhya*), there is likewise suddenness and gradualness; the text is clear enough to be understood. Below, it explains the reason for this, concerning the house...
Regarding objects such as houses that are collections of parts: if they appear without partiality, they are for the most part apprehended all at once;
if they appear with partiality, they are apprehended sequentially. Therefore, it is said that these are mostly apprehended either simultaneously or sequentially.

The former [section] explained "simultaneous apprehension" (*yugapad-grahaṇa*). The latter [section], beginning with "if in sleep or dreaming," explains "sequential apprehension" (*anupūrva-grahaṇa*).
If phenomena are dispersed and do not aggregate, they are for the most part apprehended sequentially. However, upon detailed analysis, there is also simultaneous apprehension therein;
therefore, it is taught that "some apprehend all at once. This is like eating hot honey: if there is no partial intensity, the two consciousnesses of body and tongue apprehend simultaneously.
If there is partiality [in the application], one should first take the stronger [evidence]. Thus, the characteristics appearing in these various passages can be understood.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the "object of apprehension" (*grāhya*) regarding sudden and gradual [attainment].

Hereafter begins the fourth [section]: "The nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* is eternally unchanging. This consists of two parts: first, explaining that the nature of the true mind is eternally unchanging; second...

This means that [the term] "that which" can give rise to phenomena according to conditions. Furthermore, it is said: the former explanation clarifies the gate of the supporting basis (*āśraya*), while the latter explains dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Within the context of the permanence of the nature (*dharmatā*), first comes the phenomenon, and subsequently, the aforementioned Tathāgatagarbha-mind is eternally present within birth and death, yet its nature is eternally pure.
This is not understood by ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas at the initial stage of practice.
Therefore, it is proclaimed that the nature of the mind is fundamentally pure and inconceivable. This reveals the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"The naturally pure mind cannot be defiled by afflictions, nor can it be purified by wisdom. This is the subtle and wondrous [teaching] of all Tathāgatas.

"Treasury" (garbha) explains "Non-empty Treasury. This means that within the Tathāgatagarbha, there are from the very beginning all the dharmas of essential qualities, more numerous than the sands of the Ganges;
yet not a single dharma exists as a separate, self-sustaining nature. Because it is like an image reflected in a mirror, it is called "subtle and wondrous."
The explanation of the Dharma through its textual expressions is concluded. Below, specific metaphors are introduced for further elucidation. "Like gold in its ore, its nature is eternally pure;

the true mind is likewise"—this explains dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Regarding the phrase "the mental faculty (*manas*) arises from the mind": as for "mental faculty," it refers to ignorance up to the consciousness that continues in an uninterrupted stream;
these six layers are collectively termed the "mental faculty. As for "mind," this is the *tathāgatagarbha*-mind, also called the "True [Mind]."
The mind is also called *ālaya*. This is because the seven consciousnesses are all produced by the mind; thus the text states that "the other six are likewise.
One should understand that what follows below is the concluding explanation. The explanation of the fourth section is hereby completed.
Regarding the meaning that the ālayavijñāna, from this point forward, exists in the same location as all phenomena yet its nature is neither identical nor different, there are three parts:
first, the explanation of the doctrine to demonstrate the principle; second, the citation of analogies; and third, the application of the analogy to the doctrine.

The initial passage is further divided into two parts: first, the explanation that the *ālayavijñāna* is neither identical nor different; second, the explanation that the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is neither identical nor different.

From the section beginning with "From the *ālaya*" down to "and they dwell together," the meaning of non-difference is clarified. The subsequent section, "Its nature is eternally luminous and pure," explains the meaning of non-identity.
Regarding the term "that which perfumes" (*kṣobhaka*), there are two meanings. As for the first meaning, it refers to the consciousness arising from ignorance (*avidyā*).

Up to and including manifesting consciousness (*vijñapti-vijñāna*), these are called the "perfumers" (*vāsaka*), because they perfume the true mind (*tathatā-citta*) and produce birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

As for the various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), this refers to those associated with the wisdom-consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*) and the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*); since all possess the association of a mind-king (*citta-rāja*) and mental factors, they are thus described as mental factors.
There is another interpretation which states that among the aforementioned mental factors, those that are particularly potent are selected as the "perfumers."
Excluding the inferior and indeterminate mental factors (*citta-dharma*), that which is named "capable" is called "perfuming" (*vāsanā*) from the perspective of its functional capacity.
As for all mental factors, if one speaks in terms of their essential nature (*svabhāva*), the remaining textual passages will manifest their characteristics.

Below, the explanation of the Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) as being neither identical to nor different from the various afflictions (*kleśa*) follows the same principle as above; therefore, it says "likewise. Regarding the distinction between the determinate and the indeterminate, there are two types. The first is...

The third is right determination (*samyaktva-niyata*), which refers to those of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). The second is wrong determination (*mithyātva-niyata*), which refers to *icchantikas*. The third is indeterminate (*aniyata*); this should be understood by analogy.
Although there are such distinctions between persons who are determined or indeterminate, the essence of Buddha-nature is eternally pure and stainless.

This concludes the textual explanation of the Dharma. Next, a metaphor is cited to clarify it; the text is readily visible [therein]. Below follows the application of the metaphor (*upanaya*): first, the metaphor is joined with the subject, and subsequently, [the conclusion is] raised.
The Dharma is thus revealed. Passages such as these may all be understood from their direct presentation. The preceding prose commentary has been concluded.
Below follows the extensive explanation of the aforementioned meaning through verse; therein, there are one hundred and twenty-six lines and a half of text in total.

This is divided into two sections. The first consists of forty-six and a half lines, which answer the question on "seeing things as they truly are" (yathābhūta-darśana) at the beginning of the *Prakaraṇa* chapter.
The latter consists of seventy-nine lines, which provide a detailed explanation of what was stated in the prose preceding the verses. Within the first section, there are further nine subsections:
first, eight and a half lines praising the question on seeing things as they truly are; second, thirteen and a half lines [answering] that which was not [explicitly] stated in the prose...
1. One line follows the preceding [section]. 2. One and a half lines answer the question in the prose section regarding dwelling in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*). 3.
One line answers the question in the prose section regarding the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) and not abiding in the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

4. One line explains the attainment of the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) and so forth. 5. Three lines answer the question in the prose section regarding the object of internal realization (*pratyātma-adhigama-viṣaya*). 6. Four lines.

The preceding verses are cited and re-explained point by point through successive challenges. Section Eight consists of three stanzas, which demonstrate the principles of the Mahāyāna to the various non-Buddhists.
Section Nine consists of one hundred and one and a half stanzas, answering the prose section on the practice of blissful cultivation leading to the stage of Buddhahood.

The initial section consists of three parts. First, there is one line that praises and inquires regarding the teaching according to reality. Next, there is one line that exhorts the king to transmit what he has heard to others.
Finally, there are six and a half lines that clarify the benefits obtained from hearing the Dharma. The meaning of the first two sections is clearly evident.
Within the third section, the first two phrases indicate the thesis and briefly demonstrate the benefits; the subsequent portion, beginning with "or," [provides further detail].

This extensively demonstrates the benefits according to our school’s tenets. "If a person has heard the Dharma" refers to one who has first heard this teaching during the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

"Gradually purifying the *ālayavijñāna*" means that from the stage of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*) upward, one understands the principle of the selflessness of all phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), gradually subduing the attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
Because this attachment to phenomena is subdued, the *ālayavijñāna* gradually manifests; thus it is said to be "gradually purified. This refers to starting from the stage of the spiritual lineage.
...up to the vajra stage, one finally attains the ultimate. Therefore, it is called "gradual. Below is the detailed explanation, which consists of three sections.
The first two and a half lines explain that by virtue of hearing the Dharma, one receives superior karmic retribution within the triple world.

Next, there is one line explaining that by virtue of hearing the Dharma, one attains the path of non-abiding; although remaining in saṃsāra, one is constantly in accord with joy. The final two lines...
Half [of the verse]. By hearing the Dharma, one achieves the unsurpassed fruit. The first section further has three parts. The first half-line concerns becoming a king among humans.
The next line concerns becoming a king of the desire realm heavens (*kāmadhātu*).

The final line concerns becoming a king in the fixed abodes of the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*), or becoming a king among humans—namely, various minor kings (*kṣudra-rāja*) or universal monarchs (*cakravartin*). There are four types of universal monarchs; the first governs...
Jambudvīpa; second, ruling over two continents; third, ruling over three continents; fourth, ruling over four continents, as described in the *Ratnarāśi-sūtra*.
Below, the heavens of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) are explained. There are four such heavens, yet here only four are mentioned because they are cited according to their preeminence;
the [other] four heavens are not mentioned because they are omitted in this abbreviated treatment. The remaining text is clear. Below, the two upper realms are explained. Above—
The meaning of the two lines can be understood accordingly. "Non-conceptual sentient beings" refers to the Heaven of Non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñisattva*).
Regarding "experiencing the bliss of various meditative concentrations," according to the Mahāyāna teachings, there is indeed mental consciousness within the Heaven of Non-conceptualization;

however, because it is extremely subtle, ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles do not perceive its existence. Since consciousness is present, they experience the bliss of meditative concentration. Next, the commentary explains "non-abiding in equanimity."
The path of equality. The first phrase indicates not abiding in a fixed tenet; the subsequent three phrases explain the reason for not abiding.
The initial phrase indicating the tenet can be understood by analogy. "Like the lion's roar" means preaching the Dharma to the assembly by means of the path of non-abiding.

Like the lion king, he roars without fear; one who possesses mastery over all meditative concentrations, though dwelling within birth and death to preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, is not defiled by the faults of birth and death. He is sovereign and unimpeded within dhyāna-concentration.

Even when in hell, it is like the bliss of the third dhyāna; for this reason, it is said that he is "in accord with joy and bliss. The following section explains the attainment of the supreme fruit. First:
The first line explains the method of practice; the subsequent one and a half lines explain the fruit attained. In the pure land of Ghanavyūha, difficult practices cannot be found;
therefore, it says, "seek Ghanavyūha with a single mind. This pure land lies beyond the three realms (*tridhātu*); one must generate the bodhicitta to attain rebirth there.
Thus, it says, "without being stained by attachment to the three realms. The explanation of the method of practice is concluded. Below is:

These two lines explain the fruit of practicing the means; their textual structure is evident. Below, the primary fruit is revealed. The preceding two lines demonstrate the characteristics of attaining that fruit.

Regarding the term "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*) means cessation. Because it transforms and ceases the basis of conditioned change (*pariṇāma*), it is called the "transformation of the basis."

Regarding "attaining peace and happiness": the transformation of the fruit of accomplishment, which is *nirvāṇa* without remainder, from the suffering of change (*pariṇāma-duḥkha*), is termed "peace and happiness.

Being free from the fault of clamor and agitation, it is described as "tranquility" (*śānti*). Because it transcends the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), it is termed "abiding securely" (*susthita*).

Next, there are two phrases: "honored by gods and humans," and below, two further phrases: these indicate the excellence of his station. The textual structure is clear. Thus far has been the praise of the King’s inquiry.

[This concludes the preceding section. From here below, the response addresses the question in the prior prose passage concerning "not following the ways of others. This section consists of two parts.

The first part comprises three lines, which briefly indicate the faults of external schools and concisely demonstrate the correct principle. The second part comprises ten and a half lines, which extensively refute what is grasped by external schools.
Within these three lines of verse, the first line indicates that the tenets of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are flawed and untenable.

The latter two lines briefly demonstrate the correct principle. The phrase "not like the non-Buddhists" expresses the thesis; here, "non-Buddhists" includes the followers of the Two Vehicles as well, who are collectively termed "non-Buddhists.
Therefore, the general negation states: "It is not like the non-Buddhists who claim that the destruction [of existence] constitutes *nirvāṇa*. The non-Buddhists...
The followers of the two vehicles all abide by this teaching that all phenomena exist; through the power of cultivation, they are extinguished and thus become non-existent.

The exhaustion of phenomena, where there is no [further] existence, is called *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, [the opponent] points out the fault: it is identical to the fault of conditioned phenomena dying and being reborn. The outsider objects, saying:
"As for conditioned phenomena, as long as they have not been countered, there is the fault of dying and being reborn. I cultivate the power of the counteragent."
Once dead, one does not return to birth. For this reason, the objection raised is not directed at me; therefore, you raise another objection, saying: "All phenomena are originally non-existent;
they do not become non-existent only upon cessation. Yet, due to your deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*), you claim they become non-existent only upon cessation.

To reckon that which has no existence as existing constitutes one error; to reckon the non-existence of what is already non-existent as further non-existent constitutes a second error. [To reckon] existence...

There is no calculation [of it], because both positions entail faults. To say that it is "the same" as the conditioned existence entails the fault of death and rebirth occurring again. This concludes the explanation of the first passage.
Below are two lines that briefly demonstrate the correct principle; of these, one and a half lines demonstrate the correct reasoning, while the final two phrases [serve as a conclusion].

This concludes the demonstration of the aforementioned faults. Regarding the "ten actions," these refer to the ten paths of wholesome karma; because they constitute the essence of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), they are called the "ten virtues.

Although their substance consists of ten types of action, they are divided into three grades according to the strength or weakness of the mind. There are distinctions among the three vehicles (*triyāna*); within these three vehicles, [the following applies].
The Bodhisattva is supreme; only one who is supreme cultivates the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) until their practice is perfected and attains the fruit of the three bodies (*trikāya*).

Therefore, it is said that they attain the wisdom of liberation and the subtle body of a Tathāgata. Below this, the faults are summarized, as the text clearly indicates. The first section, which constitutes the explanation, is concluded.

From here on is the second section, which restates the opponent's thesis and refutes it extensively. This consists of three parts. The first part comprises five lines, which restate the external [opponent's] position.
