There is no external object that can be traversed. This is demonstrated below by means of analogies; it may be understood accordingly. Below there is one line which exhorts one to know and provides a concluding indication.

The first two phrases exhort one to know; the latter two phrases provide the concluding indication. As for the phrase "these three," they refer to the three preceding analogies. Regarding the statement "all are manifestations of consciousness":
these three phenomena are the aspects of the perceived (nimitta) and the perceiving (darśana) that arise within manifesting consciousness; there is nothing else.
Regarding the remaining dharmas, it is therefore proclaimed that all are manifestations of consciousness. This is the exhortation to know; what follows is the concluding demonstration.
As for "this place of remoteness," there are three places called the place of remoteness. It is called "the ultimate reality" because it is the final limit of dharmas, which is suchness (*tathatā*).
Because it cannot be destroyed, it is named "ultimate reality. The preceding section, responding to the difficulties, has concluded its detailed explanation.

From here below is the sixth section, which praises the Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha). It consists of three parts. The first part, comprising seven lines, praises the Land of Secret Adornment. The next two lines praise the Teacher.
The final two and a half lines praise the excellence of the inhabitants and the excellence of their dwelling place. Within the first of these, there are two sub-sections:
the first one and a half lines consist of the disciples praising its excellence, and the subsequent five and a half lines consist of the Buddhas praising its excellence. Specifically:
Regarding "Viseṣacintī and others": among the assembly of bodhisattvas, those with preeminent supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) are called Viseṣacintī;
these are bodhisattvas from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward. As for "and Ārya-Maudgalyāyana," this refers to the foremost in supernormal powers within the Śrāvaka vehicle.
These two individuals are such that no one among the Buddha’s disciples can surpass them. Even when surveying the lands of the ten directions, none exceed the *Ghanavyūha* [Pure Land].
The Disciples finished their lamentation. Because the various Buddhas below [in the worlds] then praised him themselves, it is clearly known that he is the most supreme.

The text is divided into two parts: first, one line and one phrase, where the Buddhas of the ten directions and others speak words of truth in praise; second, four lines and one phrase, which extol his virtues.
The initial statement refers to the Land of Ultimate Bliss, the Land of Immeasurable Life, as well as the Manifest Joy, also named Wondrous Joy (*Abhirati*). This is...
The world of Abhirati in the eastern direction transcends even the lower realms; therefore, it is said "even unto.

In such a land, the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges all speak of their own accord, declaring that the Land of Secret Adornment (Guhyasamāja) is supreme. This is an exaltation of its virtues through a downward comparison, which consists of two sections.

The first has two lines, concerning the virtue of self-benefit; the latter, from "desiring" onwards, concerns the virtue of benefiting others. Its external appearance is solemn and majestic, leading those who are guided by it.

I prostrate before this majestic transformation. Such majesty does not come into being for the first time through cultivation; it is spontaneously perfected from the beginning. Therefore, it is called "natural" (*svayambhū*).
Without beginning and without end, such a Pure Land has, from the very outset, been the Pure Land inhabited solely by the Dharmakāya Buddha.
Ordinary beings have never been born in that land; therefore, it is said that from the time of the Tathāgata’s original ground onward, various textual signs appear, through which this may be known.
The explanation of self-benefit is concluded. Regarding the section below on the Buddha-activities within the desire realm, this explains the virtue of benefiting others:

it means that when all Buddhas appear in the world within the desire realm, they do so by coming from Ghanavyūha to transform sentient beings. Although these transformations are immeasurable, they do not depart from Ghanavyūha.

Because it strictly establishes fundamental right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*), it is said that one "always relies upon right concentration. The remainder of the text may be understood accordingly. The preceding section concludes the praise of the land.
From here on is the second part: the praise of the teaching that can be expounded. Within this, first there is the praise of this teaching as superior to other teachings;

subsequently, from "O Benevolent Kings" onwards, there is the exhortation to make offerings. The initial passage is further divided into two parts. First, there is one line praising this sūtra among all sūtras.
The [verse concerning] his mother follows, consisting of two lines that no other sutra can surpass; this is evident. Below, the exhortation to make offerings is also clear from the text.

Having concluded the praise of the one who can preach the teaching, the third section follows: because the inhabitants are superior, their land is also exceptionally sublime. Within this, [the text continues]:
The first line states that after having emerged from the three realms, one dwells in reliance upon the Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha); thus, one knows it to be a preeminent place.

The subsequent one and a half lines state that the palaces of this land surpass those of other places, and that all Buddhas and Tathāgatas constantly abide therein; thus, one knows it to be a superior place.
The textual characteristics are explicit and need not be elaborated further.
From here on, the seventh section consists of twenty-one lines concerning the various bodies manifested by the Tathāgata; this answers the previous inquiry regarding the "body of verbal expression.
It is divided into three parts. The first one and a half lines concern the boundless physical forms manifested by the Tathāgata.

The next seventeen and a half lines specifically clarify the various distinctions of what is manifested. The final two lines exhort one to cultivate the causes for rebirth in that land. Regarding the first part:

the upper half concerns the supremacy of remaining in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Because there is no distinction between entering and emerging while abiding in concentration, it is called "unsurpassed" (*anuttara*).
The subsequent two lines concern the arising of function within concentration. As for the "inconceivable concentration," it is constantly present within the mundane.

While performing these activities, he does not lose his meditative concentration. Therefore, Vimalakīrti said: "To manifest dignified deportment without arising from the samādhi of cessation—this is called sitting in meditation.
The second couplet below concerns the forms and other phenomena thus manifested, which ordinary and inferior persons cannot comprehend; this is evident in the text.

From here below is the second section, consisting of seventeen and a half lines, which specifically clarifies that which is manifested. Within this, there are seven subsections: first, five and a half lines indicating the various marks and forms;
second, one line indicating the inconceivable power; third, one line concerning the primary subject’s gathering and transforming of beings;
fourth, three and a half lines indicating the manifestation of preaching the Dharma; fifth, one and a half lines indicating the cultivation of the various perfections.
[The text continues with] the practice. Sixth, through two lines [of verse], it is shown that the physical forms of the people in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are perfectly complete.

Seventh, through three lines, it is shown that they possess mastery over the material requisites for their enjoyment. The first section further divides into two parts. First, there is one line which provides an explanation according to ultimate reality, showing that the physical characteristics of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas in the Land of Ultimate Bliss are all identical.
Subsequently, for four and a half lines, [it is shown how beings] each perceive [the Buddha] differently according to the depth or shallowness of their respective faculties.

The same applies here. Why is it that other pure lands (*śuddhakṣetra*) are not mentioned, but only the Western Pure Land? What is the reason for this? The answer is: It would be no harm to mention other pure lands as well;
however, because we follow the method of "abbreviated mutual illustration" (*chāyā-saṃkṣepa-anyonya-vāda-mukha*), we cite Sukhāvatī for now.
Furthermore, why is it that Ghanavyūha is not praised, but only Sukhāvatī? What is the intention behind this? The answer is: [Ghanavyūha is] the pure land of Ghanavyūha...
The "land" refers to the fundamental land; all the pure lands of the various directions rely upon the Ghanavyūha (Dense Array). This is as explained above.
In this present passage, however, only the various lands manifested from beginning to end are praised, and for this reason, the Ghanavyūha itself is not praised.
Those who practice contemplation—referring to Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and others—are called practitioners of contemplation. Their physical forms and characteristics are likewise...
"However, they are the same. This means that Amitābha Buddha and all the bodhisattvas are each fully endowed with the thirty-two marks;
therefore, it says, "all are likewise. In the subsequent detailed explanation, the first two and a half lines explain the various different perceptions of a single Buddha.
Thereafter, there are two lines concerning how different things are seen within the bodies of the bodhisattvas.

Regarding the vision of the Buddha, some see the Buddha’s body fully endowed with all the marks (*lakṣaṇa*). Therefore, it is proclaimed: "Some see the God among Gods, resplendent and imbued with manifold colors.
Within this, some see a single color, or they see two colors—meaning those who see only the color *hāridra* (yellow), or see *hāridra*..."
In Rājagṛha there were two colors; thus it continued until they saw all various forms.
There was one class who saw the ascetic’s body wearing tattered rags and lying upon a bed of grass; another class saw him like the light of a thousand suns sitting upon a lotus flower.
Thus there were such diverse visions of a single Buddha-body. From here on, for two lines, there are various differences regarding the body of the Bodhisattva.
They see it. Regarding the term "Indranīla" (Indra-blue): "Indra" refers to Śakra, the King of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; the blue jewel belonging to him is called "Indranīla.
Below this is a line [of description]: they see the body of the Bodhisattva. Among them, one class sees the body as being like a wheel;
another class sees the body as being like a banner; some see it as being like written characters; or another class sees it as being like a fish, a conch, and so forth. Or there are some...
A certain class [of beings] saw the Bodhisattva’s radiant and beautiful color like a rainbow trailing through the sky; they saw the Bodhisattva’s single body as being different [from others].
Having finished describing the manifested colors, the following line clearly shows his inconceivable power.

The next line describes the ceremonial protocol for acting as a king among men to govern and transform [the world], which can be understood by analogy. From here below, three and a half lines describe what was seen.
The teaching of the Dharma to deliver sentient beings also has different meanings. Within this, there are three sections. The first line speaks of the "objective realm" (*viṣaya*);
"white" refers to pure color, and "white" carries the sense of being clear, bright, and distinct. The objective realm of the Two Truths known by the Buddhas of the past is called the "white realm.
Next is one line, which speaks of transforming the supporting body to attain a body with illusory-like supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*). The final one and a half lines...
These various passages describe the practice of severing afflictions and realizing nirvāṇa; their textual characteristics are all manifest and need not be explained at length.
From here on, for one and a half lines, the cultivation of various practices is shown. Regarding "all pāramitās," there are briefly three kinds:
first, the six pāramitās; second, the ten pāramitās; third, the thirty-eight thousand four hundred pāramitā-gates, as in the *Bhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna*.

The *Kalpa-sūtra* states that "yan-na" (yāna) means "unrestricted" (*asaṃvara*). It refers to making offerings to all who come without any discrimination; thus it is called "unrestricted. This constitutes the practice of giving (*dāna*).
Following the sections on asceticism and the observance of precepts, the text clarifies the cultivation of miscellaneous practices, the meaning of which is likewise evident.
The two lines below clarify the primary attachments experienced by those in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Within these, the first line explains the retribution of the people of Ultimate Bliss.
It is supreme. Thereafter follows one line which no one in other worlds can equal. The initial passage is easy to understand.

As for the term "yoga," this translates as "correspondence" (*saṃprayoga*), and is also called "contemplative practice" (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). In mastery of contemplative practice, he is such that even those like Maudgalyāyana cannot equal him.
Furthermore, regarding the people of other realms, such as the Land of Peace and Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) and the Land of Radiance (*Prabhāsvarā*): [the people] of such lands...
There is a common realm [of experience], yet compared to the objects known by those in Sukhāvatī, it does not equal even one hundredth part.

Such a calculation can also be understood from the text. From here on, the next three lines explain the articles of enjoyment experienced by those in Sukhāvatī; among these, the first line is as follows:
The first row contains provisions for the body and utensils for food; next is a row where one enjoys inexhaustible bliss through wish-fulfilling jewels;
and in the final row, there are lotus flowers in the pond of incomparable adornment. The remaining text is fully present; it may be understood by comparison. As for the term "Muni":
This refers to "quiescence. Regarding the "supreme lords," this names the assembly of Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara and others.

In the following two lines, there is an exhortation for all people [to practice]. Within that, the first line exhorts them to demonstrate the practice to be cultivated and shows the benefits obtained thereby.
Within the first passage, the upper phrase exhorts faith and practice; the next phrase exhorts the cultivation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); and next...
The first line exhorts the practice of aspiration; the next line exhorts the practice of dedication.
As explained above, by means of these four practices of the cause, one attains rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. The benefits thereby obtained are evident from the textual analysis.
The preceding section concludes the explanation with verses.
From here below begins the prose section. The Bodhisattva Vajragarbha manifested his own body and preached the Dharma for the assembly.
Although he had previously expounded various teachings for the multitude, those present might fear that they would not believe him;
they might harbor doubts and say: "What has been thus spoken is merely words; the reality of the matter is not seen. Is it truly so, or not? Because of such doubts, Vajra...
The Tathāgata manifested his own body and preached the Dharma for the sake of the assembly, so that they would decisively believe and accept what was taught;
thus this text comes forth. It consists of two sections: first, from "At that time" up to "and preached the Dharma," which briefly indicates the fundamental tenet (*mūla*);

second, from "Alternatively, he preaches for Bodhisattvas" onwards, which provides an extensive explanation based on that tenet. The first section further has three parts: first, the manifestation of the subtle and minute...
The body. Next, after manifesting the Buddha-body, he manifests a great body; subsequently, he expounds the Dharma, preaching it for the sake of the assembly.
Such passages can be clearly understood through their characteristics. The explanation of the first passage is concluded.

down to "...are eternally unchanging," it explains the practice of realization (*praveśa-pratipatti*). 2. From "Some say that bodhisattvas... down to "...surrounded by a retinue," it explains the practice of conforming to existence (*anuvartana-pratipatti*).
3. From "Some say that bodhisattvas... down to "...those who do not practice contemplation cannot perceive them," [it explains the difficulty of perception].
"Those who say that bodhisattvas manifest various bodies to serve various Buddhas;
or those who say that bodhisattvas, down to those who have entered parinirvāṇa, manifest birth-bodies in the lands of the ten directions and attain parinirvāṇa;
or those who say that bodhisattvas, down to those who are like the sun or the moon, do not abide in the practice of the path."
Fifth, some say that Bodhisattvas do not remain stationary for even a single moment;

this explains that because Bodhisattvas take pity on sentient beings with a heart of great compassion, they do not retreat from the suffering of birth and death, but preach the Dharma for the sake of the multitude.

Sixth, some say "the Buddhas" and below; this explains that for the sake of sentient beings whose minds are disordered by perversion, Bodhisattvas teach the doctrine of regression according to what is appropriate for them.

Regarding the method of cultivation, the first section further divides into three parts. First, from "Entering into all stages" down to "the two kinds of selflessness," it explains the phenomena to be observed.
Second, from "Attaining the illusion-like samādhi" down to "all are non-retrogressive," it explains the virtues to be accomplished.
Third, from "Purifying the basis" down to "permanently without change," it explains the meaning of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). As for the "illusion-like samādhi":
Mastery over transformations is like an illusion or a magical creation. That which assumes a body at will is the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).

The eight kinds of mastery are called "mastery. All other textual passages may be understood as they appear. From this point downward, the second section explains the practice according to existence, which also has three parts.
First, from the passage beginning with "skillfully" down to "the path to be traversed," it explains the objects of contemplation.
Second, from "attaining Śūraṅgama" down to "none fail to achieve fulfillment," this refers to the virtues accomplished through practice.

Third, from "reaching perfect enlightenment" down to "surrounded by [a retinue]," this refers to the attainment of the fruit of Great Bodhi. Regarding "Śūraṅgama," this is translated as "Samādhi of Valiant Practice.
The "ten illusory-like bodies" are as explained above. The "ten mind-born bodies" refer to the ultimate vows.
Briefly, there are three kinds: first, severing all evil; second, cultivating all goodness; third, delivering all sentient beings.
In detail, they are immeasurable, as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. The remaining text is easy to understand. From here below is the third section:
manifesting various forms to serve successive Buddhas. This further has two parts: first, "by the power of vows" down to "serving successive Buddhas."
It is taught that these bodhisattvas manifest bodies with sovereign mastery to make offerings to all Buddhas;
subsequently, it is taught that even those bodhisattvas who are unable to perceive them manifest bodies free from the marks of existence and non-existence. Regarding "by the power of vows":
the perfection of vows is called "vows. By means of this perfection of vows, the bodhisattva manifests various forms and proceeds to the ten directions to make offerings.
Nurturing all Buddhas. The body manifested below is free from the marks of existence and non-existence. First the Dharma, then the analogy. The textual manifestation of the Dharma teaching is clear;
within the analogy there are two parts: first the analogy, then the application (the *yōga*). The textual characteristics are evident.

The preceding section presents the Dharma, followed by the analogy; both may be understood accordingly. From here below is the sixth [section], which explains the remedial teachings as appropriate for sentient beings whose minds are deranged by various inversions.
This text is further divided into two parts: first, the teaching through the Dharma itself; second, the citation of analogies as illustrations.
Regarding "thirsting craving" (*tṛṣṇā*): it refers to the affliction of sensual greed that can never be satisfied, like a parched person who knows no contentment.

Regarding "discriminative suffering" (*parikalpita-duḥkha*): it refers to the scattering and drifting of the mind, which is difficult to restrain; for this reason, it is called discriminative suffering.

First, the great assembly asks; subsequently, Vajragarbha answers. Regarding the inquiry, there are three parts: first, the listing of the inquiring assembly;

second, from "Having heard the teaching of the *Ghanavyūha*" down to "and thus bring about benefit," which explains the intent behind the questions; third, from "Then, with one mind, they addressed Vajragarbha" onwards, which constitutes the actual words of the inquiry.
Within the listing of the inquiring assembly, the "Constantly Attendant Assembly" is explained first; this refers to the assembly of Samantabhadra.
The Bodhisattvas of the ten realms, such as the Bodhisattva Mahāprabha, are listed first; next, the assembly of devas is listed;

next, the assembly of the sons of the Buddhas from Ghanavyūha is listed; and finally, the assembly from other directions who have come to hear the teaching is listed. These various passages are all clearly manifest and can be understood.
Next, the meaning of the question is explained. The text consists of two sections. The first presents what [the author] himself understands;

the second, beginning with "However, out of compassion for all," explains that the question is asked for the sake of others. Generally, there are four types of questions: first, asking despite already knowing the answer; second, asking to disturb or vex others;
third, asking because one has doubts and wishes to reach a definitive resolution; and fourth, asking with the desire to benefit others. Now...
In this passage, the question is posed both to resolve one's own doubts and to benefit others.
From here on is the third section: the actual formulation of the questions. This consists of three parts: first, a brief inquiry using a simile;

second, from "For the sake of the Yāma devas" down to "Is there a dwelling place?", which extensively explains the simile in relation to the Dharma through specific details; and third, from "Or some might say... onwards.
The citation of examples concludes the inquiry. The first section further contains three parts: first, a general investigation of the origin;
second, a request for instruction using the analogy of a potter molding clay;
and third, the formal inquiry to resolve doubts, beginning with "In this way, the world... Regarding the first part, the term "Venerable One" is used to praise the person being questioned.
"Since you possess supreme merit, I pray that you will speak for me"—this is the request that he grant his consent. "Please explain this by means of the Dharma"—this is the formal entreaty.
Below, he provides illustrative analogies; there are three types of analogies.

First is the analogy of the potter, which illustrates the seven kinds of false conceptualizations regarding the distinctions among the heavens, from the Yāma heaven down to the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu). Second is the analogy of the actor.

In the section on the specific analogies for questioning, from "all these lords of devas" down to "like the water of a mirage," there is the analogy of the three self-natures (trisvabhāva) within a single entity.

In the section on the specific analogies for questioning, from "for example, in the case of a jar" down to "the accumulation of various qualities," there is first the analogy of the potter, which illustrates the calculations of Brahmā and others.
Regarding the original calculation of the non-Buddhists, it says: "The Great Brahmā..."
"Lord": [The opponent claims] that a Lord can create the world, just as a potter creates [his wares].

When creating, he must necessarily rely on the dharmas of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), just as one relies upon a lump of clay to produce vessels, jars, or small objects. Regarding the analogy of the actors:

the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) calculate that when the world is formed, there is no single Lord capable of producing all phenomena; rather, all phenomena act together to produce a single phenomenon. Thus they speak of "all phenomena."

This refers to the time when the self (ātman), mind (manas), mental faculty (manendriya), contact (sparśa), attention (manaskāra), form (rūpa), light (āloka), space (ākāśa), and so forth, come together in combination, and only then does the eye arise;
for there is not a single dharma that can act as a sovereign producer on its own. Regarding the claim that a single entity possesses three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva):
the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) calculate that every single thing is endowed with the three natures, just as all [three] exist within a single jar.
An atom is a substantial entity (*dravya*). It is narrow at the neck and broad at the belly; it has an opening that is blocked at the bottom. It is the locus upon which qualities (*guṇa*) depend.
When filled with water, it does not overflow; this is what is called a quality. Thus, a single object possesses these three intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*).

Therefore, the great assembly cited the calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) and asked the Buddha, the Tathāgata: "Is the world as it is conceived by these non-Buddhists the same [as your teaching], or is it not?"
It is so. Within the first analogy, there is first the illustration and then the application to the Dharma; the textual form of the illustration is evident.
"The various images in the world" refers to the subject matter (*dharmin*). The two subsequent pairs of interlocking inquiries determine the cause of the world, as can be understood from the text.
In the second analogy, there is first the illustration and then the censure. "Is it not also thus with all the world?"—this is the censure.

The particle *qǐ* (how could it be? is a term of censure; it does not concern the act of establishing [a position]. Within the third analogy, there is first the illustration and then the censure. The censure says:
"Regarding worldly objects that have already attained their substantial form and characteristics, I shall provisionally grant your point for the sake of censure.

As for what you now establish—that a single entity possesses all three natures—if this has already been established, I may provisionally allow it. However, [the text] subsequently refutes it by saying: 'If it has not yet been established, then this...'"

How could it possibly be established within a single entity? The preceding section has concluded the brief inquiry by means of analogies. Second, from "For the sake of all these lords of the heavens" downward, it uses the analogy of the musician to the phenomena being illustrated, followed by specific and extensive inquiries.
Third, from "For example, as with a jar" downward, it [uses the analogy] according to all things...
The analogy is explained through detailed and specific inquiries. Within the initial section, there are three parts:
first, from "descending from the Yāma Heaven" down to "the Kinnaras," it asks whether those who possess great power within the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*) are capable of creating worldly objects.
Second, from "Is it for this reason? down to "the Brahmā Śikhin," it concerns the various devas of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) acting as the primary agents.
Can they create all things in the world? The gods of the three formless realms act as the masters; can they create all things in the world?

Is it like a potter who can create jars and the like? The meaning of the text is clear. From here on, the second section concerns the capacity to create with the gods of the form realm as the masters.
Within this, there are two parts: first, Subhūti and others represent the fourth dhyāna; second, the Brahmā Śikhin.

"The King" refers to the Heavenly King of the First Dhyāna. From here downward to the third section, it concerns how the various devas of the Formless Realm (ārūpyadhātu) are able to create all manner of things.

The explanation of the first section is hereby concluded. From here downward is the second section, which uses the metaphor of a musician to illustrate the dharma being illustrated, through specific and extensive inquiries.

The text further has two parts. The first concerns how the various powerful worldly devas, acting with a common mind, create all worldly objects—much like performers collaborating to produce music.
The second concerns that which is produced through the transformations of supramundane Buddhas and Bodhisattvas;

this is clearly visible in the text. Having concluded the section describing these views, the following portion reveals their errors and demonstrates the correct position. Within this context, [various] misconceptions arise...
"Deluded" indicates the fault. This deluded view, which perceives things like water in a mirage, demonstrates the principle of the primary causes and conditions.
What was previously refuted was the notion that one person acts as the master while others merely assist;
what is now clarified is that there is no single fixed master, but rather all people act together. The second analogy concludes above; from here below is the third analogy.
Regarding the dharma that serves as the analogy: herein, first is the analogy, followed by the restatement of the position held by the opponent.

For example, "the locus of the jar being the substratum for its qualities" is the analogy cited by the opponent; the capacity to hold water is termed a "quality," and the collection of atoms is termed the "locus of the jar.
Below is the formal application (*dharmanirdeśa*) restating that opponent's position, which consists of two sections. The first restates the opponent’s thesis.
"Those who do not possess any qualities," down to "those who have accumulated a multitude of qualities," refutes what is conceived by outsiders.
Regarding the phrase "all those in the world who abide in a locus": "abiding" means relying upon, and "locus" refers to atoms (*paramāṇu*).

This should thus be stated as: "All those in the world rely upon atoms. This cites the false thesis established by the outsider; below this, the text refutes the outsider's conception, stating: [text follows].
The term "possessor of qualities" (*guṇin*) refers to the category of the real entity (*dravya*). The term "qualities" (*guṇa*) refers to the category of qualities themselves.

The opponent maintains that the categories of the real entity, action (*karman*), and so forth are necessarily the substrata (*āśraya*), while the category of qualities is the dependent (*āśrita*). Therefore, the present refutation states: it is not the case that the categories of the real entity and so forth are necessarily subsumed under qualities.

Nor is it the case that the attributes (guṇa) are fixedly dependent upon the substance (dravya) and so forth. Therefore, it is said that the various attributes do not belong to the attributes, nor do the attributes depend upon the attributes.

This leads to the following doubt: the opponent raises an objection, asking, "If one does not conceive of the self as the substratum (āśraya) of the attributes, and the attributes as the superstrata (āśrita), how can the distinction between the superstratum and the substratum be established?"

Regarding these characteristics, such doubts arise; therefore, it is explained through a general principle: because they are joined in succession, the various virtues are collectively established. "Joining" means relying upon one another;
the virtues are provisionally accumulated through mutual dependence, and there is no fixed entity that serves as either the support or the supported.

The preceding section has concluded the detailed inquiry into specific points. From here on is the second part: restating the externalist calculations and questioning them to determine that they are not [correct]. Thus, the world...

The preceding section, beginning with "In the meantime," restates the opponent's position and is thus easy to understand. What follows is the definitive inquiry, which examines the matter through two alternatives: Is it merely a state of delusion?
Or is it that the inverted, false conceptualization of the discriminating mind is ultimately non-existent? Or does it have a basis of existence?
That is, is it something produced from causes and conditions that exists rather than being non-existent? This concludes the text of the definitive inquiry.
From here below is the third section, which cites examples to conclude the inquiry. This section consists of three parts:

first, from "Or perhaps" down to "arising through ignorance, craving, and karma," the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are set forth; second, from "The celestial seers and others" down to "all harbor doubts," examples are cited to give rise to doubt;
third, from "Because there is no substantial entity" onwards, the conclusion is reached with the definitive statement. Within the first part, furthermore—
Two parts: first, an account of the calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); second, from "ignorance, craving, and karma" downward, an account of the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*).

Within the citation of the non-Buddhist calculations, first is the account of the calculation that a person (*pudgala*) can create all phenomena; subsequently, from "or there are those who falsely cling," is the calculation that phenomena themselves can create.

Within the calculation of a person's creation, three heavens are briefly mentioned, though in reality they are numerous, such as the *ṛṣi*, *kāśyapa*, and others. These represent people of worldly wisdom; by analogy, it refers to [the aforementioned].

This can be understood. Regarding the passage beginning with "Or there are those who falsely cling... and so forth: it calculates that dharmas are capable of acting as creators. A detailed discussion of this would involve many dharmas;
however, as we are currently preserving only a brief summary, we shall cite three dharmas, which may be understood according to the text. Regarding the calculations of the Hīnayāna below:

the Hīnayāna calculation states that ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and karma (*karman*) definitely act as causes and conditions to produce all dharmas. It further calculates that the delusions regarding the *tathāgatagarbha* and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) are capable of acting as creators.
It is like water forming waves. Therefore, we now refute this by stating that ignorance, craving, and karma merely act as conditions for the arising of all phenomena;

they cannot establish the essence [of those phenomena], because the essence of phenomena is precisely the nature of dependent origination. Having concluded the exposition of the externalist views, the second section follows below.
Citing examples to raise a doubt: "The various devas" refers to the devas of the three realms; "seers" (ṛṣis) refers to those who have attained the five supernormal powers through cultivation;
"and so forth" includes the eight classes of supernatural beings (*aṣṭa-nikāya*) who possess great physical power, as well as those who have cultivated worldly meditative concentrations among humans.
Such individuals among the wise of the world may exhaust all their efforts in contemplation, yet they never fully comprehend [the nature of reality].
They understand the Tathāgatagarbha mind as the functioning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). For this reason, it is said that they all harbor doubts.

Having concluded the citation of examples to generate doubt, the third section follows, which provides the formal conclusion of the inquiry. First the principle (*dharma*), then the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding the statement "because there is no substantial entity":

the teaching of the principle is presented directly, meaning that all phenomena are the dependent origination of the true mind; they appear to exist but do not exist. Therefore, they are said to be non-existent.
"Does it have a substantial reality? Below, he provides analogies. There are nine analogies, which are grouped into five sections.
The first four analogies illustrate that although all phenomena appear to exist similarly, when sought through ultimate analysis, they are ultimately unfindable.

Next, there is one analogy illustrating that the perceived object (*nimitta*) and the seeing consciousness (*darśana*) are originally of one essence, with consciousness as their substance; it is only due to beginningless false discrimination that they suddenly [appear as distinct].
The arising of the two types of discrimination—of seeing and of appearance—is like a snake that has a single body yet possesses two heads, each performing its own distinct function.
Next are two analogies illustrating how all phenomena revolve according to causes and conditions and do not arise or perish of their own accord.

Following this is one analogy illustrating how all phenomena exist within the deluded mind and are fundamentally non-existent upon awakening. Finally, there is one analogy illustrating the impermanence of all phenomena.
It does not remain; it perishes in every moment. The above concludes the summary of the preceding inquiry through correct reasoning.

Having finished the explanation of the question, what follows below is the answer to that question. Within this, the thirty-seven verses are divided into two main parts; the first consists of two verses.
To refute the false attachments of outsiders, there follow thirty-five lines of verse that demonstrate correct principles and cause one to abandon those false attachments.

This initial section is further divided into two parts. The first one and a half lines refute the false calculations of outsiders; the subsequent two lines show that the teachings upon which outsiders rely fail to serve as valid proof.
The former part is again divided into two: the first two lines provide a general refutation of their calculations, while the following line...
This section refutes various speculative views. Within it, the first half refutes the view that a person is the creator. *Kubera* is also called *Kapiṭha*;
this is the name of a ṛṣi, and is also said to be an alternative name for one of the Four Heavenly Kings. *Indra* is another name for the Lord of Devas (Śakra).
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes other such views, which may be understood by analogy. The final two lines of the text refute the notion that those false causes can produce results.
There are two types of false causes: first, the view that one can obtain the fruit of wealth through giving at sacrificial assemblies;

second, the view that one can obtain superior fruits through sacrifices to celestial deities and the like. As worldly people say: "By offering excellent food and flavors, one makes offerings to the various gods."
Furthermore, by making offerings to powerful rishis and others, one obtains excellent fivefold sensual pleasures and enjoys them with sovereignty.

These excellent fivefold sensual pleasures arise because one made offerings to celestial rishis, and they are bestowed by those celestial rishis. Therefore, it is said that these are not the fruits of the merit from great sacrificial assemblies.
The son of heaven in that realm produces the sacrifice from his own body; thus it is called a "great sacrificial assembly. This explains the basis for the following interpretation.
The proof is not established. Regarding what is called the *Veda*: as stated above, the three *Veda* treatises are named *Veda*.
As for the cause they propound, the *Veda* speaks of the *Prakṛti* (Primal Nature). Furthermore, it is said that at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), this treatise was expounded;

[it claims] that the eternal cause can spontaneously produce all phenomena. This is contradictory, as an eternal cause producing an impermanent effect is mutually inconsistent. Therefore, it is taught that [their doctrines] are mutually contradictory.

Definition: This concludes the refutation of the aforementioned false attachments regarding the arising of all phenomena—from the "Primal Nature" (*prakṛti*) acting spontaneously, down to the karma of craving.
Hereafter, the correct [view] is demonstrated, which consists of six sections.
The first, spanning eighteen and a half lines, clarifies that the cause of the world is solely dependent [on conditions].

The first three and a half lines clarify that this is not the same as non-Buddhist doctrines. Next, there are three and a half lines answering the metaphors such as "like an illusion" mentioned in the preceding prose section.
Next, there are three and a half lines answering the question in the preceding section regarding "the various forms and images of this world.

Next, there are three and a half lines answering the passage in the prose section concerning beginningless discrimination involving the grasping subject and the grasped object. Finally, there is one and a half lines answering [the remaining point].
In the preceding inquiry, there were analogies such as the walking corpse (*vetāla*). The subsequent four and a half lines summarize the principle of Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātra.

The initial section further consists of seven parts: first, three lines indicate the causes of the world; second, two and a half lines distance [the teaching] from non-Buddhist views (*tīrthika-dṛṣṭi*).
Third, two and a half lines: only Buddhas and Bodhisattvas know that it exists. Fourth, three and a half lines: following the dharmas it upholds, it flows constantly without ceasing.
Fifth, one and a half lines: the body is not separate from consciousness. Sixth, six and a half lines:
although it can maintain the seed-nature, it undergoes prior transformation. Seventh, two lines: ordinary beings do not know that it exists. The first section has two parts; the first...

The first line establishes the thesis (*pratijñā*), sets forth the essence (*svabhāva*), and provides the name. The subsequent two lines explain the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, it is not that there exists beforehand a causal agent capable of sustaining the world; this constitutes the thesis. "Ālaya" is the designation of the name.

"The consciousness of the Great Being (*puruṣa*)" sets forth its essential nature (*svabhāva*). Among the eight consciousnesses, this consciousness is supreme; therefore, it is called the "Great Being. This is dependent origination.

Within the exposition of the meaning, first comes the principle (*dharma*) and subsequently the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). Regarding "that which moves throughout all things": this refers to the totality of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), which pervades all phenomena (*dharmas*) and exists nowhere it is not present.
This is illustrated by the analogy of water giving rise to waves; within the waves, the water is everywhere and remains below them. Thus, the analogy is introduced.

There are six types of analogies, all of which are evident in the textual form and can be understood accordingly. From here on, the second section concerns the established thesis (*pakṣadharma*), which differs from that of the outsiders (*bāhya*).
The Treatise consists of two sections. The first section comprises one line, which demonstrates that the worldly cause—the ālayavijñāna—is distinct from all the views held by non-Buddhists.
The second section comprises two and a half lines, which demonstrates that it is not [merely] a provisional teaching but the correct principle. Regarding the first section:

the first half refutes the attachments of the non-Buddhists, while the latter two phrases clarify that the ālayavijñāna is free from external false views; the meaning of the text is evident. From here on—

Second, the present passage does not demonstrate the correct principle. Within it, the first half reveals what is not the case, clarifying that the *ālayavijñāna* is not an object of experience for other persons.

The latter half consists of two lines, which demonstrate the correct principle. Regarding the initial text, the phrase "not sought by wisdom" refers to discursive investigation (*vitarka*), conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), the mind of attainment, external mental constructions beyond reason, and the false grasping of boundaries and established positions. Therefore...

It is called "knowledge. Because that which is not understood by such knowledge is therefore proclaimed to be the domain of non-knowledge, it is therefore proclaimed to be realized through internal wisdom.
The following [verse] immediately overturns this by exposing the fault of contradicting reason; the first half is an exposition in terms of phenomena (*dharma*).
The root and the branches are mutually dependent; therefore, it is proclaimed that if the fundamental *ālaya-vijñāna* did not exist, the seven consciousnesses would likewise not exist.
Below is a single line which uses a metaphor to demonstrate the meaning of the relationship between the fundamental and the derivative as being neither identical nor different;
this can be understood by examining the text. From here on is the third section: the subtlety of the *ālaya*, which is not the domain of others, but is known by Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The text consists of two parts. The first, spanning one and a half lines, cites an analogy to demonstrate that [this stream] is not within the domain of other persons.

The latter, consisting of one line, applies the cited analogy. This can be understood according to the text. Below this is the fourth section, which follows the supported dharma as it flows constantly and without ceasing.
The text further consists of three sections. The first line states that it can sustain the world without any loss or failure.
The next line shows that dependent origination can establish phenomena. The final one and a half lines show that the sustained phenomena flow continuously without ceasing.

Within the first line, the initial phrase provides the doctrinal explanation; "ālayavijñāna" is an abbreviated name for the *ālaya*. The middle two phrases provide an analogy to illustrate [the point].
It is shown that just as a pearl has a string threading it so that there is no risk of loss, the Tathāgata possesses two wheels capable of carrying and transporting things;
the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is likewise able to maintain and transport phenomena, turning according to the winds of karma. This concludes the explanation.
This means that according to good and evil karma, one transmigrates within the six realms of existence. The subsequent [verses on] dependent origination establish the phenomena.

The first two lines cite a metaphor to demonstrate this; the latter two lines apply the metaphor to conclude the demonstration. The rest of the text is easily understood. Regarding the *ālayavijñāna* and the various elements (*dhātu*):
the *ālayavijñāna* alone cannot, through dependent origination, produce the phenomena of the world. Likewise, if there were only the various elements, they could not be established. It is as follows:
Water alone cannot produce waves; where there is no water, waves cannot abide. Therefore, the concluding statement says that through combined power, nothing is not accomplished.

The following one and a half lines follow the meaning of the *Anupada Sūtra*, which states that the flow of the secondary [phenomena] is constant and uninterrupted. The two preceding lines [refer to this].

The preceding section explains the teaching through direct exposition. The following line cites an analogy to demonstrate it; the text is clear and may be understood as it stands. This concludes the section on the constant flow following after the secondary [causes].

From the next point, one and a half lines follow: the body does not depart from consciousness. The first line provides the analogy, and the latter half of the line applies it to the subject being illustrated;

the text is clear and may be understood as it stands. From the next point, two and a half lines follow: although it is capable of sustaining the seeds of both the defiled and the pure, its essence is non-existent...
Regarding transformation: therein, the first line explains the meaning of maintaining the seeds, while the subsequent one and a half lines concern the essence which is without transformation.

The first two lines of the initial section are the analogy, and the following two lines are the application; the text is explicit and thus easily understood. Within the section on the unchanging essence, the first line is the analogy.
The latter half of the verse is combined; it may be understood by comparison.

For example, in the seventh section of the text beginning with "Just as the eyes have pupils," it explains that the *ālaya-vijñāna* constantly dwells within the body, yet ordinary fools do not know it exists.

Within this, the first line concerns the fact that the substance of consciousness is ever-present yet unknown to exist; the subsequent line concerns the fact that there is a superior functional capacity yet unrecognized. First, above...

The first half is the simile; the second half is the application of the simile. The textual structure is evident. Regarding the subsequent practice: the first phrase explains the function of being able to maintain; the second phrase is the simile;
the second half of the verse combines them—this may also be understood. Thus far, the explanation of the causes for maintaining the world is concluded.
This is the second section from here on, which provides answers through analogies such as that of an illusion. It consists of three parts: first, one line restates the calculation of the externalist;
next, one line sets forth the method for refuting that calculation; finally, one and a half lines demonstrate the correct principle.

Ordinary fools do not know that the world is like an illusion and lacks inherent existence, yet they give rise to false conceptualizations, such as that cows and other animals possess horns, while rabbits [do not].
They are equal in being without horns. Although there is the entity of non-existence, because one takes what is non-existent to be existent, existence is itself non-existence.
Yet, ordinary beings who see that cows have horns while rabbits have none do not understand that the world is like an illusion or a dream; thus, they perceive existence and cling to non-existence.
Therefore, it is certainly said that one should not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the two dharmas of existence and non-existence.
From here below is the third section, consisting of three and a half lines, which answers the preceding question: "Are these various forms and images of the world merely delusive confusion?
Within this, there are two parts; the first three lines of verse address this from the perspective of the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) by way of causes and conditions.

There are various forms and images; they are not non-existent phenomena as seen by one who is deranged. There are two subsequent lines which state that it is only when the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is realized that the continuity [of these appearances] is severed.
The initial passage further consists of three parts: first, one and a half lines concerning the objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) that give rise to mental factors;
second, two lines regarding the internal, immediate cause (*samanantara-pratyaya*) that gives rise to the perceiving mind; and finally, one line explaining all worldly [phenomena].

Regarding the reason why there is no interruption between [moments], first, the first half of the verse explains that when the mind arises, it necessarily arises in dependence upon an objective referent (*ālambana*).
The final line provides an analogy to demonstrate this: a "whirling firebrand" refers to seeing the flame on a finger-tip as it rotates and forms a circle;
or seeing one's own eyelashes as a "wheel of hair" due to an optical disorder (*timira*). Such things must rely upon what is seen in small increments.
Consciousness arises conditioned by [the storehouse consciousness]; consciousness does not arise of itself. Below are two phrases: [it shows that] worldly phenomena arise from internal seeds.
The first phrase conversely demonstrates the absence of internal seeds. "Lacking" means non-existent; because there is no cause, the fruit does not arise of itself.
For this reason, it is said that "this awakening is itself non-existent. Below is one line which explains the underlying rationale.
If, as stated above, nothing arises without a cause, then from what cause does this productive cause itself arise? Therefore, it is explained:

"The mutual conditioning of names and characteristics has no limit. This means that because names and characteristics are mutually conditioned, they give rise to discursive investigation and conceptualization.
Seeking names and grasping at perceptions arise constantly and without ceasing; therefore, the seeds thus perfumed are likewise without limit.

This constitutes the inexhaustibility of internal and external causes and conditions, which is why the world is never severed. All various conceptualizations that arise together with the mind constitute the continuity of the world;
this is not due to causes alone, but arises by depending upon and taking false mentation as its support. Thus it is said.

There is no interruption; this is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). The preceding section has concluded the discussion on how, according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there are various delusive distinctions based on conditions.
From here, the two following lines demonstrate that it is only when realizing ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) that [delusion] is severed and no longer continues. This concludes the third section.
The fourth section from here below answers the previous question regarding the beginningless conceptualization of the grasper and the grasped. The text is divided into three parts.
The first consists of two lines, which state that because one has lost sight of the principle, mental conceptions arise in vain.

The next consists of one and a half lines, which distinguish the differentiation between the "seeing" and "image" aspects within a single mind. The final line explains the reason for this. Regarding these:
In the initial passage: "all false objects" refers to the five dharmas—names and characteristics—which constitute the false objects. "Proliferation" (prapañca) refers to the discriminating mind.
Because names, characteristics, and discrimination mutually condition one another, they perfume and form seeds, which in turn give rise to the six consciousnesses.
It is said that "various kinds of minds arise. This is truly because all phenomena are solely the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Since beginningless time, due to ignorance and deluded thoughts, one has failed to know the true meaning; [the mind] flows outwardly and scatters, giving rise to the various consciousnesses. For this reason, it is said that "various kinds of minds arise.
The preceding section concludes the discussion on how errors arise from delusion regarding the principle. From here on, for one and a half lines, [the text] divides [the mind] within a single mind.

Regarding "seeing" (*darśana-bhāga*) and "appearance" (*nimitta-bhāga*): that which is called the "grasper" (*grāhaka*) is the seeing-portion of the mind; that which is called the "grasped" (*grāhya*) is the appearance-portion, the objective field (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the "self-nature of the mind" (*cittasvabhāva*): this refers to the self-substance-portion (*svābhāvika-bhāga*). The fourth [aspect] reveals consciousness, which is named the self-nature of the mind;

it means that from within the self-substance-portion of this revealing consciousness, the two portions of seeing and appearance suddenly arise, as well as objects of enjoyment such as jars, garments, and so forth. Thus it is said.
Phenomena (dharma), apart from their own intrinsic nature, cannot be found as something distinct. Therefore, it is said that "apart from mind, nothing exists.
There are two ways to explain the meaning of "apart from mind": one explanation states that if one examines consciousness, the phenomena described therein cannot be established as existing.
There is another interpretation: if one is separated from the true mind, there are no separate dharmas outside of the mind;
therefore, it is taught that nothing exists apart from the mind. Here, "apart" (li) means "non-existent. The following two lines conclude the point that nothing exists apart from the mind.
The subsequent line explains the reason for this: because, according to the preceding text, all things—both the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived—are entirely non-existent.
The opponent raises a doubt, saying: "If it is as stated above, how can there be a distinction between the subject (the grasper) and the object (the grasped)?

Therefore, [the author] now provides a general explanation, stating that the nature of the grasper and the grasped naturally evolves in this way. "Nature" (*svabhāva*) refers to the self-substance (*svabhāga*) of manifesting consciousness (*vijñapti*).

"Naturally" (*svataḥ*) is also called "suddenly" (*akasmāt*); it means that prior to the manifesting consciousness, the aspects of seeing and form did not yet exist, yet because they gradually become coarse, they reach the stage of manifestation.

At the time of consciousness, it suddenly divides into the two parts of the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*). Since these two parts originally have no self-nature (*svabhāva*), they are said to be "spontaneous" (*svayambhū*).
This spontaneity does not mean that they arise without a cause. Furthermore, a doubt may arise: "If phenomena are thus, why do ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles not know this?
Therefore, it is explained: "The mind is agitated and turbid by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*); the foolish and ignorant cannot see [it]. This concludes the fourth section above.
The section concludes.
Below this is the fifth [section], which answers the question from the previous inquiry regarding the movement of a *vetāla* (reanimated corpse). The text consists of two parts:
the first two lines cite a metaphor to illustrate the point; the subsequent line of text applies it to that which is being illustrated—namely, that the Tathāgatagarbha cannot arise of its own accord.
Thus, all phenomena arise from causes and conditions; they cannot arise by themselves, just as a corpse can only move through the power of a mantra.
This serves as the analogy for the manifestation of the textual marks. In the subsequent application (*upanaya*), the first half of the verse corresponds to the arising of the essence of the mind.

The second half [of the verse] sets forth the distinctions in the functional activity of consciousness; these are all clearly manifested in the textual phrasing. Thus concludes the preceding explanation of how the Tathāgatagarbha, following conditions, arises as the various phenomena of the mundane world.
From here below is the sixth section, which concludes by demonstrating the principle of Mahāyāna Vijñaptimātra (Cognition-Only). This consists of three parts.

First, there is one verse explaining why the Tathāgatagarbha is the basis of all phenomena (*dharma*). Second, there are two and a half verses clarifying why a single mind is divided into the two aspects of the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*).
Finally, there are two verses concerning the principle of Vijñaptimātra as the domain of the Noble Ones (*ārya*), which is not accessible to others.
Regarding the objective realm (*viṣaya*): the first half of the first verse demonstrates this by means of an analogy.

Although the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) lacks the discrimination of "this" and "that," it can serve as the universal basis for all phenomena. The latter two lines should be understood as the application of the analogy.

From here on is the second section: within a single mind, it is divided into two parts. The first one and a half lines demonstrate this by means of an analogy, and the final line applies it; this is the application.
Regarding the statement in the text that "this is the mind," there are two different interpretations. One interpretation explains it as follows: "This mind" refers to the *tathāgatagarbha* mind.
As for "its objective sphere," it is because this is an object constituted by the dependent origination of the true mind;

therefore, it is called the objective sphere of words. There is yet another interpretation: the "seeing-part" (*darśana-bhāga*) is called the mind, while the "image-part" (*nimitta-bhāga*) is called the objective sphere. These two...

The commentary on "attaining both" states: That which is universally present throughout the three realms and consists merely of the dualistic discrimination of the perceived and the perceiver is the dharma of ordinary beings within the three realms.
Because the noble ones only realize the principle of the single flavor, they do not perceive the distinctions or boundaries between the perceived and the perceiver.

Therefore, it is said that [consciousness] pervades the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). From here on, the two following lines concern the profound principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (representation-only), which is realized by the noble ones (*ārya*).
The foregoing concludes the response to the question. Although there have been various textual variations above, the general explanation of the second cycle of questions and answers is now complete.
From here below is the third section of questions and answers, which extensively elucidates the merits of the Pure Land of Ghanavyūha.
It is divided into two parts: first, the general question and brief answer; second, the specific questions and detailed answers from within the assembly at that time. The first part has two sections:
first, from "At that time" down to "I pray that the Honored One will expound it," the great assembly poses their questions; second, from "Vajragarbha" onwards, the brief answer is given.
The preceding inquiry consists of two parts. First, Vajragarbha emits light to gather and sustain the future assembly of the Sahā world.
Second, from "At that time, the sons of the Buddha" onwards, it clarifies how the great assembly present within the Ghanavyūha requests him to preach the Dharma.
The first of these sections also has two parts: first, Vajragarbha emits light to reach those who are spiritually receptive; second, from "Those sons of the Buddha" onwards...

Seeking to go to Ghanavyūha, the first section further divides into three parts: first, the meditative concentration as the basis; second, the phenomena manifested within the light (beginning with "Next, he saw immeasurable...");
and third, the actual emission of light (beginning with "After arising from that concentration...").

Within the first part, the phrase "having finished speaking these words" concludes the preceding section, while "sitting in silence" refers to what follows. "Abiding in no fixed location" demonstrates the characteristic of being free from faults.
The Bodhisattva abides in suchness (*tathatā*), free from the faults of the two extremes of "this" and "that," and does not cling to either extreme, but always dwells in the Middle Way;
therefore, it is called the subtle and wondrous dhyāna. Regarding the phrase "roaming the gateway of the dharmadhātu": the dharmadhātu is the true suchness dharmadhātu (*tathatā-dharmadhātu*).
It possesses two meanings: first, the meaning of support (*āśraya*); second, the meaning of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Because it has the function of support, it is eternal.
Quiescent. Because it arises through dependent origination, it is quiescent yet constantly active. Such a Dharma-gate is fully realized by the Tathāgata;

therefore, it is said that "one who wanders through the gates of the Dharma-realm enters the sphere of all Buddhas. This refers to great compassion observing all sentient beings, which is called the "sphere of the Buddha.

The phrase "seeing there are immeasurable [beings]" below refers to the capacities previously reached by his teaching. "Immeasurable sons of the Buddha" cites those whom he transforms and instructs. As for "should... [the text continues].
