The latter two lines describe the constant presence of the faculty of wisdom free from outflows (*anāsrava-indriya*), which is characterized by the absence of self and the absence of conceptual correspondence.
This concludes the explanation of abandoning faults. Following this, there is one verse-line praising the virtues thus accomplished.
The first half-verse praises the perfection of the cause; the latter two lines describe the excellence of what is attained, as can be understood from the text itself.
The following two lines show the excellence of the secondary environment (*upabhoga*) of the Ghanavyūha realm, which may be seen by referring to the text and need not be described at length.
The following two and a half lines praise this excellence and exhort one to practice the cause; therein, the first half-line praises the superiority of the land, followed by one line.
The first half [of the text] exhorts the cultivation of its causes; the latter half concludes with the practice. The initial passage is easily understood. Regarding "the most supreme practitioner":

those from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward are termed "most supreme. Regarding "progressing through each stage": this refers to the generation [of the resolve] starting from the first stage up to the tenth stage; hence the expression "stage by stage" (*bhūmi-bhūmi*).
"Thoroughly knowing that all phenomena have the mind as their nature" refers to the accomplishment of the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha-caryā*). This is well explained.

Below "Ālaya" [is] the practice for the benefit of others. Regarding the "Dharma," there are five dharmas; the remainder of the text is self-evident. The above concludes the explanation of the "Chapter on the Body of Wondrous Birth.
Next is the "Chapter on Womb-Birth."
Regarding the "Chapter on Womb-Birth": this chapter is introduced because one wishes to manifest superiority by contrasting it with inferior and weak characteristics.

Furthermore, since the birth of those possessing bodies in the preceding chapter was not like that in the Land of Secret Adornment (*Guhyavimala*), this "Chapter on Womb-Birth" is now spoken in response to those remarks.
Within this chapter, there are two major divisions: first, from "the bodies of sentient beings" down to "surrounded by the assembly of the sons of the Buddhas."

Regarding "circumambulation" (*parivarta*): this explains the phenomena that constitute the cause of a sentient being's body. Following the section on the body within the womb, it explains the falsity and loathsomeness of the resulting retribution one obtains.

The initial passage is further divided into two parts. First, from the beginning up to the end of the cycle through the various realms of existence (*gati*), it demonstrates the phenomena that are to be loathed.

Second, from the phrase "If there is a wise person" onwards, it concerns the benefits gained from such loathing. The first of these [two] parts is further divided into four sections. First, from... [the beginning].

Regarding the bodies of sentient beings, from their initial growth together with [the elements] down to the first moment of receiving a body: at the time of first receiving a body, it is formed by relying on conditions.
Next, from passing through nine months down to undergoing immeasurable suffering: this explains how, while in the womb, one is oppressed by manifold sufferings upon emerging from the womb.
Next, regarding these various sentient beings down to being born within this [world]: they revolve without end within the three realms.

Regarding the section beginning with "After it has already been produced through meditative concentration," it concerns the present creation of karma that brings about future retribution. Within the initial passage, the nine substances that constitute its nature are as follows:
the four characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) constitute four, the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) constitute four, and the impure semen and blood together form the ninth.

These are called the nine substances. Regarding the phrase "constantly bound by immeasurable karma," this explains the reason: namely, that the aforementioned nine substances cannot constitute a body on their own;
rather, because they are bound by the ropes of karma, they combine to form a body. Below, an analogy is cited for illustration:
just as every branch and leaf of a poisonous tree can kill a person, so too is the body; [it is composed of] greed, hatred, and delusion.
This is the dwelling place of those [beings]. The rest of the text is clear. According to the sutra, they remain in the womb for nine months;
whether descending from among humans or otherwise, they all undergo suffering, as is evident in the text. Below, the commentary explains the ceaseless rotation within the three realms.

In this present passage, eleven types of persons are cited by way of illustration; were one to discuss them in detail, there would be immeasurable varieties. These various texts should be understood accordingly.

This can be understood. From the passage beginning with "Once born," it refers to the period after emerging from the womb; within the present body, one further creates new karma that brings about retribution in the future.
Such various texts clearly manifest this meaning.

Regarding the passage beginning with "If there is one who possesses wisdom," it concerns the benefits obtained by those who weary of faults and rejoice in the wholesome. Within this, there are two parts:

first, from "If there is one who possesses wisdom" down to "should manifest as appropriate," which concerns the accomplishment of the practice of cultivating causes; second, from "Those born thus" onwards, which explains the fruition that is accomplished.
The first section further divides into two: from here down to "the Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha" refers to the practice for one's own benefit (*svārtha*).

Accomplishment. Second, regarding the section "In immeasurable billions [of eons] below," the practice for the benefit of others is accomplished. In the first passage, it says: "If there is one who possesses wisdom.

One who possesses mundane and other-worldly knowledge, and who has faith, interest, and aspiration, is called "one who possesses wisdom. At the beginning of initiating practice, this is called "meeting a spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Hearing the Dharma constitutes the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*); reflecting upon it constitutes the wisdom of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*); and that which results in understanding and realization is the wisdom born of cultivation (*bhāvanāmayī-prajñā*). Next, this is clarified.
"Free from faults": because of the aforementioned cultivation of wisdom (*prajñā*), one does not cling to words and letters and is free from inverted conceptualization (*viparyāsa-vikalpa*).

"Entering the three gates of liberation" refers to the perfection of the practice of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). "Perceiving the true principle of phenomena" refers to non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*), which is the perfection of the practice of wisdom (*prajñā*).
"Supremely pure" means that within the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), afflictions (*kleśa*) are entirely exhausted; therefore, it is called supreme. "Supremely and supremely pure" refers to...
In the tenth stage, all subtle habitual tendencies are completely exhausted; therefore, it is said to be the "supremely supreme purity.
Those who thus fully accomplish all the practices of the Buddhas are born in Ghanavyūha. Therefore, the conclusion states that they come to dwell in this Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha.

The explanation of self-benefit is finished. From the passage beginning with "immeasurable hundreds of millions" below, the practice of benefiting others is clarified; the text is evident for inspection. Explanation complete.
The causal practices having been completed, the following section on "those who are thus born" clarifies the fruits attained. There are three kinds of fruit-virtues:

first, the virtue of liberation, which refers to the passage stating that one has eternally attained liberation from the perilous realms of saṃsāra; second, the virtue of renown, which refers to the passage stating that one is called a "great man" (mahāpuruṣa) and so forth;
third, the virtue of supporting all other qualities, which refers to the passage stating that one is surrounded by a multitude of "Buddha-sons" and others.
This is the third section from here on: regarding those born from the womb, whose karmic retribution of birth and death is false and loathsome. Within this, there are three parts.
First, from the body born of the womb down to these humans who are reborn in the Land of Secret Adornment (Ghanavyūha), he explains what is to be loathed and afflicted.
Next, regarding those practitioners of meditative concentration, from the lowest level down to those who are bound by samādhi:

the worldly, out-flowing (*sāsrava*) samādhis they attain cause them to receive bodies within the three realms, and they are unable to achieve liberation. Later, as for "abiding in samādhi" and below:

the samādhi that accords with the principle of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) serves as the cause for being born in the Guhyasamāja Realm (Ghanavyūha). The first section further has two parts; the first is the indication.
It is loathsome. As for the question "Why is this so? that follows, it explains the reason. Regarding "false and unreal":
because the body is a composite of impure and empty things, it is false and unreal. There are many kinds of "impurity," but as we are treating this briefly, we shall discuss five types.
The first is impurity of the seed, which refers to the various karmas and afflictions of past lives, as well as the semen and blood of the present parents.
First, impurity of blood: because it serves as the seed for birth. Second, impurity of the dwelling place:
because during the ten months of gestation, the body is situated between the stomach (āmāśaya) and the large intestine (pakvāśaya). Third, impurity of its own characteristics:
because impurities flow forth from the nine orifices. Fourth, impurity of its own substance: because the body is composed of thirty-six kinds of impure things.
Fifth, they are ultimately impure: buried, they become earth; burned, they become ash. Upon ultimate investigation, not a single mark of purity is found.

For this reason, it is said that they are false and unreal. "Not produced by way of intrinsic nature" means they do not arise from causes such as the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), atoms, or the nature of the world as postulated by the non-Buddhists. Therefore, it is refuted by saying: "not produced by way of intrinsic nature," nor...
Regarding the phrase "produced by ignorance, craving, and karma," this refutes the attachments of the Hīnayāna within the Buddha-dharma.
This is because the Hīnayāna does not know that ignorance and the other factors are empty and non-existent; they instead cling to ignorance and the rest as being capable of producing birth and death.
Now, using reasoning to refute this, it is said: "nor are they produced by ignorance, craving, and karma. Why is this? The following passage explains the reason for this.
This is the question posed by an outsider: "What is the reason that ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and karma (*karman*) are not the causes of birth and death (*saṃsāra*)?

In the Buddha’s sūtras, it is taught that starting from the link of ignorance as the condition for volitional formations (*saṃskāra-pratyaya*), and volitional formations as the condition for consciousness (*vijñāna-pratyaya*), [the links] continue in succession up to old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).
For what reason, then, is it said that ignorance is not the cause of birth and death? Therefore, he asks: "For what reason? Now, the Buddha responds:

It is said: Ignorance, craving, and karma exist only as mutual dependencies; they have no substantial reality, being like what is seen in a dream. Therefore, they cannot produce a body subject to birth and death.
This explains the reason why [existence] is to be loathed. Regarding the passage "If one can thoroughly understand... and below, it clarifies the benefits gained through such loathing.
From "If one can thoroughly understand" down to "and by means of discrimination," it refers to the benefit of being free from faults. Such a person will then be born [in a pure realm].

In the Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha, where brilliant virtue brings about benefit, if one can thoroughly comprehend the principle of the emptiness of phenomena—that the intrinsic nature of ignorance is fundamentally unarisen—then, since it lacks an intrinsic nature, how could it serve as a cause to produce the body of birth and death?

For this reason, it is said that all are extinguished without remainder; not only is there no substance, but even names do not exist. Because of names, one relies on them to engage in false discrimination.
The mind, too, is non-existent. Having completed the section on the elimination of faults, the section on the perfection of virtues follows; its characteristics appear and may be known.
Regarding those who possess meditative concentration—down to those bound by samādhi—leakage-tainted (*sāsrava*) samādhi cannot lead to transcendence.

Within this, there are three sections. First, regarding "those who possess meditative concentration" down to "the path of distraction": these are persons who have attained concentration but have not yet...
Because they have severed the seeds of afflictions consisting of attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*), they give rise to conceptualizing thought (*vikalpacitta*).

For this reason, it is taught that the mind has an object of focus (*ālambana*). Because there is an object of focus, grasping and attachment arise toward the six sense objects, such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth.

Although they are able to enter samādhi constantly for a long period of time, for this reason it is concluded that this is called the path of distraction (*vikṣepa-mārga*). Next, by the power of samādhi, [the teaching] descends to this person.
Those who are bound by samādhi are those in tainted (*sāsrava*) samādhi; it serves as the cause for the three realms and increases birth and death, with its characteristics manifest and recognizable.

Later, when dwelling below [the level of] samādhi, [the text] explains untainted (*anāsrava*) concentration as being in accord with the true nature (*dharmatā*). Although there are the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*), they are non-existent.

This is what is being distinguished. Therefore, it is concluded by saying: "This is called a person who practices true contemplation. If one wishes to be born in the lower realms, the method for cultivating the correct causes should be understood by analogy.

Regarding why this chapter follows to demonstrate that one's own actions are created by oneself: the preceding section clarified that both the "wondrous birth" (*upapāduka*) and the "womb-birth" (*jarāyuja*)—these two phenomena, which may be either desirable or loathsome—are produced solely by the mind.
Since there is no phenomenon apart from the mind, this chapter is presented to reveal the profound principle of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only). Therefore, [this chapter follows].
The text that follows. Within this, there are two further sections. First, Vajragarbha establishes his own reasoning to explain the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

Second, from the passage beginning "At that time, Ratnacūḍa... onwards, he further elaborates on the reasoning through a series of questions and answers. The first section, in turn, has three parts. First, from "The mind has eight kinds...
down to "...its fundamental mind is firm and immovable," he establishes the thesis and provides a brief explanation. Next, "The causes of the world... [and so forth].

Regarding the passage from "down to those who merely deceive the foolish," this is a broad explanation based on the tenet (*siddhānta*). Regarding the subsequent section, "each of the Buddha-sons" and so forth, this demonstrates the formal exhortation to practice.
The first part of this text is further divided into two. As for the statement, "the initial mind has eight kinds, or perhaps nine," this constitutes the formal proposition (*pratijñā*).
It subsequently descends together with ignorance. This explains how the eight and nine [consciousnesses] are established as their basis.

Why is the number of consciousnesses not fixed at eight or nine? It is because the true mind possesses two gates: first, the gate of support (āśraya), and second, the gate of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).

If one does not differentiate these gates and speaks of the system of the eight consciousnesses, there are eight; if one differentiates the two gates, there are nine consciousnesses explained—namely, when the true mind of dependent origination is discussed.
That which is named *ālaya* is the support for the true mind, which is named *amala*. For this reason, although their enumerations may increase or decrease, their essence remains no different.
Therefore, the established tenets state that there are eight or nine [consciousnesses]. Below, the reason for this is explained:
by what principle can such a true mind serve as the cause for the various phenomena of the world? Thus, the explanation clarifies: together with ignorance, it serves as the world...

Regarding the "intermediate causes," the term "mind and mental factors" (*citta-caitta*) has two interpretations. According to the first interpretation, within the true mind, the ignorance-driven evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*), and so forth, there are no mental concomitants (*caitta*).
Within the manifesting consciousness (*khyāti-vijñāna*), the two divisions of subject (*darśana-bhāga*) and object (*nimitta-bhāga*) suddenly emerge.

Upon reaching the cognitive consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*), specifically the consciousness that discriminates phenomena, only then do mental concomitants arise. From the manifesting consciousness onward, there is only mind without mental concomitants; this refers to the cognitive consciousness.
Since the time of consciousness, there have also been the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*). Furthermore, there is another principle:

the eighth and ninth [consciousnesses] are called only "mind" (*citta*) and not "mental factors" (*caitta*); apart from these, everything else is called only "mental factor" and not "mind-king" (*cittarāja*).
Thus, because these seven consciousnesses belong to the true mind, they are called only "factors" and not "mind. Both principles are valid. However, in this text, the World-Honored One...
Regarding the statement that "all that appears in the interim is mind and mental factors," this combines two meanings to form the term "mind and mental factors.
Such mental factors, once arisen, continue in a stream and flow on without cessation;

this is because they undergo transformation without interruption due to the false causes and conditions of the karma of ignorance, just as water arises from wind, where after one wave, waves follow one another in succession, arising without end.

This is explained according to the dharma-gate of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). As for the fundamental mind being firm and immovable, this is explained from the perspective of the gate of establishment based upon support.
It is like water giving rise to waves while its moist nature remains unchanged. The brief exposition of the established tenet is now complete.

From here below is the second section: the extensive explanation according to the school’s tenets. This consists of three parts. First, from "All worldly causes and conditions" down to "their nature is not firm":
all worlds exist solely through false causes and conditions; they possess no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The passage from "Next, in the land of Ghanavyūha" down to "crossing to the shore beyond birth and death" contrasts the preceding state of false defilement to reveal actual purity.

The subsequent section from "Within the bodies of sentient beings" down to "merely deceiving the foolish" demonstrates that, according to principle, there is no such thing as insentient existence among the phenomena of the world.

The initial section further consists of four parts: 1. From "From the worldly causes and conditions there are twelve links" down to "those who are free from all causes and conditions," this explains the scope and limits of what is encompassed by various causes and conditions.

2. From "The internal and external worlds" down to "having destruction as their nature," this explains the scope and limits of that which is free from the phenomena of the four characteristics (*catur-lakṣaṇa*).
3. From "The subtlety of the various consciousnesses" down to "the distinctions in the characteristics of the mind."
This principle of the eight consciousnesses is not an object of knowledge for ordinary, ignorant people.

Fourth, even if there were someone whose nature was as weak as grass, yet who practiced with diligent effort through a distorted mind, they would still be unable to escape the burning house of the triple world. Regarding the initial passage:

Regarding the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*): first, the title indicates the fundamental principle and enumerates the number; then, from "whether faculties or objects," the twelve bases are explained in detail.

Now, these twelve bases are of two kinds: first, the objective conditions (*ālambana*) that serve as the basis for manifestation, which clarify the twelve bases—namely, the six faculties and the six objects, which constitute the twelve bases;
second, the combination of the producer and the produced, taken together as the twelve bases. Here, the "producer" refers to the six faculties.
That which is produced is consciousness. Within this gateway, the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) are not grasped because they are remote; this may be understood from the text as it stands.

As for "perishing in a single moment," this demonstrates the principle of impermanence (*anityatā*). As explained above, phenomena such as the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are pure and empty beyond the realm of rational thought, for they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since they do not exceed a single thought-moment and perish as soon as they arise, they are described as impermanent. Below is the explanation.
The limit [of the realms] from the Brahma-world down to the Sphere of Neither-Perception-nor-Non-perception is precisely the extent reached by the twelve links of dependent origination.
Only the Tathāgata, who is free from dependent origination, demonstrates the place where the twelve links do not reach. Question:
If it is said that only the Tathāgata is free from dependent origination, why does the Sūtra state that this is because he has brought the six pāramitās to full completion?
Is the realization of bodhi called the *vipākabuddha* (Reward Buddha)? The answer is: The Buddha’s teaching has two aspects.
First, the teaching door of practicing relinquishment as an antidote; second, the teaching door of destroying marks to enter realization.

If one explains according to the teaching door of practicing relinquishment as an antidote, the Tathāgata is free from those twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of birth and death; therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata is free from causes and conditions. However...
When the cultivation of the six perfections is perfected and awakening is realized, for this reason the Tathāgata is also called the *vipākabuddha* (Retribution Buddha).

If one explains according to the teaching on entering realization by means of the deconstruction of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-bhaṅga*), all dharmas do not move from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"All sentient beings are themselves the mark of nirvāṇa; they do not need to be extinguished again. By this principle, the various faults that were to be extinguished were originally...
Since it does not arise in the future, what could possibly cease in the present? Against what, then, would one cultivate the dharmas that are practiced in order to realize bodhi?
Therefore, it is said that they are free from causes and conditions.

The second section below demonstrates the boundaries between the four characteristics and that which they characterize. "Internal" refers to the internal body; "external" refers to the external vessel-world.
"Moving" refers to the karma of the desire realm; "unmoving" refers to the phenomena of the two upper realms. All such phenomena as these are impermanent.
As we observe in the world objects such as jars and garments, it is precisely because of this principle that the four characteristics do not remain still for even a single moment.

From here begins the third section: the principle of the eight consciousnesses, which is not within the sphere of ordinary fools. Within this, there are two parts; the first begins from "all consciousnesses."
From "subtle" down to "that which can be known and seen," one should explain that the eight consciousnesses are subtle and difficult to know.

From "the various seers and non-Buddhists" down to "the distinctions of mental characteristics," one explains the reasons for this [difficulty]. In the initial passage, the statement that "all consciousnesses are subtle" explains the essence of the various consciousnesses:
they appear to be unitary and permanent, yet they are neither permanent nor annihilated; ordinary and ignorant people do not understand this and thus engage in false conceptualization.
First, they conceive of permanence; yet because [the mind] undergoes flux, it is not permanent, and because it is swift, it is not unitary.

Such are the eight consciousnesses, which only Buddhas know, as they are not the domain of the world. The following explains the reason for this: because non-Buddhist practitioners and heretics are bound by the afflictions of craving, they are unable to discern the distinctions between the eight consciousnesses.
From here below is the fourth section: regarding that which is not a cause, one falsely conceives it to be a cause and practices with a perverted mind;

thus, one cannot escape the burning house of the three realms. This section consists of two parts: first, an exposition of the Dharma to demonstrate the calculations of the perverted mind; second, from "Do you not know?

onwards, a command to abandon the perverted [view], followed by an illustration of the faults through parables. Within the Dharma exposition, the phrase "exhorting those who practice with diligence" refers to the foolish people of the world who desire—
Seeking long life, they rely on the *Veda* methods, chanting songs to worship the gods and attending upon the deities of fire sacrifices;

yet through such various heterodox practices, they ultimately cannot attain a peaceful and secure lifespan. Regarding the term "Veda," it refers to treatises composed by worldly scholars, which are thus called *Veda*.
Therefore, he concludes by pointing out their faults: "In the end, they too shall regress. From the words "You do not know" onwards, he exhorts them to abandon these heterodoxies. (3)
Regarding the *Veda*: first, the discourses on desire produced by Brahmā; second, the various virtuous discourses of Śakra, Lord of Devas;
and third, the various theories of a self (*ātman*) held by non-Buddhists. Based upon such treatises, the unwholesome practices that arise result only in the impermanent fruits of the three realms.
Therefore, it is said by way of analogy: "For example, the nature of the plantain tree is not solid. Thus far, the general explanation of all worldly [views] has been concluded.

Having concluded [the section on] the fact that intervening phenomena lack intrinsic nature, the second section from here on demonstrates their actual purity in contrast to the preceding emptiness and defilement. This section consists of three parts: first, from "Thus, all Tathāgatas...
down to "...should practice well," which cites the excellence [of the goal] to exhort practice; second, from "Those within the Ghanavyūha... down to "purity"... [and so forth].
"Free from cloud-like obscurations" refers to the excellence of the karmic fruit obtained based on its causes.

"All Buddhas, down to those who have crossed to the further shore of birth and death," refers to the excellence of the activities performed by the people in that land. "The Buddha-land of Ghanavyūha" is mentioned as an example of seeking after excellence.

Regarding "those who delight in liberation" and so forth, this encourages them to cultivate the causes; this may be understood according to the text. From here below is the second section, explaining the excellence of the attained retribution.

The passage from "having no retinue" down to "that which is free from defilement" clarifies the excellence of being free from faults. The passage beginning with "like a lotus flower" clarifies the distinction of the essence of the retribution;
the text is explicit and thus easily understood. From here below is the third section, explaining the excellence of the performed activity. Within this:
There are three phrases. "Constantly and collectively sustained by all Buddhas" is the first phrase.
"Receiving the power of empowerment, bathing in the stream of pure precepts, and drinking the essence of wisdom" refers to practicing the conduct of the Buddhas; this is the second phrase.
"Because their practice is sublime, they attain true understanding and cross to the shore beyond birth and death" refers to the sublimity of the fruition; this is the third phrase. As it is said:
These textual passages may be understood through their manifest characteristics.

From here on is the second section: the extensive explanation based on the tenet system. Within this, the third part concerns how the world is non-existent in principle yet possesses the appearance of existence.

Among these, first the non-existence of the world in principle is explained; subsequently, with the eye and forms as conditions, it is explained how all worlds, though non-existent in principle, are delusively perceived.
Within the realm of emotion, it constantly appears as if real. In the first passage, the phrase "the bodies of sentient beings" below serves to state the general while revealing the particular.

"The various realms" refers to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*). The "five aggregates" (*skandha*) consist of two types: the five aggregates that constitute persons and the five aggregates that constitute phenomena.
"Consciousness and so forth" refers to the eight consciousnesses. All such phenomena are like what is seen in a dream—non-existent yet falsely perceived; upon awakening, they are [seen as empty].
Fundamentally quiescent. Therefore, the concluding statement says that all things are non-existent. From "the eye and forms as conditions" onwards, the explanation appears to suggest they exist;
within this section there are eight parts: first, the meaning of how various consciousnesses arise from conditions;

second, from "all objective spheres" down to "following the lodestone," the conditions that give rise to consciousness are established in dependence upon consciousness itself; third, from "again, like a mirage" down to "but merely... [text continues].
The transformations of the minds of ordinary beings can produce the four great elements, yet these are empty and lack intrinsic nature.

Just as the four [elements] are like those in a city of Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*), so too are all activities from the lowest level of movement and conduct; this applies to worldly actions such as the four modes of deportment (*iryāpatha*).

5. "Appearing to exist but lacking reality" refers to the five aggregates and other phenomena, which are logically non-existent despite being perceived as existent, from the phrase "like what is seen in a dream" down to "originally quiescent.
6. "The combination of the earth element and so forth" refers to coarse, manifest objects composed of the four great elements;
these are non-existent phenomena that are falsely perceived, from the phrase "down to all worldly phenomena" down to "are likewise thus. 7. "All worlds... [and so forth].

Regarding the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), they exist as mental objects but lack substantial reality. Within the eight realms of existence, the following concludes by demonstrating their faults.

In the first section, there is first the teaching and then the analogy: consciousness cannot arise by itself; it must depend on the conjunction of conditions, just as fire requires the condition of wood to ignite and blaze.
Regarding "all objective spheres" and below: secondly, the objective spheres that serve as the objects of consciousness are [unrealizable].
It is established by itself; it necessarily depends on the consciousness that arises from it, and is established in accordance with that consciousness. Therefore, an analogy is cited:

"Just as iron moves and shifts following a magnet," and as stated below under the section on "mirage": thirdly, this explains how the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which constitute [matter] are non-existent yet appear to exist.
First the analogy, then the application. The analogy is clearly visible in the text. In the section on the application, first the principle is established, then the application follows;

this merely serves to resolve lingering doubts below. Regarding the phrase "In this there are no such things as a creator and so forth": this refers to the absence [of such things] according to principle. "This" refers to the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
Within this principle of emptiness, there are no such things as a creator or the created. Having completed the establishment of the principle, what follows is...

Resolving Doubts: There is a doubt beyond the text. If the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth do not exist within the ultimate principle (*tattva*), how can one perceive the existence of these dharmas such as the four great elements that are able to create all things?
The teachers of the Hīnayāna raise this difficult doubt. The Sūtra itself resolves it by stating: "These are merely transformations of the minds of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Although they do not exist within the ultimate principle, they appear to exist through deluded sentiment. This is as explained below in the fourth section on the City of Gandharvas (*gandharvanagara*).
All activities and the four modes of deportment existing in the world appear to exist but are not real. The analogy is presented first, followed by its application;

the text is clearly visible. In the section beginning with "As seen in a dream," the fifth [point] explains that while phenomena appear as objects of the mind, they lack reality in principle; the text is clearly visible.
In the section beginning with "The combination of earth and so forth," the sixth [point] explains the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) of the coarse, manifest objects produced by the four great elements.

The accumulation of material objects is, in principle, devoid of sentience. First is the teaching (*dharma*), followed by the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*). Within the analogy, there are two sections: first, the citation of the analogy as an illustration;

second, the immediate application (*yoga*) of it to the teaching. Regarding the first analogy: it illustrates that while phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, the deluded mind falsely conceptualizes them as if they were present.
Regarding the second analogy: it illustrates that once phenomena have arisen, they manifest through their own continuity, and there is nothing else capable of causing them to arise. As it is said:
These various passages may be understood by inference. "You, sons of the Buddha, should diligently observe" is the concluding exhortation to practice, which is likewise understandable.

Regarding the phrase "all worldly things, down to those that are deceptive and unreal": the seventh section concerns the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), demonstrating the existence of the phenomenal world (*yod pa*).
Within this, there are five subsections. As for "things subject to movement and fluctuation," these refer to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which is the primary phenomenon.
The subsequent metaphors may be understood by analogy. "Perceptions such as those of a jar or clothing" refers to the insubstantiality and unreality of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

"Suffering and pleasure among the various feelings" demonstrates that the phenomena of the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) are unreal in their nature. "Formations are like the plantain tree" demonstrates the unreality of formations (*saṃskāra*).

"Consciousness is like a magical illusion" demonstrates the falsity of consciousness (*vijñāna*). These various passages are all evident and can be understood through direct observation. The three realms...
Within this [section], the faults are summarized and demonstrated. These phenomena—such as seeing what does not exist—are originally quiescent according to the awakening of the noble ones (*ārya*).
Yet ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and children do not understand these dharmas; they perceive only empty appearances and, clinging to them as real, are thus deceived.
Therefore, it is concluded that these merely delude the foolish. The preceding explanation of how things exist conventionally but do not exist ultimately is now complete.
From here below is the third section, which demonstrates the correct exhortation to practice. Within this, there are three parts. First, from "If, O sons of the Buddha...

down to "...the land of Ghanavyūha," it exhorts practice by highlighting its benefits. Second, from "All worlds... down to "...not within the range of the mind," [it describes the state of realization].
It demonstrates the correct principle. Following the passage "After all marks... and below, it demonstrates the limits of faults and exhorts one toward liberation.

Within the first section of the text, there are three kinds of benefits: first, the benefit of attaining fearlessness regarding phenomena; second, the benefit of severing hindrances through the fire of wisdom (from the passage "With the fire of wisdom... and below);

third, the benefit of the body dwelling in a superior state (from the passage "Immediately producing sublime bliss... and below). The characteristics of these textual passages are all manifest; they should be understood accordingly.
This can be understood. From the passage "All worlds are devoid of characteristics" onwards, the correct principle is demonstrated. First, the correct principle is shown;

subsequently, from "All various characteristics are the dharmas of the three realms" onwards, the faults of these characteristics are revealed. Regarding the statement "All worlds are devoid of characteristics":

within the mind of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), one falsely calculates and clings to various characteristics. If one awakens to this principle, then characteristics are themselves non-characteristics (*animitta*). It is not...

The characteristic of cessation is subsequently termed "signlessness" (*animitta*). Just as the characteristics within a dream are themselves signless, it is not the case that they become signless only after waking from the dream;
this is a general demonstration of the true principle. Ordinary beings are deluded regarding this principle and falsely grasp at signs;
unaware that signs are empty, they reckon them to be truly existent. The Noble Ones realize emptiness and do not grasp at signs. Therefore, the Tathāgata himself judged and declared:
"Characteristics (lakṣaṇa) constitute bondage; the absence of characteristics (alakṣaṇa) is liberation. The following passage explains the reason for this. There is a doubt outside the text:

"For what reason do characteristics constitute bondage, while the absence of characteristics constitutes liberation? What is the meaning of this? Now, the text provides a comprehensive explanation: Characteristics are the objects of the deluded mind;
because they are grasped by the deluded mind and are not real, it is said that characteristics constitute bondage. As for the true Dharma...

The realm of wisdom is free from all characteristics; therefore, it is not the domain of deluded mind. For this reason, it is taught that the absence of characteristics (*animitta*) is itself liberation.
In the passage beginning "All characteristics," the faults of characteristics are demonstrated. First, the faults are shown;

subsequently, in the passage beginning "If one can [regard] characteristics," there is an exhortation to abandon all characteristics, which will certainly bring benefit. These two sections are clearly discernible as such. Thus far, Vajragarbha himself...

Having established the principles and completed the explanation of the meaning of *vijñapti-mātra*, the second section from here on consists of a detailed explanation through questions and answers of the meanings previously stated. This is divided into two parts: first the question, and then the answer.

Regarding the inquiry within the text, it is further divided into two parts: first, praising the virtues of the speaker; second, from "For what reason" onwards, the actual formulation of the question.
Within the praise of his virtues, there are four sections: first, praising his gathering of all virtues, meaning he is the foremost leader among the assembly of Bodhisattvas;
second, praising his wisdom-virtue, meaning he has attained the supreme wisdom, as indicated by the following passage; third, [he is] in *yogācāra*...
The first section below praises the virtue of transforming others. The fourth praises the virtue of eloquence, specifically the passage beginning with "able [to teach] for an eon" (*kalpa*).
The first passage is easily understood. Regarding the second passage, "immeasurable *siddhāntas*":

*siddhānta* is a Sanskrit term translated here as "tenet" (*zōng*), also rendered as "establishment" (*chéng*), or "principle" (*lǐ*). This is analyzed in detail in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Now, regarding *siddhānta*:
The meanings are briefly of four kinds: first, the worldly *siddhānta*; second, the ultimate *siddhānta*;
third, the therapeutic *siddhānta*; and fourth, the individual *siddhānta*. These are explained in detail as found in the sub-commentary to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*. To discuss them separately:
The twelve divisions of the sūtras and the eighty-four thousand gateways to all dharmas are all subsumed herein.

Now, this scriptural text provides a detailed explanation according to specific categories; therefore, it speaks of "immeasurable *siddhāntas*. The remaining text is easily understood. Regarding the third section:

Regarding the term *yogī*: "Yogī" is a Sanskrit sound; here it is translated as "contemplative practice" (*guanxing*). This Vajragarbha dwells among the assembly of those engaged in contemplative practice and is able to resolve the doubts of others.
Furthermore, he knows the fundamental source of the bodies of sentient beings. There are three such sources: first, craving and karma constitute the fundamental source of the body;
second, ignorance constitutes the fundamental source of the body; and third, the true mind constitutes the fundamental source of the body.
Section One. Those of the Two Vehicles know only that the coarse arising of the karma of craving and ignorance constitutes the fundamental root of the body;
they do not know the primordial, subtle ignorance nor the true mind. The Bodhisattvas, however, know that the bodies of sentient beings are established based upon these three roots.
For this reason, he proclaims the origin of the body’s foundation. Below, he praises his virtue of eloquence, stating that within a single kalpa, or perhaps a single...

Even after the remainder of an eon, one could never finish speaking [of it]. Therefore, he concludes by stating that he expounds it without weariness; "weariness" here means exhaustion or reaching the limit.
Thus ends the preceding praise of his excellence in teaching.
"Why is it not for the lower [state]? This is the formal inquiry, which consists of five sections: 1.

From "Why is it not for the lower" to "affection is a firm bond," this section rebukes the previous failure to speak and requests an explanation of the causes, conditions, and correct principles regarding the reasons for bondage and liberation.
2. From "Sentient beings, below... to "...by ignorance, craving, and karma, they are turbid and disturbed," this section requests an explanation of the confusion of consciousness.

The flowing current is difficult to restrain. Third, regarding those within the bodies of sentient beings who manifest even the most subtle colors: please explain how false thoughts act as the masters of false phenomena.
Fourth, as for the question "Why do you, O Benevolent One, not explain such a meaning?": this is a general reproach for not speaking.

Fifth, from the passage beginning "Furthermore, like various colors" onwards, it concludes by praising the speaker’s capacity for exposition. Within the first section of the text, there are two sub-sections.

First, it indicates what was not previously explained in the preceding text; subsequently, the passage beginning with "thereby enabling all wise ones" explains the reason for this. This specifically demonstrates that which was not stated in the text:
namely, the true dharmas that are distinct from all causes—whether contrary or conforming, apparent or non-apparent.

Such meanings were not mentioned in the prior text; therefore, they are now set forth in response to the request so that they may be explained. Regarding "contrary," this refers to those who flow downward toward the three evil realms.

The Path. That which is "conformable" leads upward toward the realms of humans and devas, for it conforms to human sentiments. According to another interpretation: delusive phenomena violate principle and run counter to the intentions of the Sages;
thus they are called "contrary. The practices arising from the teachings conform to both principle and sentiment; thus they are called "conformable. Question:

Contrary phenomena may be abandoned, so it is appropriate to speak of "distancing oneself" from them. Conformable phenomena may be relied upon; why then do you speak of "leaving" them? Answer: [See following response].

It is said: Speaking in terms of principle (*li*), there is nothing to be accepted or rejected regarding the two dharmas of opposition and conformity; one simply knows them as empty appearances. Speaking in terms of emotional sentiment (*qing*), there is both opposition and conformity.
Now, speaking from the perspective of principle, one remains detached from both. As for "resembling yet not resembling," the meaning encompasses two interpretations.
First, regarding the principle of the mutual production of cause and effect, one speaks of "resembling yet not resembling" by means of the production of effects from afflictions (*kleśa*).

The *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body) is designated as "non-similar" because it is not of the same class. What kind of affliction gives rise to a subsequent affliction is called a "similar cause," because they are of the same class.
Karma is also like this. Second, this is explained by means of the principles of formal logic (*pramāṇa*). For example, as in a thesis statement:
"Sound is impermanent. The reason (*hetu*) is stated as: "Because it is produced. This reason is pervasively present within all impermanent phenomena.

Because they appear similar to one another, it is called a "semblance-reason" (*sādṛśya-hetu*). However, regarding the "produced cause" (*kṛtaka-hetu*), although the produced nature is the same, there are distinct causes:

a jar is accomplished through poverty (i.e., human effort), whereas [a cloth] is accomplished by being fired with fire. Sound is also a produced phenomenon; if [the reason were applied], it should likewise be accomplished by being fired with fire.
This reason is dissimilar. Furthermore, there is another thesis: "Sound is eternal," for which the reason is stated as "because it is formless."
This reason is inconclusive. If an incorporeal cause were to establish that sound is eternal, then all minds and mental factors, being likewise without corporeal obstruction, should also be eternal.
Because this reason is inconclusive, it is not similar to the true dharma.

The *tathāgatagarbha-citta* and its functioning through dependent origination are free from the defects of the aforementioned [erroneous] dharmas; therefore, they are called "true. The explanation of the principle of causes and conditions is hereby concluded.

This causes those who possess wisdom to descend. [The text] explains the reason for "releasing bonds and attaining liberation. Regarding the phrase "those who possess wisdom": those in the world who are clever and intelligent but lack correct faith are called "those who possess wisdom.

Furthermore, within the Buddha-dharma, a Bodhisattva of the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-carita*) who has not yet attained the stage of practice through understanding (*adhimukti-carita*) is called a "wise one" (*jñānin*).
One whose mind is pure and free from doubt is exhorted to believe in the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), thereby dispelling and eliminating doubt and confusion. "Pure" refers to faith.

Regarding those who quickly attain liberation by abandoning the causes and conditions of the aggregates (*skandha*), this is an exhortation to practice through the presentation of benefits; the signs will appear so that they may be known.

Below, concerning "Dharma and non-Dharma," the essential nature of the causes and conditions of the aggregates is set forth. Wholesome phenomena (*kuśala-dharma*) are called "Dharma" because they are to be rejoiced in; unwholesome phenomena are called "non-Dharma" because they are to be loathed and abandoned.

Here, the terms "wholesome" and "unwholesome" together refer to the causes and conditions of the aggregates, as explained in the *Yogācārabhūmi* (The Stages of Yoga Practice) in the section on the abundance of meaning.
Regarding the "accumulation of non-benefit" and the "accumulation of benefit," they are identical to the "Dharma and non-Dharma" mentioned in this text.

Below the passage "Wisdom can liberate one from suffering," the essential nature of bondage and liberation is set forth. Thus, concerning these aggregates (*skandha*), who attains liberation and who is bound?

Therefore, the statement regarding their essential nature says: "Wisdom can liberate one from suffering; craving is the firm bond. Below the phrase "the mind of sentient beings," [the author] requests an explanation of the confused consciousness of ordinary worldlings.

Because it is difficult to restrain when it rushes toward its objects, we shall first explain the conditions upon which it relies. To speak in terms of ultimate reality, all six consciousnesses are like this;
however, in this text, we shall discuss the visual consciousness for now, while the other consciousnesses may be understood by analogy.

When visual consciousness arises, it does so through conditions such as visible form, light, and mental attention (*manasikāra*); it cannot arise of itself. Because it depends on a multitude of conditions, it is devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). However...

It appears to have a substantial nature and moves with great speed; because ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) do not realize its falsity, it is said to be difficult to perceive.

The reason for this will be explained later. As for why ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles do not recognize that [phenomena] lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), the reason is explained below:
they are turbid and disturbed by ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and karma. This is precisely because those of the two vehicles have not yet severed the seeds.
This [passage] concerns the failure to realize that the nature of the six consciousnesses is empty. It is situated below the section on sentient beings' bodies.

Third, it requests an explanation of how deluded thought and all deluded phenomena act as the master and the root. This is divided into two parts: first, the explanation through the Dharma; second, the citation of analogies.

Within the explanation through the Dharma, "various phenomena" refers to the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense bases (*āyatana*), which are termed "various phenomena. Furthermore, there are the three categories of form (*rūpa*), mind (*citta*), and so forth.

The phenomena of the aggregates have various conditions as their cause. With the mind as the precursor means that, following ignorance and karma, the six kinds of deluded mental activity intimately obscure the true mind, transforming it into the coarse aggregates, elements, and sense bases; therefore, it is said that the mind is the precursor.
Regarding the statement that "the mind is the most swift": deluded thought deviates from principle and is superficial and empty beyond it;

within a single moment of thought, it cannot remain stable. Among all things that are impermanent, this mind is the first. It is called "most" because it is the first, not because there is any difference in the length of its moments (*kṣaṇa*).
This is because, whether coarse or subtle, moments are identical in nature and possess no progression or regression; since it is the very beginning, it is designated as such.
"Supreme" (*manas*) means that which is preeminent. It reveals that within the state of consciousness, the appearance of the perceived object suddenly manifests;

furthermore, it is capable of sustaining the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all phenomena so that they do not cease. Because it possesses this superior capacity, it is called "preeminent. Regarding the phrase "according to whatever phenomena [exist]":
this explains how various deluded phenomena appear within the deluded mind, just as various images manifest in a clear mirror. Therefore, it concludes by stating that the mind is [the basis].

Regarding its nature, it is illustrated below by means of a metaphor: "Just as a *maṇi* jewel manifests various colors according to what is appropriate, why do you, O Venerable One, not explain such a meaning?
This concludes the reprimand for not explaining; the text is clear enough to understand.

From here until the end, the concluding praise of the speaker’s capacity to teach is presented, first through a metaphor and subsequently through the teaching of the Dharma; these passages are likewise clear enough to understand. Above.

Having finished the inquiry, the second section follows, in which Vajragarbha provides the answer. This text is divided into two parts: first, the prose response; second, the extensive response in verse.
Within the prose section, it is further divided into five segments. The first begins from "Most tranquil" and extends down to "respective[ly]."

Regarding the distinctions: 1. "The body is eternally pure" and "not a phenomenon subject to destruction by external conditions" explain the self-enjoyment realm (*svasaṃbhogakāya*) and the dharma-nature realm (*dharmatā-kṣetra*).

2. "The second is the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*), from consciousness down to the objects of its activity" explains the Pure Land of Secret Adornment (*Guhya-vyūha*), the stainless and pure abode.

3. "The third is the dwelling place of the Tathāgatas, down to the net of darkness" explains that the Pure Land of Secret Adornment is not... [the latter part of this section is missing from the source text].

1. The fruits produced by various false causes; 2. The four *āryasatyas* (noble truths) down to the realm of pure wisdom (*viśuddhajñāna*), which cannot be measured by the false cognitions of worldly people;
3. [The point that] from "O virtuous ones" onwards, it is permitted to explain extensively.
Regarding the first section of the text, it is divided into three parts. The first consists of four phrases, which originate from the essential nature of the Pure Land of Enjoyment.
Next, from the phrase "Furthermore, it is wisdom" down to "the place where one rests," [it describes] how all practitioners reach the ultimate limit of their practice.

Regarding the phrase "subsequently, because it is originally and eternally abiding, down to its various distinctions": external false conditions cannot cause its success or failure. Regarding "most tranquil":
it is called tranquil because it is a place not reached by external clamorous conditions. Regarding "this Great Nirvana is the wondrous liberation":
it is nirvana because the fruit obtained through cultivation in the land of self-enjoyment is perfected; it is free from affliction.
Therefore, it is liberation. This pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is the pure land of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Because it is the nature of all phenomena, it is named the "dharma-realm.
Such a pure land is the ultimate place of rest for those who practice meditative contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).

For this reason, it is proclaimed that this is also the place where those who practice wisdom and the various supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) abide. [The following explains why external conditions cannot bring about accomplishment.]
The defeat [of the opposing view] consists of three further sections. First, the essential nature of the Pure Land is eternal; it is immovable and unchanging.
Water cannot moisten it, nor can external conditions bring about its formation or destruction. That which is primordially abiding is the Dharma-nature Pure Land;

because it has never moved from the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) since the beginningless past, it is called "eternal. Because it lacks any characteristic of interruption, it is called "indestructible. It is free from...

Because there is the characteristic of existence and non-existence, it is said that they do not perish. The following section explains that external conditions cannot bring about their formation or destruction; this text is divided into two parts.
First, from "Water cannot moisten them" down to "they are again destroyed," explains that conditions cannot cause destruction.

Second, from "It is not because of various similar causes" down to "because each is distinct," explains that conditions cannot cause formation. The first of these sections is further divided into two: first the principle (*dharma*), and second the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The signs appear and can be known. Below, it is explained that the conditions cannot be established. This means that the thesis (*pakṣa*), reason (*hetu*), and example (*dṛṣṭānta*) of this school of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are not established.
This is because the Pure Land is utterly beyond the sphere of representation and conceptual investigation (*vitarka*); whereas inference (*anumāna*) operates only within the sphere of representation.

As for what is called a "pseudo-reason" (*hetvābhāsa*), it is merely an impermanent phenomenon (*anityadharma*) that uses the exertion of effort as its common ground to establish the reason; it is solely a phenomenon.
They are distinct. Because their causal function is the same and they resemble one another, they are called "similar causes" (*sādharmya-hetu*).
As for "dissimilar causes," these are established by the proponents of the science of sound (*śabda-vidyā*): they take the thesis that "sound is eternal" and offer the reason "because it is formless.

This reason is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*), for phenomena such as greed and hatred are also formless yet are impermanent; thus, they do not resemble the thesis of eternality. Therefore, this is a dissimilar cause. [In the] *Ghanavyūha-buddha*...
Earth. Such an inference is not established. Why? [The text] below explains the reason for its non-establishment:
"If the thesis and its members are indeterminate dharmas," this refers to establishing a thesis of permanence in contrast to impermanent dharmas; the case of impermanence is likewise.

If there were no impermanence, the thesis of permanence would not be established; the same applies to the reason (*hetu*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). This is because they are mutually dependent and provisional.

Because it is a dharma [established by] logical reasoning, it lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Therefore, it is said that the thesis (*pakṣa*) and its various members (*avayava*) are indeterminate dharmas.
As for the various distinctions among theses and reasons—such as the theses of permanence and impermanence, each having its own specific limits—the reasons are likewise distinct;

thus, they cannot establish the Land of Secret Adornment (*Guhyasamāja-buddhakṣetra*). This is because the Pure Land pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein there is no distinction between "this" and "that."
There is nothing to counter it; thus, neither the thesis (*pakṣa*) nor the reason (*hetu*) is established. For this reason, it is taught that the various theses and reasons are each distinct.
Regarding the "consciousness of the transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti-vijñāna*): from here on, the second section concerns the pure state free from faults.

As for the consciousness of the transformation of the basis, because it is free from the faults of birth and death and has exhausted them without remainder, it is called the "consciousness of the transformation of the basis. It transforms into all untainted merits (*anāsrava-guṇa*), and is also called "transformation" (*parāvṛtti*).
"Relying [on this], one transcends the discriminating mind; it is not an object traversed by various deluded sentiments.

This means that within the *vajra-citta* (diamond-mind), ignorance and false conceptualization are entirely exhausted without remainder. Furthermore, even the discrimination of untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*) cultivated through conditioned practice is entirely exhausted without remainder.
Only by means of true cultivation of the untainted can realization be attained. Therefore, it is said that this is not an object traversed by various deluded sentiments.

Regarding "this is the abode of the Tathāgata": this is the third section from here below, which explains that the Ghanavyūha realm is inhabited solely by the Buddhas and is not a fruit produced by worldly or heterodox causes.
Within this, there are three phrases; the first is "this is the abode of the Tathāgata. "Without beginning and without end" refers to the *tathatā* (suchness).
The "coming" is the subject; it is able to dwell in the Pure Land. It has dwelt there eternally from the beginning, not starting only today;
therefore, it is called "beginningless. Because there is no time of decay, it is called "endless. That which is able to dwell and that which is dwelled in both lack beginning and end.

Because it is beginningless, it is not the past; because it is endless, it is not the future. Since there is no conjunction of conditions, it is also not the present. Therefore, it is said to be "non-existent."
It has no beginning and no end. Furthermore, it is not produced from atoms, nor is it obtained through false causes. Within this, there are three points.
First, regarding the passage from "not produced from atoms" down to "produced by Śiva": the Pure Land is not produced from false causes. Second, it is not produced by ignorance, craving, or karma.
Even the twelve links of dependent origination taught in the Buddha-dharma cannot produce the Saṃghāṭa-vyūha (Ghanavyūha) Pure Land.

Regarding the "land" (*bhūmi*): subsequently, from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward, where there is only non-conceptual effortlessness (*anābhoga*), the self-enjoyment land (*svasaṃbhogakāya-bhūmi*) arises with non-conceptual wisdom as its cause.
Within the first section [of the text], there are four types of false causes imagined by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*):

first, they imagine that atoms (*paramāṇu*) are eternal and indestructible, and are capable of producing all phenomena; second, they imagine the primal nature (*prakṛti*), also called the obscure principle (*avidyā-tattva*); third, they imagine pleasure (*sukha*).
That is to say, when the Brahma King is joyful, he can give rise to wholesome dharmas; when he is angry, he gives rise to unwholesome ones.

Some reckon that Maheśvara, the Heavenly King, can give rise to all dharmas. Such false causes do not produce the Pure Land. Next, it should be understood by analogy that the causes and conditions taught within the Buddha-dharma do not produce the Pure Land either.
Finally, the correct cause is shown: it is only from the eighth stage (*bhūmi*) upward that there is non-effort (*anābhoga*).
Because it arises with wisdom as its cause, it transcends the three realms; this is clearly evident in the text.

Below the section on *āryasiddhānta*, it is stated that this is not something to be measured by the false wisdom of worldly beings. Within this, first, it explains that it is not revealed by the false wisdom of the world;
second, from "even those who possess the provisions" (*sambhāra*) onwards, it explains that even those at the stage of non-realization do not comprehend it.
The phrase "afterwards, only the Tathāgata" and below indicates the person who has realized the truth. In the initial passage, the term *ājñāsiddhānta* is a transliteration of the Indic sound;
it is translated here as the "First Noble Truth" (*paramārtha-satya*) *siddhānta*. It is also called the "tenet established by wisdom. This refers to the correct [view];

it is not the same as the "inferential logic" (*hetuvidyā*) mentioned below, which serves to exclude false tenets. There are four types of false tenets: first, inferential logic (*hetuvidyā*); second... [text continues].
These are: first, the doctrine of Primordial Matter (Prakṛti); second, the doctrine of the Self (Ātman); third, the doctrine of Maheśvara; and fourth, the doctrine of the Grammarians (Śabdika).
Regarding the term "Veda," it refers to the three Vedas as described above. Such heterodox systems cannot reveal the Tathāgata’s Pure Land.

Furthermore, they cannot be fully understood by the wisdom of Bodhisattvas at the stage of Provisions (sambhāra-avasthā) who have not yet reached the stage of Realization (adhigama-avasthā). Only the Tathāgata—referring here to the one who has attained correct realization—can [reveal it].

Only the Buddha, and no others, [attains it]. That is to say, having cultivated all practices throughout the ten stages (daśabhūmi) until they are ultimately perfected, such wisdom reaches the nature of phenomena (dharmatā).
For Bodhisattvas of the ten stages, because they have not yet exhausted it according to their respective degrees, it is still not called their "object" (viṣaya).
This is the fifth section from here below, which permits a broad and detailed exposition. First, because worldly beings are deluded by false attachments, he gives rise to a mind of compassion.
Then, with the words "Now I," and so forth, he permits a broad exposition for their sake. Regarding those who are deluded about what constitutes karma and what does not in the world:
this is because the world is created solely by the one mind; yet ordinary people do not know this, and instead perversely seek causes such as atoms. For this reason, it is said:

Delusion within the world is created solely by the mind; it is the mind alone that constitutes karma, for body and speech are not karma in themselves—they are designated as karma only because they follow the movement of the mind.
Karma means movement. Because the mind is deluded, it turns outward; therefore, it is called karma.

I shall now, at this very moment, grant permission to proclaim this extensively, so that all those established in meditative concentration may attain peace and happiness. This is the statement of its benefit.
From this point downward is the second section: the detailed explanation in verse. Within this, there are fifty-eight and a half lines, divided into five sections.
First, from the beginning up to "all arise from the mind," there are eight lines of text;
these answer the prose questions concerning the minds of sentient beings and so forth. Second, from "this sublime samādhi of Ghanavyūha" down to "there are none who do not... [the text continues].
1. "The accomplishment of coming" (28 lines and a half) explains the prose response concerning the *Ghanavyūha* Buddha-field (*Ghanavyūha-buddhakṣetra*).

2. From "The threefold analysis of all forms" down to "In this way, arising, abiding, and ceasing," etc. (seven lines), answers the preceding question regarding the causes and conditions for abandoning the aggregates (*skandha*).
3. From "Whether it be karma or [the fruit of] karma" (five lines and a half), it explains the preceding prose.

Regarding the passage beginning with "All ordinary beings among those who practice" and continuing through the five lines starting with "The mundane is not the supreme nature," there are nine and a half lines that conclude by demonstrating the correct principle.
The first section further divides into two parts; the initial four lines respond to the prose section concerning the cause of the minds of sentient beings, which are [dependent upon] form and light.
The aforementioned passage concludes with four lines that answer the subsequent prose section concerning the various phenomena within the bodies of sentient beings.
Within the first part of this text, the initial one and a half lines demonstrate the correct principle:

they answer the preceding question by showing that because the mind arises from a multitude of conditions such as form (*rūpa*), it is thereby known that the subject-object body arises only by relying upon the perceived objects (*ālambana*) as its support.
The final two and a half lines concern ordinary beings and those of the Two Vehicles who, being deluded regarding this principle, give rise to conceptual discrimination in vain.
The initial passage is further divided into two parts. The first two lines present the correct principle; the subsequent line explains the reason for it. Regarding "all internal and external things":

"internal" refers to sentient beings, while "external" refers to mountains and rivers. "That which is seen" refers to grasping (*upādāna*). As stated above, both the internal and external are entirely mind.
Because it is an object of perception, it is called "that which is seen. The phrase "only one's own mind" demonstrates the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only).

All internal and external phenomena are manifestations of a single mind; they are like what is seen in a dream. Just as there are no objects outside a dream—existing only because of the activity of the mind—it is said to be "only one's own mind.

The following passage explains the reason for this. There is a doubt regarding the implicit meaning: if there is only consciousness and no external objects, why is it that we currently perceive [objects] as being seen?
The two aspects of appearance exist and are not non-existent; therefore, it is said in general that the dual nature of the sentient being’s mind consists of the grasper and the grasped.

"The sentient being’s mind" refers to the mind of the seeing-consciousness (*darśana-vijñāna*). This indicates that within consciousness, the aspect of appearance manifests; hence, it is called "dual nature.

Regarding the statement that "the essence of the mind has two gates," the "essence of the mind" is precisely the manifestation of its own substance, which is nothing but representation-only (*vijñapti-mātra*). It has two [gates].
The "gatekeeper" refers to the seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) and the image-part (*nimitta-bhāga*). These are precisely two.

As for the statement that "the mind itself sees all objects," this reveals that the seeing-part manifested within consciousness takes back the image-part manifested by its own mind; therefore, it is said that "the mind itself sees all objects.

This concludes the demonstration of the correct principle regarding the various [parts]. Below this is the second section: the ordinary beings and those of the two vehicles who recklessly give rise to these parts.

This is distinct. Within it, there are two sections: the first one and a half lines concern the commonality with ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), while the subsequent one line distinguishes the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*).
In the first section, the initial half-line points out their faults, and the following line explains the principle of universal penetration;
such passages are evident for those who know. Below, regarding the false discrimination common to the Two Vehicles, the term "various sages" (*ṛṣi*) refers to the persons of the Two Vehicles.

Because they subdue and suppress manifest afflictions and delight in tranquility, they are called "sages" (ṛṣi). Those whose wisdom is inferior—namely, the followers of the Two Vehicles—only take as their object the suffering, impermanence, and so forth of all phenomena;
they suppress and suppress the arising of afflictions but cannot contemplate True Suchness (tathatā) with equanimity to sever the seeds [of affliction].
Therefore, they are said to be "inferior. Regarding those who cannot know clearly: in all phenomena, there is originally nothing...
Because they have arisen, they are now without cessation. Enveloped in delusion, one fails to recognize this and falsely calculates that the extinction of all phenomena constitutes the beginning.

For this reason, it is said that one cannot clearly and fully know that the signless *tathatā* (suchness) is called the true principle, whereas phenomena with signs are called the path of conceptual discrimination.

This is the second section from below, answering the prose passage concerning how, within the bodies of sentient beings, all various phenomena are preceded by the mind (*manas*), as explained in the subsequent text.
This section is divided into three parts: first, a single line stating the thesis; second, one line and three phrases citing a metaphor to demonstrate it;
and third, two lines of prose providing the formal explanation and conclusion. Regarding the phrase "this mind," the fourth [section] clarifies that consciousness is what is so named.

Regarding the statement that "the mind has two natures": when consciousness evolves from ignorance to manifesting consciousness (*nirbhāsa-vijñāna*), the distinction between the two gates of the perceived (*nimitta*) and the perceiving (*darśana*) suddenly arises.
For this reason, it is said that this mind has two natures. This is the answer to the preceding passage which stated that "intention (*manas*) is the precursor.

Within the section on citing metaphors, there are three sentences that cite the metaphors and one sentence that provides the summary and explanation. The phrase "like a mirror containing various images" is the metaphor.
The first two natures take the mind as their essence; there is no separate dharma that constitutes these two natures.

Just as a reflection in a mirror arises rapidly and perishes instantly, the answer to the preceding passage is that the mental faculty (*manas*) is most swift. Furthermore, regarding the analogy of the moon appearing in water:

the moon and the water coexist and exist in mutual correspondence. This serves as a metaphor for how the deluded mind and all phenomena act as the fundamental support, just as water supports [the reflection].
The Moon replied: "The meaning of the previous question is that [the object] is preeminent. As for one with cataracts seeing a net of hairs, this is merely a visual aberration;

it takes the eye as its substance, just as all phenomena take the deluded mind as their substance. There are no phenomena outside the mind. This answers the previous question, wherein those phenomena are all said to have the mind as their nature.
The connection can be understood from the following lines of text. Below this are two [sections].

This explains by analogy that all twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) revolve endlessly; the text is clear enough to be understood.

The preceding section concludes the explanation through the Dharma (*dharmadeśanā*). Below, analogies are cited, consisting of the simile first and its application later. The simile-text has three sections.

The first, from "For example, like a stone woman" down to "the initial birth and subsequent end," serves as an analogy for the preceding textual passage concerning how kinsmen and associates bind one another.
Next, the dream of descending into mountains and rivers corresponds to the passage in the preceding text beginning with "the ninth or tenth month.
Furthermore, the passage beginning with "again, there are those with many desires" corresponds to the passage in the preceding text beginning with "I observe all sentient beings.
The passage beginning with "all worldly affairs" synthesizes the cited metaphors. Thus, the characteristics of these textual passages are clearly manifest; one may understand them accordingly.

"Know this. You have thus failed to cultivate [this practice] below such a state of meditative concentration. This concludes the second section above, which exhorted the cultivation of superior causes by demonstrating faults to induce weariness with cyclic existence.

From here on is the third section, consisting of seven and a half lines, which compares the superior and inferior qualities; within it are three sub-sections, the first of which consists of four lines and one phrase.
The first two lines and one phrase explain that what is practiced by those of the three vehicles is inferior and weak;

next, the subsequent section explains the practice cultivated by great bodhisattvas. Finally, the line beginning with "the world" (*loka*) compares their respective superiority and inferiority against the preceding two lines.
Regarding the first section of the text, it first identifies those who practice: namely, the followers of the two vehicles and those of the bodhisattva vehicle.

Among these, for a beginner bodhisattva within the stage of equipment (*sambhāra-avasthā*), whose own benefit (*svārtha*) comes first while benefiting others (*parārtha*) is secondary, their practice is similar to that of the followers of the two vehicles;
thus, they are explained together in one place. This follows the passage beginning with "next, in a secluded place."
There are three types of abodes where [beings] dwell. Regarding those dwelling below Jambudvīpa, they manifest the signs of practicing their respective karmas.
As for these abodes, there are generally three kinds. First, those who dwell from beneath the Ocean of Milk down to the Snowy Mountains (Himavat) reside among the mountains.
One version refers to them as Mālaya, which is translated as the "Seven Golden Mountains. Sūdaya and Piṇḍata are translated as "level plains."
This refers to the flat earthen walls existing between the Seven Golden Mountains and the Milk Ocean.
