The answer, "They do not abide in anything else," addresses the preceding question; the text is clearly visible [in its meaning]. From here on, the [author] restates the [opponent's] views and demonstrates the correct reasoning.
First, the opponent’s position is restated: they claim that consciousness arises from the conjunction of four factors—the self, the mental faculty (*manas*), the object, and the dharma.
Having restated the opponent’s view, the following demonstrates the correct principle: in our Buddhist teaching, consciousness arises solely from the conjunction of the mental faculty and the object;

there is no such thing as a "self" (*ātman*). Such is what is shown. Within this, there are two parts. The first part, from "the mental faculty" down to "mental factors," is explained according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti*).

[The section on] the Truths. To demonstrate the principle of selflessness: following this, from "In this regard" (*atra*) onwards, it demonstrates the principle of selflessness according to the principle of ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

This section further consists of three parts: first, the direct explanation (*dharmadeśanā*) demonstrating the principle of selflessness, which refers to the passage beginning with "Originally there is no self" (*ātma naivāsti*);

In the second section, "all worlds" refers to the objects of what has been heard. All the various phenomena existing within all worlds—namely the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)—are called "all the various phenomena existing within all worlds.

As in the answer below regarding the names of the four aggregates (*catuḥ-skandha*), these are names that have a referent. All such cases are concordant names; the rest of the text is self-evident. Below is the inquiry concerning the essence (*svabhāva*).

Regarding such phenomena as these: do they possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or are they devoid of an intrinsic nature? Therefore, it is asked: "In what does the intrinsic nature of those phenomena abide?

From this point downward is the second section, which poses the question in verse. The first one and a half lines constitute the actual phrasing of the inquiry; the subsequent half line [introduces the response].

"Name" refers to the designations of all phenomena; "perception" (*saṃjñā*) refers to the mind that establishes those names.

The mind is able to exhaustively measure and establish the names of phenomena. Names are able to draw forth the arising of conceptual thought (*saṃjñā*). Thus, name and concept act as mutual causes for one another.
Among all worldly phenomena, they exist though appearing as if they were real. Within these five factors, "name" refers to the naming of phenomena;

"concept" refers to discrimination; and "equality" refers to grasping at signs. To grasp only these three factors while not grasping right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*) is to depart [from reality].
Because it is neither worldly nor non-worldly, it is not grasped herein; other textual characteristics appear.
The preceding section concludes the questions. Below this begins the second part: Vajragarbha’s response. This consists of two sections:

"If all phenomena possess nothing but names, by what cause do those names exist? Therefore, it is explained to resolve this: they are merely established through conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).

Therefore, the concluding statement that "the name is distinct from the referent" means there is no other meaning [to this distinction]. Next follows one verse-line which explains the reason for this.
The first half answers the reason for the term "associated" (*saṃprayukta*) mentioned previously; the second half answers the reason for the term "non-associated" (*viprayukta*) mentioned previously.

This is because the phenomena of the four aggregates consist merely of names and lack substantial characteristics (*nimitta*); they are conventionally established upon names. Thus, "name" is associated with "name. As for the term *māṇava*: [it refers to] one who is designated by a name.

Because it is not established as a designation upon the "superior," the term "non-associated" is used. Below are two lines explaining that the general name is established as a designation upon the characteristic of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
This is divided into two parts: first, one line citing scripture to establish the proof; second, one line concluding by demonstrating the underlying principle.

Explanation. From here below, four lines explain the name "world" (*loka*). It arises from causes and characteristics. This section is divided into three parts:

Among these, the first line concerns the absence of marks (*animitta*) as explained; the second line concerns the lack of substantial reality (*avastuka*) as spoken of according to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

This is clear from the text itself. Below, there is one line which concludes by exhorting [the reader] to understand. The first half exhorts [one] to act according to the principle; the second half provides a comprehensive explanation.

Therefore, it is now stated in general terms: "The ability to know the arising of various consciousnesses has no corresponding objects of knowledge," and so forth; this passage provides a comprehensive explanation, which may be understood according to the text.

Next, there are two lines clarifying that phenomena (*dharma*) are not established. Within these, the first line—titled "Because phenomena are mutually guests"—shows that both [subject and object] are unestablished.

The benefits have now been presented. From here on, for seven and a half lines, the text explains the benefits obtained. This section consists of three parts: first, two lines at the beginning provide a doctrinal exposition (*dharmadeśanā*) to state the thesis;

Because the designation of differentiation abides in the name of intrinsic nature, how could the path abide in the name?

As for "discrimination arising from the conjunction of two," this refers to the discrimination arising from the conjunction of the jar and its qualities. Furthermore, the measure (pramāṇa) of the name does not exist either; it is the discrimination that arises from the conjunction of these two.
Arising is merely conventional arising and lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). The name "that which gives rise" is likewise so; as a name, it lacks intrinsic nature and is unapprehendable.
Therefore, it is said that even the measure of names does not exist. "Measure" (*māna*) refers to the act of measuring.

As for the "threefold conjunction," it consists of the faculty, the object, and contact; because of this threefold conjunction, consciousness is produced. Furthermore...

As for the statement that sound issues from a drumstick striking a drum, or that a sprout grows from a seed in the earth, this is intended to clarify the principle that dependent origination involves specific causes for each phenomenon without confusion. The meaning of the remaining text is evident.
Thus, because these phenomena depend upon the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*), they are called the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
Below is one line that clarifies true reality (*tathatā*). If a phenomenon is untainted (*anāsrava*), this suchness-phenomenon is not produced by outflows;
therefore, it is called "untainted. Regarding "that which cannot be abandoned": "abandonment" means destruction. The remainder of the text is clear.
The preceding section concludes the explanation of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

From here below, nine lines clarify the intent behind establishing the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). Within this, there are two sections: the first consists of four and a half lines, which establish the intent for the *parikalpita-svabhāva*;

The reason for clarifying the nature [of the three natures] is as follows. The next three and a half lines cite analogies to demonstrate this. Question: Why does this passage appear here? Answer: Someone might harbor a doubt, thinking:

"Since it was stated above that all phenomena are produced by the single mind alone, and thus all dharmas are characterized by the nature of signlessness (*animitta*), why is it now established that there are three natures (*trisvabhāva*)?
What is the underlying intention? Because such a doubt exists, the text now provides a comprehensive explanation according to its [context].
Regarding the *dharmalakṣaṇa*, three natures (*trisvabhāva*) are taught. If the gateway of the three natures were not proclaimed, the teaching of the *dharmalakṣaṇa* would not be clear;

this passage is introduced precisely to refute the attachment to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*). The first two lines conclude the preceding section, while the latter two lines explain the reason for this.
Next, analogies are cited to illustrate it; there are two metaphors that liken worldly phenomena to being existent yet unreal.

this is consistent with the preceding [argument] that although the three natures (trisvabhāva) are established, there is no contradiction, for they are produced solely by the single mind and are, like suchness, devoid of intrinsic nature.

The next verse-line provides an analogy: worldly phenomena revolve according to conceptual construction, lacking both substance and utility. This should be understood in accordance with what preceded. As for the establishment of the three natures, it is merely in accordance with pervasive [delusion].

[This is] the calculation. Furthermore, the intrinsic nature does not contradict the principle of the single mind of suchness (*tathatā*). From this point downward is the second section: establishing the meaning of the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
First, there is one line of verse that uses a metaphorical illustration; next, half a line of verse provides the application; finally, three lines of prose [follow].
This explains the underlying reason. In the first analogy, it says, "nor is it that there is no cause," meaning that vapors rising from the earth are mistakenly perceived as a city;

the appearance of other phenomena can be understood by applying this principle accordingly. In the third section, one line and one phrase state the doubt of the opponent, while the subsequent one line and three phrases demonstrate the correct reasoning.
The opponent’s doubt is as follows: "In the world, we currently perceive the sun..."
The moon, the various mountains, houses, and other objects have distinct essential characteristics; they have never been confused with one another, whether as self, other, or both.
Why, then, is it now said that they are like a *gandharvanagara*—not a city but appearing as one?

Because such a doubt arises, he provides a general explanation: "Their essential nature is entirely unestablished; they are merely what is conceptually constructed (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). Below, there are five phrases [to explain this].

The two natures are briefly established as follows: the nature of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) appears as if it exists within the mind of false attachment, yet it does not exist in reality as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises from various conditions. It is like imagining a snake in a rope;

the snake does not arise through causal production, but the appearance of the snake's form manifests within the mind of conceptualization without arising from causes. Nor is it entirely without cause; it exists due to cognitive error.
Therefore, it is said that they are not without cause. Thus, such false views regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth, are all merely attachments of deluded sentiment and nothing else.
The preceding section, based on the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), has completed the analysis of the designations and their bases.

The following five and a half verses clarify that the five dharma-treasuries (*pañca-dharmas*) are what the designation rests upon. Within this section, there are two parts: first, one verse clarifies the characteristics of the five dharmas;
second, four and a half verses explain the reasons for this. Regarding the initial passage, it concerns the sequence in which the designation, the characteristic, and the conceptualization arise.
As for the phrase "that which arises from conceptualization": the two factors of designation and characteristic arise from conceptualization.
However, the sequence in which names (*nāman*) and characteristics (*nimitta*) arise through conceptualization (*vikalpa*) varies across various sūtras and śāstras.
For instance, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts, they arise from the mind that conceptually constructs names and characteristics.

In contrast, according to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, and this very sūtra, both the two phenomena of name and characteristic and the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arise from the mind of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita*). The second half of the verse below correctly [expresses] this.
Because wisdom is suchness (*tathatā*) and free from conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), it is neither born nor extinguished.
From this point downward, for four and a half lines, the reason for this is explained; the text is divided into three sections.

First, one line shows that the two phenomena—the characteristic of mind and [its object]—mutually induce one another. Next, two lines further explain away lingering doubts. Finally, one and a half lines demonstrate impermanence.

The principle is to remain far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism. Regarding the first passage, "the mind appears as the aspect": here, "mind" refers to the fourth consciousness, the manifesting consciousness (*vijñapti*).
This means that at the time of manifestation, the two parts—the subjective aspect (*darśana-bhāga*) and the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*)—appear simultaneously and instantaneously.

The manifested aspect serves as the object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the wisdom-consciousness and other aspects; therefore, it is said that the aspect is the support of the mental faculty (*manas*). This "mental faculty" is precisely the fifth [consciousness].
The sixth and the second minds are called "mind" (*manas*). Because these two minds mutually depend upon one another, the six consciousnesses arise.
As with waves, they are said to be "two" based on their verbal designation. When the mind arises from discrimination, there is no objective referent (*ālambana*);

yet, what is it that discriminates and gives rise to those appearances? Therefore, it is generally stated that the mind appears as appearances, yet the mind does not know its own appearances; it merely creates its own conceptualizations.

Regarding external objects of perception, when one discusses the mind in terms of its ultimate reality, it appears exactly as its characteristics; for there are no characteristics existing separately from the mind.
Next, there are two lines [of verse] that resolve a doubt arising from the preceding explanation. If, as stated above, the mind is able to produce its own characteristics, one wonders:
does the mind create itself, or does it have something upon which it relies? Because such a doubt arises, this [verse] provides the resolution.
It is said that the mind also has a basis, namely, the objects of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time, which exist perpetually.

When habitual tendencies give rise to the mind, these objects are able to delude and confuse it. The first line of verse demonstrates this principle; the next line of verse concludes and explains the reason for this, the text of which is clear enough to understand.
From the following one and a half lines onward, it clarifies the principle that although all worldly phenomena are impermanent, their continuity is never severed.
Because it enters the past, it is not eternal; because it continues into the future, it is not annihilated. The meaning of the text is evident.

From here on, for six lines and a half, the provisional views are restated to demonstrate the correct principle. First, two lines restate the externalist positions. Next, two lines refute those views to reveal the correct teaching.
Following that, two lines explain the underlying reason for this. Finally, half a line concludes by demonstrating the benefit.
Furthermore, the first of these consists of one verse-line that restates the theory of a self (*ātman*). Next, there is one verse-line that restates the theory of a creator (*kartṛ*).
The textual characteristics of these are evident. Following this, within the demonstration of the correct principle, the first two lines refute attachment and reveal the correct view;
the subsequent two lines explain the underlying reason for this. Within the first of these lines, the upper half refutes the conception of a creator, while the lower half reveals the correct view.
[The text] observes: Next, one line refutes the conception of a self (*ātman*). Outsiders conceive of a self as eternal; they hold that this eternal self can create things.
[They argue that] the *ālayavijñāna* taught by the Buddha is no different in meaning from what we have described, and thus it too should be able to create things.

Because such a conception exists, [the text] generally states that because the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* is eternal, it is not produced through conditions, nor does it arise by acting as a condition for others. It is not like [the self].
You reckon that the "I" can create things; therefore, it is said that the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) also does not take as its object that which produces various things.
Of this [verse], the first half refutes the attachment of externalists, while the second half demonstrates the correct view. Regarding the phrase "there is no triadic conjunction":

if there were a triadic conjunction of sense-faculty, object, and contact, such is permitted even by the Buddha-dharma. However, in this passage, the conjunction of the self, the sense-faculties, and so forth is being refuted.

Consciousness produces the appearance of objects. The following two lines of verse explain the reason for this. Because the preceding text states only that the *ālayavijñāna* manifests as if it were an object, a doubt arises outside the explicit words:
"If the *ālayavijñāna* transforms into something resembling an object, it must be impermanent.
Therefore, the text clarifies that the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* is eternally abiding. Upon hearing that the essence of the *ālayavijñāna* is eternal...
Because it abides [permanently], another doubt arises: "If its essence is eternal, it cannot be that which is accumulated by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the various dharmas.
Therefore, he explains comprehensively: "The various consciousnesses and the store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), if they were solitary, could not be perfumed or accumulated by habitual tendencies;

however, because they are inseparable from the various consciousnesses, they are able to maintain the perfuming of dharmas. The first line of the verse explains that the essence of consciousness is not separate from the other consciousnesses.
Together. Next is one line. It shows that the continuity is uninterrupted. Regarding the first half-line, it explains the reason through the teaching of the Dharma;
the second half-line provides a simile. Next is one line. The first half explains its own continuity, while the latter half continues with the words of others:

"From this, habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) arise. This refers to the place where the *ālaya* and the seven consciousnesses are inseparable; the textual characteristics are clear. Below is a half-line.
Verse. A concluding summary of the benefits. Passages such as these clearly manifest the characteristics [of the teaching].

From here below is the third section, "Refining and Returning to the Source," which is divided into three parts. First, there are three lines explaining how the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) eliminates all faults.
Next, there are two lines explaining that the principle of Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*) is eternally present within the body. Finally, there are seven lines.
The Buddha-nature possessed by all beings cannot ultimately be seen by those who do not diligently practice; this initial section consists of three parts.
First, one line provides a simile for the practice; second, one line applies the simile; third, one line indicates the benefit through verse.

Within the first line, the first half serves as a simile for the elimination of birth-and-death in segments (*paricchinna-bhava*), while the latter half serves as a simile for the cessation of birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-bhava*), gradually removing all states of existence.

Regarding "outflows" (*āsrava*): this refers to the exclusion of the three obstacles of *paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa* (segmented birth and death). Next, one practice brings about the eternal cessation of *pariṇāmi-jarāmaraṇa* (transformative birth and death).

Next, one practice is divided such that the first half demonstrates the benefit of the path of realization (*darśana-mārga*), while the second half demonstrates the benefit of the path of instruction (*śāsana-mārga*).

Within the second textual unit, it is further divided into two lines: the first line provides a simile, and the second line applies the simile to the subject at hand; this may be understood accordingly.

From here below is the third section, consisting of seven lines of verse. The mind of the *ālayavijñāna*, being shrouded by various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), can never be perceived unless one practices meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Among these, the first line provides a simile, the text of which is clear and self-evident. The subsequent five lines praise its excellence to encourage practice.
Of these, the first two lines of verse praise the excellence of the place where one is born as a result of the causes for cultivation. First...

The first line praises the cultivation of the cause for rebirth through wisdom; the next line praises meditative concentration as the cause for the Pure Land—the text is clear and may be understood as it stands.
The final three lines praise the excellence of their virtues, encouraging one to cultivate them so as to attain realization. "Manifest activity" refers to the assembly of followers;
"accomplishment" refers to their majestic spiritual power; and "light" refers to their radiance. Thus, these various merits are as perfect as the sun and moon, abiding in the stage of practice.
The term "those" (*te*) praises the assembly of those who have realized within themselves; the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are called the stages of practice. "Abiding" (*sthita*) refers to realization.

Non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is what is meant by "abiding in the ten stages. "Proclaiming the corresponding meaning" (*yoga-artha-nirdeśa*) praises the assembly of those who transform others externally; that is to say, the teaching that corresponds with realized wisdom is called the "corresponding meaning.
Next, there is one line [of verse] which, together with the subsequent phrase, collectively expresses the *tathatā* (suchness) that has been realized. This is the next phrase.

It is manifested through the gradual sequence of practice. The final two lines bestow the prediction (vyākaraṇa); the textual structure is clear. There is one subsequent line which clarifies the function of simultaneous contemplation;
this may be understood according to the text.
From here on, the prose section follows by providing a detailed explanation.

Although the preceding portion extensively clarified that the *ālaya-vijñāna* serves as the foundational locus for all phenomena, it did not yet fully exhaust the underlying principles; therefore, this text follows. Within this section, there are twenty points.
First, the *ālaya* possesses the nature of dependent origination, remaining constant throughout birth and death without interruption or cessation. This is divided into two parts; first:
From "This proclamation" down to "neither annihilated nor eternal," this expresses the fundamental tenet and demonstrates the principle.

Next, from "Furthermore, all sentient beings" down to "are called holy ones," there are two types of persons—ordinary and holy—who, though differing in their delusion and awakening, do not depart from the *ālayavijñāna*.
The first section further contains two parts: first, from "The *ālaya*" down to "saṃsāra continues without end," which expresses the tenet through an explanation of phenomena (*dharmadeśanā*).
The second section, "Like the ocean," and below, uses metaphors to illustrate this. The subsequent text also consists of two parts: first, the faults resulting from delusion;
next, "If one understands for oneself," and below, which shows that awakening results in the fulfillment of one's purpose. The text is clear and can be understood as it stands.
Second, the seven consciousnesses are deluded and give rise to various attachments. The manas that clings to a self is called the "defiled mind" (*kliṣṭamanas*). There are two kinds of mind:
first, the "delusive mind," which refers to the continuous succession from ignorance up to the sixth consciousness;

it gives rise only to attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) and not to attachment to a person (*pudgalagrāha*). Second, the "defiled mind," which refers to the evolving consciousness (*pravṛttivijñāna*) that subsequently gradually...

It arises coarsely. Before reaching the intermediate stage of the sixth consciousness, the defiled mind (*kliṣṭa-manas*) suddenly arises, taking the wisdom-consciousness (*jñāna-vijñāna*) and so forth as its object.
It falsely clings to them as being "one" and "constant," grasping at them as a self (*ātman*), yet it does not give rise to attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). Question:

Since the defiled mind only grasps at [the object] as a self and does not calculate it as "mine" (*mama-kāra*), why is it said that it grasps at both self and what belongs to the self? Answer: There are two explanations for this meaning. One explanation states: This...
The text of the *Madhyāntavibhāga* explains this in terms of general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*). What is the meaning of this?

It means that at the time when cognition (*vijñapti*) arises, the mind-king (*cittarāja*) and its mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) only then acquire their functional distinctions, yet they possess no separate substance. Therefore, when the defiled manas (*kliṣṭamanas*) arises and gives rise to grasping, it grasps by way of these general characteristics alone as being "self," without distinguishing individual mental factors.
Nevertheless, among those various objects of perception, there exist both mind and mental factors; [the manas] takes the side of the mind as its object and, based upon it, [grasps].

This is explained as the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*). Regarding the mental factors (*caitta*), it is conventionally designated as the grasping at what belongs to the self (*ātmīya-grāha*). There is no separate grasping of "I" and "mine" apart from these.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: within the afflicted manas (*kliṣṭa-manas*), there is in reality no separate reckoning of a self or what belongs to the self.

However, in this text, the mention of "reckoning what belongs to the self" is because when that manas serves as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) to reckon a self and what belongs to the self, it acts as such.
The faculties (*indriya*) are able to give rise to the grasping at "mine. Based on what is produced [by them], one conceives of a self and what belongs to a self (*ātman-ātmīya*).

Why, then, is false conceptualization (*vitarka*) not mentioned here? False conceptualization is attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*); it is obstructive outside the realms (*dhātu*) but faultless within the realms.
Within the realms, attachment to a person (*pudgala-grāha*) is more gravely faulty; therefore, it is explained universally. The meaning of the text is evident.

Third, regarding the distinct functions of the three minds, the text is divided into two parts. The first provides the doctrinal explanation (*dharmadeśanā*); the subsequent section, beginning with "like a cataract-afflicted eye," employs metaphors to illustrate this.
Within the first part, it states that "the mind accumulates karma. Here, "mind" (*citta*) refers to *layana*, meaning it serves as the locus of support when all phenomena arise.
"Karma" (*karman*) refers to action; it is called "karma" because it arises from accumulation through activity. It does not refer to the [retribution] induced by wholesome or unwholesome [actions].

The fruit is called "karma. Regarding the term "intention" (*manas*), there are two types. If we discuss the deluded intention: following the consciousness of ignorance, the karma-consciousness moves outward;
therefore, it is called "karma. The rest of the text is understandable. Having concluded the explanation of the Dharma, the reason is now explained through an analogy.

It is like a person with cataracts who sees floating hairs; though they are not wheels, he perceives them as wheels. In this same way, within the manifestation that appears as form through one's own gateway, though there is no form, one reckons it as such.
Regarding "form":
the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally pure. When in the state of an ordinary being (*pṛthagjana*), it manifests as the various forms of the phenomena of birth and death;

when in the body of a sage (*ārya*), it is fully endowed with meritorious qualities. Within this, there are two phrases: first, the analogy of the *maṇi* jewel, which serves as a metaphor for the supporting basis.

Section on the Door. Next is the analogy of milk, which illustrates the door of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). In the initial passage, there is first the analogy and subsequently the application; this may be understood by comparison.

Within the section on the door of dependent origination, the initial analogy of milk transforming into curd illustrates how the dependent origination of nature (*prakṛti-pratītyasamutpāda*) resembles the arising of all phenomena.
Apart from dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), no separate dharma can be found. It is like waves arising from water; there are no waves apart from the water.

This is illustrated by the analogy of the cataract-afflicted eye, which represents how ordinary beings falsely grasp at real dharmas within dependent origination. First is the analogy; next, the section beginning with "all sentient beings" connects [the analogy to the teaching].
The text is readily understandable. The passage beginning with "this perceived form" demonstrates the principle of causes and conditions.
Among these, there are four passages. First, the analogy of a mirage generally explains that all five sense objects are manifested by the transformation of the *ālayavijñāna*.

Next, the section beginning with "relying upon the eye and forms" specifically addresses the sense object of form, showing how it is produced by the *ālayavijñāna* as something false and devoid of reality.
The passage beginning with "Next, all various forms" and below explains that, apart from these, the other four sense-objects have no separate substantial entities.

The passage beginning with "Next, all sentient beings" and below shows that although the forms within the six destinies differ from one another, they are in fact nothing but the maturation (*vipāka*) of the single *ālayavijñāna*. This text consists of three sections.
From the passage beginning with "initially, from all sentient beings" down to "those who falsely give rise to grasping," there is an explanation of the Dharma along with a metaphor.

The metaphor [shows] that the *ālayavijñāna* is not form (*rūpa*), yet it resembles form. Next, from "like a magnet" onwards, [it shows] that the *ālayavijñāna* is not the self (*ātman*), yet it resembles the self.
Next, "like water in a vessel" explains the *ālayavijñāna*: although it lacks volition or cognition (*saṃjñā*), it functions throughout the body.
Regarding the six realms of existence, such passages as these all manifest their textual characteristics; there is no need for further elaboration.

As for the section beginning with "Just as two elephants... and ending with "...covered and not appearing," this clarifies that although the ālayavijñāna possesses a pure portion, it undergoes birth and death due to its defiled portion.
Within this, there are four textual passages; the first concerns two elephants fighting with the strength of their trunks.
The first simile illustrates that while the ālayavijñāna follows conditions and remains within the defiled state, its essence is not extinguished.
Next is the simile of the lotus flower, which illustrates that once the ālayavijñāna is freed from defilement, it serves as the body venerated by all Tathāgatas.

Next is the simile of the wondrous jewel, which illustrates that the ālayavijñāna is no different in essence from both ordinary beings and sages, neither increasing nor decreasing. Finally is the simile of the beautiful jade submerged in water.
The analogy—that the *ālayavijñāna* is obscured by habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and thus fails to manifest—is clear from the textual context.

From the passage beginning with "There are six [aspects] of the grasper and the grasped" down to "the Lord of the World," it describes how foolish ordinary beings are deluded regarding the dual grasping of subject and object manifested by the *ālaya*.
They grasp at forms and conceive views such as the existence or non-existence of a self. The first part is the analogy; the latter part is the application (*yoga*).
This can be understood according to the text.

Regarding the passage from "Although there are various manifestations" down to "views of existence and non-existence": this refers to being deluded regarding the sentient beings transformed by the ālayavijñāna;

though they merely appear to exist through transformation, they lack any real ontological status. One thus falsely gives rise to attachments to various [theories] such as atoms (*paramāṇu*) or a primal nature (*pradhāna*).
Regarding the various views: herein, first the principle, then the analogy, and finally the application; these may be understood according to the text.
As for the passage from "The eight types of mental intentions can differentiate" down to "they all immediately turn and cease":

false mental intentions merely function by taking the illusory phenomena manifested by the causal mind as the root of birth and death. The initial explanation of false mental intention shows that because it arises from differentiation, it accords with birth and death.

[The section on] "Flowing. Next, from "If there is... onwards, it correctly observes one's own mind to sever birth and death. Regarding the beginning [of this section], first is the principle (*dharma*), next is the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and finally is the application (*upanaya*).
As for the meaning: within these six kinds of mind, the fifth and sixth are termed "mind" (*manas*).

That which is able to discriminate refers to the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) manifested at the time of the manifesting consciousness, and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) of the mind that is the continuity of wisdom-consciousness. This is discrimination.

Regarding those characteristics: in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts, it is stated that the objective referent (*ālambana*) of the ālayavijñāna is unknowable, and furthermore, because its fundamental nature is conceptualization, its own essence is also conceptualization;
these statements are all made on this basis. Furthermore, there are ten metaphors, which can be understood according to the text.
From the words "If there is one who [practices] herein" onwards, it refers to correctly contemplating one's own mind, whereby birth and death naturally cease.
The textual characteristics are clear.
Regarding the passage from "The ninth, the ālayavijñāna, is the basis for all dharmas such as the manas... down to "...is indestructible and inexhaustible":
the ālayavijñāna is free from the faults of conceptualization and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), and it is capable of accomplishing all untainted (*anāsrava*) meritorious qualities. Within this...

First, there is a general explanation of that which is abandoned and that which is accomplished. From the passage "If all bodhisattvas... and below, the benefits of what is accomplished are specifically revealed.

Regarding the term "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*): it refers to the Tathāgatagarbha, True Suchness (*tathatā*), and the Dharma-nature (*dharmatā*, *dharmatā*), which are called "outflow-free" because they are free from faults.

Because one realizes and accords with the fundamental nature, it is said to be "accomplished. Therefore, it is proclaimed that the outflow-free is eternal, just like space; this is what is accomplished.
Regarding the virtues within [the Tathāgata-garbha], there are briefly four kinds: first, the virtue of mastery over practice, which refers to the six kinds of merit such as meditative concentration;
second, the virtue of mastery over vows, which refers to the ten ultimate vows; third, the virtue of mastery over birth, which refers to the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*);

fourth, the virtue of the transformation of the basis, the details of which may be seen in the subsequent text. As for "the element of consciousness is eternally abiding": "consciousness" refers to the seven consciousnesses, and "element" refers to the true mind.

Because it is the nature of all entities, it is called the "consciousness element" (*vijñāna-dhātu*). This nature of consciousness is called "abiding" because it is free from the four characteristics [of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing].
Regarding the passage from "The Tathāgatas see everywhere" down to "and even iron is not destroyed," this is also like that;
it explains that all sentient beings are originally quiescent and by nature in *parinirvāṇa*. Within this, there are three phrases: the first accords with reason and explains the absence of increase.
[The section] beginning with "The reduction" has its text clearly visible. Next, from "If one is liberated" onwards, it overturns the existing faults.
Next, from "Therefore, one should know" onwards, it concludes by exhorting [the reader] to understand; first the teaching (dharma), then the analogy—the textual structure is clear.

From "The ocean of the ālaya" down to "appearing as if they were objects," this clarifies that the ālayavijñāna, being struck and stirred by conditions, [manifests] the five dharmas and the three natures (trisvabhāva).
The waves of the various consciousnesses appear as if they exist though they do not; the meaning of the textual phrasing is clear.
From "The eleventh, the ālayavijñāna, functions within the aggregates" onwards, [the text] clarifies the reason why the ālayavijñāna resides within the aggregates.

This means that when the ālayavijñāna functions within the aggregates, it cannot act by itself. Because the karma-consciousness of ignorance cannot comprehend the true mind, deluded thoughts suddenly arise.
Due to the movement of these thoughts, one flows toward birth and death; therefore, it is taught that the manas is the precursor.
Once it has arisen, it continues to arise in succession by taking objects through the six consciousnesses and so forth, without interruption, thereby assisting the manas.
Because of the continuity of the mind, the ālayavijñāna is constantly present within the aggregates, just as water gives rise to waves due to the wind;
since the water is already present within the waves, it is for this reason that the conclusion states there is nothing that is not the ālayavijñāna.
The meaning can be seen by examining the text.

From "the twelve [bases] together with life-force (*āyus*), warmth (*uṣman*), and contact (*sparśa*)" onwards, it clarifies that at the present time, each of the various consciousnesses has its own distinct basis:

namely, the *ālayavijñāna* abides in conjunction with life-force, warmth, and contact; the *manas* abides in the *ālayavijñāna*; and the remaining six consciousnesses [abide in their respective bases].
Each abides in its own faculty.

From "the thirteen mentalities, minds, and consciousnesses" onwards, it clarifies that the twelve links of dependent origination revolve in an endless cycle. Within this, first is the teaching on phenomena (*dharma*).
Next is the analogy, followed by the application; the text is clearly visible.
From "The fourteen [factors], warmth, life-force, and consciousness" onwards, it clarifies the disintegration due to the deficiency of conditions; the textual structure is evident.
The passage beginning with "Fifteenth, the storehouse consciousness is mind" and below sets forth the substance of the three minds; the remainder of the text is easily understood.

Regarding the statement that "that which clings to a self is called *manas*": if one speaks of the defiled *manas*, it clings to the *ālayavijñāna* and gives rise to the clinging to a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*).

If one discusses the deluded *manas*, it suddenly moves outward and, because it discriminates phenomena, gives rise to the clinging to a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātman*). For this reason, it is said that that which clings to a self is called *manas*. This may be inferred accordingly.
[The Buddha] knew that the sixteen moments of mind can sustain the body and those below it. This clarifies the functional activities of the three types of mental factors (*caitta*).

Because these minds exist, [the body] does not decay or rot; the *manas* clings to the person and phenomena, and thus does not depart from the six realms of existence. For this reason, it is taught that the *manas* is attached to the various destinies.
The remainder of the text may be understood.
From the passage beginning "Seventeenth, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) as cause" onwards, it clarifies the number of conditions present when a consciousness arises;

this is stated in such a manner because it refers to those conditions that are particularly dominant. However, if discussed comprehensively, the mental faculty (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five sensory consciousnesses all possess four conditions.
The passage from "The eighteen bodies are like a reanimated corpse" onwards clarifies that there is no self in the body. First is the analogy, followed by the application.
In the application, the phrase "it is not false" means that it is not like the falsely imagined real self; therefore, it is said to be not false. The rest of the text is understandable.
From "the nineteen consciousnesses, such as the mental faculty" onwards, the meaning of the simultaneous arising of the three minds is clarified.
Just as waves do not arise where there is no water, so it is with consciousness: if the true mind (tathatā) is absent, the seven consciousnesses do not arise. Thus, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states:
"If there were no Tathāgatagarbha, the seven dharmas would not abide. This is identical to the present passage. The term "great earth" is used here figuratively.
All living beings arise depending upon the earth; likewise, all consciousnesses arise depending upon the mind.
From the section beginning with "The twenty [types of] ālayavijñāna" onwards, it clarifies the emptiness of all phenomena. Within this, there are two parts.

First, from the point where it says "From this [point] onwards" down to "the various internal and external phenomena arise therefrom," it explains how the ālayavijñāna evolves in accordance with conditions.
It manifests appearing as if it were a phenomenon. Next, for all ordinary beings and those below them, Samantaprabhā-śūnyatā exhorts them to practice;
the meaning of the text is clear and can be understood. Thus concludes the extensive explanation of the questions regarding the meaning by Vajrasattva.
From here below is the second section, consisting of the dialogue and inquiry between the Bodhisattva Sovereign King of All Colors (*Sarvarūpavara-rāja*) and Vajragarbha.

This is divided into two major parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the question, there are further two sub-sections; the first is the inquiry by the Sovereign King and others directed toward Vajragarbha.
In the first section of the text, there are five lines of verse divided into two parts.
The first two and a half lines constitute the request for the manifestation of the teaching; the subsequent two and a half lines [constitute the second part].
Please explain the profound and subtle meditative dharma of the *Ghanavyūha*. The initial section consists of three parts: first, one line praises the virtues of the speaker;
second, one line sets forth the dharma requested; third, half a line concludes with the request for its exposition. The textual structure is clear.

From here, the following two and a half lines request the explanation of the meditative dharma: the first line praises the virtues of the speaker, and the subsequent half line requests the teaching of the dharma.
Following this is a single line that cites evidence for its profound attainment. Above, [the Buddhas] such as the Most Victorious King (*Vajraśekhara*) requested that [the teaching] be expounded.
From here below is the second section: the assembly led by the Tathāgata Candradhvaja being purified through the preaching of the Dharma. This is divided into four parts.
1. Tathāgata Candradhvaja preaches the Dharma for the assembly. 2. From "Those bodhisattvas... onwards, it describes the questions and answers of the assembly at that time.
3. From "While remaining in meditative concentration... onwards, it addresses the doubts of the sentient beings at that time. 4. From "Having formed this thought...

onwards, it describes how they were able to see Vijayottama arriving and gathering in this assembly. Regarding the phrase "those who are fearless" in the first section, it refers to the Perfectly Awakened One within the Vajra-mind.
The Bodhisattva has no doubts or difficulties regarding any phenomena; therefore, he is fearless in each case. The remainder of the text is understandable.
Next, the second passage concerns those whose minds do not delight in the joy of right abiding (*samyak-sthiti*). To realize the unconditioned tranquility of *nirvāṇa* is called "right abiding.
From here below is the third [section], concerning the doubts of the great assembly. There are two types of doubt: first, regarding meditative concentration (*samādhi*) itself...

[The passage] below addresses the doubt regarding the accomplishment of the meditative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Second, from "Those sons of the Buddha" onwards, it addresses the doubt concerning the Dharma requested.
Question: When one is actually in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), there is no verbal expression. For what reason, then, is it said that "each mind thinks and speaks"? Answer:

If one were in another meditative concentration (*samādhi*), there would truly be no verbal expression. However, because this concentration involves the contemplation of the eight stages and above, one is able to preach the Dharma even while remaining in that concentration.
Thus, the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa* states: "To manifest dignified conduct without arising from the concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*)—this is true sitting in quietude.
The rest of the text is clear. Regarding the passage beginning with "those sons of the Buddha," there are four kinds of doubt concerning the Dharma requested [by them].
"What is that which is concentrated? asks regarding the essence of concentration. "How is it that something is not concentrated? he asks in response. "In what is one concentrated?
One is concentrated in that which is undisturbed. "What is the condition upon which that concentration depends?
It is constant dwelling in a quiet place of forest retreat (*āraṇyaka*), diligent cultivation and refinement, moderation in food, sleeping late and rising early, and self-restraint.
Guarding the body and mind—such things as these can assist the concentrated mind; therefore, they are called the "conditions upon which it depends.
Having formed this thought [as stated] below, one perceives that the supreme leaders have gathered for this assembly.

Within this, one first sees the Bodhisattva supreme leaders, followed by those various Bodhisattvas and others who have come from lands in other directions to gather for this assembly. The preceding inquiry has now been concluded.
From here below is the second section: Vajragarbha’s reply. Within this reply, there are two parts: first, the reply in verse;
second, the prose section containing the verses of praise and prostration by the great assembly. The text consists of seventy-eight and a half stanzas, divided into four sections.

The first has three lines, answering the previous question as to what constitutes meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The second has fifty-five lines, answering the previous statement that it is "not."
Concentration consists of nine and a half modes of activity. This answers the previous question regarding what is concentrated upon. There are forty-one and a half modes of activity.
This answers the previous question regarding which conditions are required for that concentration.
Regarding the initial passage, it is divided into two sections. The first one and a half lines present the thesis (*mata*) as a general explanation and an exhortation to practice;

the subsequent one and a half lines provide a specific explanation based on that thesis. Within the first section, the upper half exhorts and urges one to practice, while the lower half presents the thesis as a general explanation;
the text is clearly visible. Within the specific explanation, the first line of verse clarifies the stage of the First Dhyāna (*prathamadhyānabhūmi*), followed by the next half...

Regarding the composition of the text: to clarify the sequence of the remaining meditative concentrations, there is the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*). Within the realm of desire, afflictions such as the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and the view of extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) are all unwholesome (*akuśala*);
these are precisely what is to be abandoned. For this reason, it is said that one "leaves behind all desires and unwholesomeness. Following this, there are two phrases.

The essence of the first dhyāna possesses five factors (*pañcāṅga*), which constitute the body of the first dhyāna; namely, the factors of vitarka (applied thought), vicāra (sustained thought), prīti (joy), sukha (bliss), and ekāgratā (one-pointedness of mind).
The term "tranquility" refers to one-pointedness of mind. The following phrase is the concluding text, the meaning of which is manifest. This concludes the explanation of the first dhyāna.

Regarding the phrase "thus gradually in succession," it clarifies the progression from the first dhyāna up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*); hence, it is called "gradual succession. 4.

These are the four immeasurable concentrations (*catur-apramāṇa-samādhi*). Regarding the "eight," there are two: first, the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*); second, the eight bases of mastery (*aṣṭābhibhv-āyatana*).
Regarding the "ten," these are the ten totalities (*daśa-kṛtsnāyatana*). Although concentrations are infinite, their essential framework lies herein. This concludes the answer to the first question.
From here below is the second section, which answers the preceding question regarding the lack of certainty. This is divided into two parts:

first, six and a half lines, which cite the opponent’s tenets and demonstrate the correct reasoning; second, from "earth, water, etc. onwards, forty-eight and a half lines, which refute the false attachments of other schools.
In the initial summary of the calculations, it is briefly divided into three parts. First, there are three types of practitioners:

those non-Buddhists who cling to a self and the followers of the Two Vehicles who cling to the notion that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Although they practice various spiritual disciplines, they cannot attain the Samādhi of the Secret Adornment (*Guhyasamāja*).
The second section consists of one line, which cites the error of those non-Buddhist outsiders who hold views of emptiness and thereby deviate from the Middle Way.

The third section consists of two and a half lines, which cites the correct meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) belonging to the Buddhist school. Regarding the first part, the three lines identify the person who harbors such attachments, citing and demonstrating their specific calculation:
namely, the non-Buddhists who calculate a self, regarding their own calculated self as a state of peace and happiness, and thus practice various concentrations; all of whom [the] Two Vehicles [fear].

Those who seek nirvana from the suffering of birth and death also cultivate this samādhi; yet, although they cultivate it, they do not know that their own bodies are the very mark of nirvana, and thus they seek realization outside the body.
For this reason, what they cultivate is not true samādhi. Regarding the phrase "it is likewise" (*tathāpi*):

while the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) concerning the self and those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) regarding phenomena differ from one another, it is nonetheless "likewise" in the present context.
They grasp only the phenomena they cling to, but do not grasp the mind that clings; therefore, it is said to be likewise. Next, there are two lines that cite their conceptualization:
namely, that those of the Two Vehicles conceive thus—that all worldly phenomena each possess their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

Although there are aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*), they are like an empty village, for within them there is no self (*ātman*). Although they speak of "no-self," they establish these characteristics as existing external to the mind.
Therefore, I shall now set it forth. Within this, the first line merely calculates the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*); that there is no self within phenomena is evident from the text.
The next line states that although there is no master, things move and act through the power of causes and conditions, like a mechanical puppet or a reanimated corpse.
There is merely the coming together of the three—the sense organ, the object, and the self—wherein arising and ceasing occur; this is not as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) claim.
They calculate that there is an agent who can produce all phenomena; for this reason, it is said that "originally there is no agent," which restates the calculation of the two vehicles.

The following line of text, beginning with "The practitioners of external paths cultivate meditative concentration," restates the calculation of the view of emptiness, namely, regarding all phenomena.

It is neither existent nor empty, like a dream or an illusion. Although it exists within the midst of existence and non-existence, those who grasp at it as definitively non-existent and thereby deny the world are called "those with the view of emptiness.
Next, there are two and a half lines that demonstrate the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only) according to the Buddha-dharma school. A question is asked:
For what reason do those of the Two Vehicles, though knowing that the aggregates (*skandhas*) are selfless, fail to eliminate all views? As for Bodhisattvas...
"The aggregates are selfless; this can eliminate all views. What is the meaning of this? The answer is:

For those of the Two Vehicles, it is simply because they perceive that within phenomena there is no self or sovereign that they speak of "selflessness," yet their clinging to phenomena remains. Consequently, they are unable to eliminate all views.
A Bodhisattva, however, does not merely see that the aggregates are not the self; he sees that the aggregates themselves are fundamentally non-existent, like a dream.
Since the phenomena within [the middle way] are not non-existent from the start of awakening, one is able to eliminate false views.

From here below is the second section, which refutes the heterodox attachments of other schools; this is further divided into two parts. First, nineteen and a half lines refute the attachment to the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

Next, twenty-three and a half lines refute the attachment to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). The initial passage is further divided into two, the first of which consists of nineteen and a half lines.

Verse: Extensively refuting the tenets held by other schools, two and a half verses demonstrate the principle of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only). The initial section is further divided into two parts:

first, fourteen verses refute the attachment to the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in the tenets; second, five and a half verses cite the correct [view] to distinguish it from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The first part is divided into two: first, nine verses refute their [conception of] *dharmalakṣaṇa* (the characteristics of phenomena); second, five verses refute their [conception of] *dharmatā* (the true nature of phenomena). The first...

The text further consists of three sections. First, there are two lines of verse which refute the false notion that the derived matter (upādāya-rūpa) of the six sense bases is real by demonstrating its conventional nature.

Next, there are three lines of verse concerning the contemplative practices cultivated by followers of the Two Vehicles, showing how they falsely conceive of what is not meditative concentration as being concentration.

Following this, there are two lines that present the correct view to refute the erroneous one, and another two lines that cite those misconceptions to demonstrate their faults. As for "the various things such as earth and water": [this refers to the objects of perception].
The statement that "all that is cited as being refuted arises from discrimination" expresses the fundamental tenet of the Buddha-dharma.

The proponents of the Two Vehicles (Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas) maintain that the dharmas of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) merely produce form themselves and are not created by anything else; since their own substance is capable of the three [characteristics], they state, for the sake of demonstrating the principle, that [form] "arises from discrimination.
They do not realize that the four great elements have the mind alone as their essence, and thus they grasp at the various derivative forms (*upādāyarūpa*) and cause them to be destroyed.

That which is contrary is called "unpleasant form" (*durvarṇa*). That which is conducive and beneficial is called "pleasant form" (*suvarṇa*). Non-manifest form (*avijñaptirūpa*) is described as "form-like.
All indeterminate forms (*avyākṛtarūpa*) are called "remaining forms" (*śeṣarūpa*). The phrase "likewise" (*tathā*) applies to the following two lines as well.
Such forms are like the colors of clouds and rainbows in the sky; because they are phenomena lacking intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), it is said that "they are likewise."
The following three verses concern the various meditative concentrations (*samādhi*) practiced by followers of the Two Vehicles (*dviyāna*), which are not what is truly grasped as concentration.
Because followers of the Two Vehicles do not know that all phenomena are produced solely by the mind and instead posit them as existing external to the mind, these are said to be "not concentration.

Regarding the contemplation of the skeleton: this refers to the eight bases of mastery (*abhibhvāyatana*) and the liberations (*vimokṣa*), wherein one universally contemplates the colors of the four great elements, such as white bones. When this contemplation has matured...
At that time, among the beings in the world, one sees only bones and does not see flesh or blood; therefore, it is said that [this] pervades the world.
Regarding the "perception of the universal bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana-saṃjñā-vipaśyanā*): the ten *sarvāyatanas* are called the perception of the universal bases.

This refers to the eight previously mentioned—earth, water, fire, wind, blue, yellow, red, and white—plus the two meditations on the sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), which together constitute the ten.

The "all-encompassing bases" (*kṛtsnāyatana*) are so named because they involve contemplation through mental construction (*parikalpa*). One who contemplates in this manner observes the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). Regarding "the body possessing form":

because one internally possesses the mark of form while externally observing forms, it is called "the body possessing form. Regarding "the body lacking [internal] form": because one does not observe the internal body, it is called "internal.
As for the meditative concentration on the mark of formlessness, one constantly and attentively reflects; the following three phrases are presented to illustrate this.

The Correct Principle (*nyāya*) is as follows: When a practitioner of meditative concentration contemplates phenomena and realizes that there is only a single mind, such an object of focus is said to be pure.
Next, there is a further practice which, by way of inversion, demonstrates the faults [of the former view]:

if those previously mentioned skeletons and so forth were distinct external objects of focus separate from the mind, then they would neither be meditative concentration nor the state of one in concentration; they would merely be a deluded mind.
This refers merely to the meditative concentration (samādhi) of the Middle Vehicle; it is not the concentration cultivated by those of the Mahāyāna. Those of the Two Vehicles ask:

"If, as you have said, that which we cultivate is not the true dharma of concentration, then what is it? Therefore, [the text] now cites the correct [view] to demonstrate that their concentration has faults:
when a person is in a state of concentration, because they all rely upon the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), all deluded dharmas are completely extinguished, and one attains...
This person of supreme meditative concentration is able to proclaim the dharmas of all dhyānas and samādhis, and is also able to destroy all external phenomena—
objects of knowledge for the deluded wisdom of those of the two vehicles and others.
From here below are two lines that cite the [opponent’s] position and demonstrate its error. The first line cites the position; the second line demonstrates the error.

"If a person possesses little wisdom" cites the wisdom possessed by those of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), who know only that there is no self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*) within the aggregates (*skandha*), but do not know that the dharmas of the aggregates are originally unarisen and likewise do not cease;
therefore, they are called those of "little wisdom. If one considers them in relation to the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), based on the world...
The wise but deluded grasp at the characteristics of various dharmas—such as the six categories and the twenty-five principles—as well as at "self" and "what belongs to self.

Therefore, they are called those of "small wisdom. Of these [four] lines, the first two involve grasping at dharmas and the self; the latter two involve adhering to the teachings of the Hīnayāna, taking the meaning literally according to the words, and claiming their own assertions to be the truth.
Thus, they calculate the Hīnayāna teachings to be the ultimate reality, yet they do not truly know suchness.
When coming to nourish the child, one should skillfully provide cooked food. If raw food were given, the child would immediately fall into madness;

because he does not understand this, he takes [the teacher's] words to be the ultimate truth. Those teachers of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) who are skilled in explaining various dharmas each compose their own treatises, asserting "I am right and others are wrong";
for this reason, they are said to be "skillful in explaining various dharmas. Next, their faults are shown: they cling to [the existence of things] external to the mind.

Regarding the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*): because one slanders the Mahāyāna Dharma, one falls into the prison of the triple world; therefore, it is said that one "destroys oneself.
Furthermore, regarding "also destroying others": this is because, by clinging to the words of the Small Vehicle as being the ultimate truth, one instructs others to slander the Mahāyāna Dharma.

Therefore, it is said that they destroy others. Regarding "that which has no capacity to characterize": the four great elements and the four characteristics are empty and devoid of essence or marks; this is called "having no capacity to characterize. Regarding "that which has nothing to be characterized":

when phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and so forth do not exist, one speaks of them as empty. The remainder of the text is easily understood. Thus far, the refutation of the attachment to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*) is complete.

From here on, in five lines, the attachment to the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-grāha*) is refuted. Based on worldly affairs, it is clearly known that there is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). First:
The first three and a half lines clarify that worldly affairs each have their own specific capacities, which counteract and mutually negate one another.

The next one and a half lines show that because they mutually negate one another, it should be understood by inference that they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). Of these, the first two lines concern the various capacities within worldly affairs.

The subsequent one and a half lines state that because illnesses are not of a single kind, the medicines prescribed are numerous; likewise, because sentient beings and bodhisattvas are numerous and not of a single kind, [the remedies] are likewise manifold.

The teachings of the Buddha are manifold and diverse. The following one and a half lines reverse and reveal the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*). Such passages can be understood through their manifested characteristics.
The refutation of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus complete.

From here downward, for five lines and a half, the text sets forth the correct [view] and distinguishes it from non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Within this, the first two lines set forth the correct principle (*yukti*), while the subsequent three lines and a half distinguish it from other non-Buddhists.
The initial passage reveals the characteristics [of the view]; within these subsequent three lines and a half, there are six propositions in total.
The first two lines refute the calculation of a creator. The following two lines explain that when the kalpa is destroyed, all subtle atoms are dispersed throughout the ten directions;
when the kalpa is about to be formed, each atom comes together to assemble and form the world. "Calculating [it] as non-time" refers to the Tīrthikas who calculate time;
"non-primal nature" (a-prakṛti) refers to the Tīrthikas who calculate primal nature; and "the three dharmas calculating it as self" refers to...
The Path is also not without cause. Next, the theory of spontaneity (*svabhāva*) is refuted. As for the term *guṇa*, it is here translated as "sovereignty" (*svatantra*).
The remaining text may be understood through its own context.

From here on, for five lines and a half, the principle of *vijñapti-mātratā* (consciousness-only) is demonstrated. This section is divided into two parts. The first consists of two lines, which provide a general exposition.
In the Vijñānavāda school, there are next three and a half lines that provide a detailed explanation by way of specific dharmas.

Regarding the phrase "karmic habitual tendencies" (*karma-vāsanā*) in the initial passage, it refers not only to the three types of karma—meritorious, non-meritorious, and immovable—but also to all afflictions (*kleśa*) that produce activity, which are likewise termed "karma.

The preceding section concludes the general and abbreviated explanation. In the following detailed explanation, the single line concerning jars and so forth refers to coarse [objects] within the mundane world.
Because it is revealed that the substance of things is mind, it is said to be empty and without reality. Second, regarding the practitioner:

from the perspective of the world, because form is a transformation of the ālayavijñāna, it appears as if it exists. Third, regarding sentient beings: from head to foot, everything is the ālayavijñāna and there is no separate dharma.
Next are two phrases which conclude by demonstrating delusion. Thus far has been the refutation of the attachment to the existence of dharmas.
[The preceding section is] concluded. From here on, twenty-three and a half verses refute the attachment to the view of emptiness (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*). This is divided into four parts:

first, five and a half lines present the Middle Way principle to demonstrate the faults of the view of emptiness; second, the two and a half lines beginning with "For example" refute [the view of emptiness].
Seeing people who hold the view of emptiness as superior, the remaining text is self-evident.

Third, regarding the "three non-observations," there are five lines of verse starting from "the horns of a rabbit" which refute their shifting defenses, demonstrate the correct principle, and exhort the abandonment of false attachments. Fourth, there are five and a half lines.
This explains away external doubts. The initial section consists of four parts: first, one and a half lines concerning the Middle Way school;
second, one line showing that the current [position] entails a double fault; third, one line stating that the demarcation between emptiness and existence must not be discussed recklessly;
fourth, two lines on the intent behind the Tathāgata’s teaching of emptiness. The preceding lines, in verse, illustrate how the Middle Way school is free from existence.
Regarding the absence of marks (*animitta*): next, there is a section on the "single practice" which cites worldly objects to explain the underlying reason. The explanation of this reason states:
"If objects were empty, there could be no object that is the refuter and no object that is the refuted, for both the refuter and the refuted would be non-existent.

If objects possessed a substantial essence, they likewise could not be refuted. Therefore, being neither existent nor non-existent, we provisionally speak of the distinction between the refuter and the refuted. Next...
This reveals a grave fault. That is to say, those who cling to a self practice various dharmas for the sake of attaining peace and happiness for that imagined self;

whereas those with the view of emptiness negate cause and effect and sever all roots of goodness, from which they cannot be turned back. Thus, it is said that this evil fault is greater than the former.
Next, there is one verse that explains the division between emptiness and existence; for the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is neither existent nor non-existent.

It cannot be said that there is nothing; yet, because there are sentient beings who grasp at phenomena as being existent and thereby lose the Middle Way, one provisionally speaks of "emptiness" to strip away this attachment.
If one understands it in this way, it becomes nectar. This applies to the characteristics of causes and conditions within the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
To deny emptiness is itself to become poisoned. Following the passage beginning with "All sentient beings," there are two lines of verse.
The first line praises the intent behind the Buddha-Tathāgata’s establishment of the teaching; the second line praises how clinging to that teaching results in error.
Thus far, the essential tenet has been set forth.
The following two and a half verses refute the attachment to the wisdom that understands emptiness held by those who hold the view of emptiness.

Within these, the first verse presents an analogy to demonstrate the point, while the subsequent one and a half verses provide the formal teaching to show the correct view. An opponent argues: "All causal phenomena and dharmas are empty;
this wisdom that perceives emptiness is supreme above all else. One merely speaks of the emptiness of dharmas, but does not say that wisdom itself is empty. Therefore—
Now, an analogy is cited to refute that cognition: it is like fire burning wood; when the wood is exhausted, the fire also extinguishes.

Your claim that the cognition of emptiness is superior to other cognitions is not reasonable, because it conforms to worldly characteristics. The next one and a half lines provide the formal teaching to demonstrate the correct view.

First is the wisdom of cultivation through conditions; next, for half [the duration], it clarifies the wisdom of true cultivation. At the time of the adamantine mind, the wisdom of cultivation through conditions arises.
When all views are severed, even your [subjective] seeing is extinguished. When all afflictions are purified, the cultivation through conditions is also extinguished.
Just as when fire burns wood, once the wood is exhausted, the fire also ceases; so too, after the cultivation through conditions has been completely extinguished, true cultivation becomes perfected.
He is therefore named a Buddha. For this reason, it is said that one is liberated within the *Ghanavyūha*.

Having concluded the demonstration of the correct [view] by refuting attachments, the third section below consists of five lines of verse which refute those attachments. They [the opponents] attempt a rebuttal, saying: "All dharmas..."
Although [things] are empty and utterly non-existent, one has not yet seen the time when emptiness exists; thus, it is impossible to make phenomena such as enemies and kin non-existent.
Since there is such a defense, we now refute it: "If phenomena were empty and non-existent, one could not avoid [the consequences of] horns touching or a great mountain being destroyed.
This section is divided into three parts: first, two verses concerning the contradiction with worldly experience; next, one and a half lines concerning the characteristics of emptiness and form.

This refers to their being of one and the same essential nature (*ekasvabhāva*). The following one and a half verses cite an analogy to demonstrate this. Regarding the phrase "not seeing [contact] with a rabbit’s horn" and so forth:

if you maintain that although things are empty and non-existent, at the time one is unaware of their emptiness, there still occurs the matter of contact, formation, and destruction, then I shall challenge you:
you ought to see a rabbit’s horn strike and shatter a great mountain; yet such has never been seen. By this standard, it is known that all [things are likewise].
Dharmas should not be entirely non-existent, for the text is clearly visible. The next one and a half verses state that emptiness and form are of the same substance, just like water and waves.
Outside the waves there is no water; apart from water there are no waves. Emptiness and form are likewise so.

Now, in the Mahāyāna, arising and ceasing are simultaneous, and existence and non-existence are of the same substance. It is not the case that the dharma of emptiness only exists after form has ceased, according to the text.
It can be seen. Next, there are one and a half lines that cite a metaphor to demonstrate this. The first half of the line cites the metaphor;

the subsequent line of verse synthesizes and concludes the preceding metaphor. When discussing form (*rūpa*), it points to space as being form; outside of space, there is no separate form. Space is likewise so.
It points to form as being empty. For this reason, it is said that all purposes are accomplished. The preceding section has finished refuting the opponent’s shifting attachments.
From the line "This body is like a corpse" onwards, five lines of verse clarify the intent behind the Buddha-Tathāgata’s establishment of the teachings.

Within these, the first two lines explain the establishment of the teachings through the principle (*dharma*). The subsequent three lines of verse provide illustrations to demonstrate this. Regarding the first of these:

The first verse explains that the body has no intrinsic nature and is provisionally established based on conditions. The subsequent verse sets forth the intent of the teaching. Regarding the term "wise person": this refers to one who holds the view of emptiness;
such a person is intelligent and of sharp faculties, and it is precisely because they give rise to the view of emptiness that they are called a "wise person.

The remaining text clarifies the meaning through analogy. Within the analogical section, the first verse consists of three lines, which illustrate how phenomena rely upon conditions; the following verse consists of one line.

Since the Dharma is free from existence and non-existence, one should not adhere to either extreme. Such textual passages as these clearly demonstrate that the intent of the teaching has been fully expressed.

From here on, for five lines and a half, the opponent sets forth a critique of the teaching; this consists of two sections. The first section comprises two lines of verse, which formally present the words of the critique.

The subsequent three lines and a half explain and resolve the critique, which can be understood once the seed [of the argument] has been established. Within the explanation of the words of the critique, the first half [of the verse]...
Even if one were to grant that [the distinction] is entirely without fault, the ancient sages spoke only of avoiding the horns and said nothing of other things.
Ordinary people, deluded by confusion, give rise to false conceptualization and are unable to realize the Dharma; they merely follow the words of others and ultimately fail to understand.
If one must engage in conceptualization, it only serves to produce further false attachments. Therefore, what is the use of proclaiming conceptualization? If one is free from conceptualization...
Below, the answer is given by way of benefit. The preceding section answered the question as to why [the text] is not a definitive scripture.
Now follows the third part, consisting of nine and a half verses, which answers the question regarding what it is that is "definitive. Within this, there are five metaphors:
first, the metaphor of the celestial palace, which illustrates how the seven consciousnesses are sustained by the power of the latencies (*vāsanā*) within the *ālayavijñāna*.
1. The analogy of the wheel: It represents how [the storehouse consciousness] revolves incessantly within the six realms of existence. 2. The analogy of the great earth:
